ROSES AND THE NIGHTINGA: In my garden it is night-time, Bat a still time and a bright time, For the moon rains down her splendour, And my garden feels the wonder Of the spell which it lies under In that light so soft and tender. While the moon her watch is keeping All the blossoms here are sleeping, And the roses sigh for dreaming Of the bees that love to love them When the warm sun shines above them Asd the butterflies pass gleaming. Could one follow roses' fancies, When the night the garden trances. Oh, what fair things we should chance on! For to lilies and to roses, As to us, soft sleep discloses What the waking may not glance on. But hark! now across the moonlight, Through the warmness of the June night, From the tall trees' listening branches, Comes the sound,sustained and holy, Of the passionate melancholy, Of a wound which singing staunches. Oh, the ecstacy of sorrow Which the music seems to borrow From the thought of some past lover Who loved vainly all his lifetime, Till death ended peace and strife-time, And the darkness clothed him Over! .oh, the passionate. sweet singing. Aching, gushing, throbbing, ringing, Dying in divine, soft closes, Recommencing, waxing stronger. Sweet notes, ever sweeter, longer, Till the singing wakes the roses! Quoth the roses to the singer: "Oh, thou dearest masic•bringer, Now our sleep so sweetly endeth, Tell us why thy song so sad seems, When the air is full of glad dreams, And the bright moon o'er us bendeth." Sang the singer to the roses: "Love for you my song discloses,. flenee the note of grief it borrows." Quoth the roses, "Love means pleasure." Quoth the singer, "Love's best measure Is its pure attendant sorrows." —Hargr's ifagazine.

A•young lady remarsed that she thought the sleeetest I words were on lozenges. Careful Housekeeper at breakfast : "Bridget, Bridget there is a fly in the room!" " Yis, indade ma'am, I know there is. It got in this mornin' when me ba.ck was turned." A good story is told of a young married man who dnring his "courting days was very bashful." One day he was in- vited to attend a tea party at the house of an uncle of his sweetheart, and when seated at the table the hnstess requested him to ask a blessing, which so "broke np " the already bewildered young man that he unconsciously stam- mered out; "I don't cars for any, thank you." Judah P. Benjamin, the famous Queen's conirel, lately dead, knew how to charge client, and often described, with a relish, his plan for making a bill. "First," he said, "I charge a retainer; then I charge a reminder; next I charge a refresher; and then I charge a finisher." He was exceed- ingly liberal, and had no love of money for money's sake. Some less scrupulous lawyers charge a " finisher " to begin

with. Charles Lamb gives some advice about making speeches, which Might be applied with advantage to other occasions. He says a speaker should not attempt to empress too much, but should leave sometaing to the imagination of his audi- ence; and he tells bow, being called on to return thanks for a toast to his heAlth„ be rose, bowed to the audience, and said—" Gentlemen." lie then sat down, leaving it to their . _

imagination to supply the rest. A Lessois IN Citentry.—lt is related of the late Mr. Peter Cooper. an American benefactor, that he was one day watching the pupils in the portrait class connected with the Women's Art School ot Cooper Institute. About 30 pupils were engaged in drawing likenesses of the same model from various points of view—some in profile, some full face, some nearer and others farther from the 'light, and so forth. After studying the scene for a while Mr. Cooper said, "Stich a eight as this should be a lesson in charity, when we per- ceive how the same person may be so different, according to the way he is looked at by various people." Tern Boor •ligis.—Few little folk have any idea of the labour that bees have to expend in the gathering of honey. Here is a calculation, which will show how industrious the " busy" bee really is. Let us suppose the insects confine their attentions to clover fields. Each head of clover con- tains about sixty separate flower-tubes, in each of which is a portion of sugar not exceeding the five, hundredth part of a grain. Therefore, before one grain of sugar can be got, the bee must insert its proboscis into 500 clover-tubes. Now there are 7,000 grains in a pound, so that it follows that 3,500,000 clover-tubes mast be sucked in order to obtain but one pound of honey.—Little Folks' Magazine. THE Dock AND van TELEPHONE —An intelligent dog was recently discovered wandering about the streets of an American city, by a gentleman who knew it. He at once asked its master by means of the telephone whether he had lost his dog. The reply came " Yes ; have you seen it ?" To whiela the further instruction was sent, "Suppose von call him through the telephone." Accordingly the dog was lifted up, and the ear-piece placed at its ear. "Jack! Jack!" shouted its owner, whereupon Jack, recognising the voice, began at once to yelp most vigorously, and licked the telephone in a friendly way, evidently thinking that its master was inside the machine.—Little Folks' Magazine. A story is told of a college president who suspected that some of the students had planned to rob his hen roost. Near the enclosure were two large apple trees at the back of the house; so he quietly went out and waited till they •came. Of the two, one ascended the tree, the other waited below. When they were ready to commence operations the doctor made a slight noise, and the one below started off with an exclamation of surprise. Tile one in the tree asked, in a whisper. " What's the matter ?" To which the doctor replied, also in a whisper, "All's right." "Here, catch hold," maid the upper one, handing down a rooster," here's Old Prex." And handing down a, hen, "Here's Mrs. Prex. And here," handing down a chicken, "here's Miss Prex. I guess that'll do." The doctor quietly gut over the fence with the fowls, and went to his house. The poor robber of the hen roost descended to find his companion gone. What they said when they met will probably never be known; hat in the morning the two young gentlemen received a polite in- vitation to dine with the president, an honour they could not very well decline. Possibly they were embarrassed when, seated at the table, they saw three fowls roasted for the dinner; and we can imagine their isensations when the doctor said, "Now, young gentlemen, will you have a piece of Old Prex, Mrs. Prex, or Miss Prex ?" How the' dinner passed off, and how the delinquents got off, deponent sayeth not. On that theme history is dumb. But nothing more was said of the escapade, the doetor thinking that the !nor, tilication was sufficient plinishment. Tau SUPREMACY OF THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE MD rirnagrran.—President Eliot, of Harvard, discusses the queer tion," What is a Liberal Education?" in the Jane Century. Its importance lies in the fact that so prominent a scholar sod edncatoe should take such strong ground in favour of making the sciences and the English language leading branches in the college course. While admitting that Latin and Greek are valuable studies, he says of English, "The first subject which, as I conceive, is entitled to recognition as of equal academic value or rank with any subject now most honoured is the English language and literature. When Greek began to revive in Europe. English was just acquir- ing a literary form; but when Greek bad won its present rank among the liberal arts, Shakepeare had risen, the Eng- lish language was formed, and English literature was soon the greatest of modern literatures. How does it stand now, with its immense array of poets, philosophers, historians, commentators, critics, satirists, dramatists, novelists, and orators? It cannot be doubted that English literature is beyond all comparison the amplest, most various, and most splendid literature which the world has seen; and it is enough to say of the English language that it is the lan- gaage of that literature. Greek literature compares with English as Homer compares with Seakspeare; that is, an infantile with adult civilisation. It may be further said of the English language that it is the native tongue of nations which are pre-eminent in the world by force of character, enterpriee, and wealth, and whose political and social insti- tutions have a higher moral interest and greater promise than any which mankind has hitherto invented. To the original creations of English genius are to be added trans- lations into English of all the masterpieces of other litera- ture, sacred and profane. It is a very rare scholar who has not learned much more about the Jews, the Greeks, or the Romans through English than through Hebrew, Greek, or Latin. And now, with all this wonderful treasure within reach of our youth, what is the position of American schools and colleges in regard to teaching English? Has English literature the foremost place in the programme of schools ? By no meats; at best only a subordinate, place, and in many schools no place at alt. Does Enelish take equal rank with Greek or Latin in our colleges? By no means; not in the number and rank of the teachers, nor in the Consideration in which the subject is held by faculty and students, nor in the time which may be devoted to it by a candi(late for a degree. Until within a few years the American colleges made no demand noon candidates for ad- mission IR regard to kilowiedge of English; and now that some colleges make a small requirement in English, the chief result of the examinations is to demonstrate theyotta I Ignorance of their own language and literature which pre. vailLatnong the picked youth of the country." He details working, is well worthy of notice as an example of what can be effected by hard work, cleanliness, and skill. To the the agricultural instruction given in elementary schools, east of Ulverston, at one time, was a large tract of land, and in concluding his report Mr. Jenkins describes the agri- situate between the town and Morecambe Bay, forming a cultural stations, the chief agricultural societies, and enters peat moss. In many parts yet it is literally a bog, and is into the instructive and stimulating effect of the competi- under water daring periods of heavy rains. From its flat tions. state it is most difficult to drain, there being no outlet. Here is situate the farm of Greenhills, for some forty-two years in the occupation of Mr. James Wright, and for the I past two or three years occupied by his two sons. It is some 46 acres in extent, and these two do the whole of the work connected with the farm, and occasionally find time to put in a few days for their neighbours. It forms a veritable oasis in comparison with some of the surrounding land. At present there are four acres of oats, and 21 acres divided into potatoes, swedes, and carrots, two acres of seed grass, and 11 acres of meadow haygrass—the rest is pasture. There are 18 head of cattle, bred from a shorthorn bull, comprising seven milch cows, four heifers between one and two years, and seven calves. Two brood mares are kept, one aged horse, and a yearling; in summer, 14 or 15 sheep (bat they never winter any); two sows (one with 13 young pigs), and a store pig for family use. The milk is made Into butter, and the skim milk and buttermilk fed to calves and pigs. Of the land and the crops, I have not seen cleaner and better on any farm more favourably situated, and the hedges are trim and neat. Some years ago portions of the land were badly infested with charlock, and great as was the labour, a persistent hand weeding has effec- tually cleared the pest, a refutation of the oft-repeated assertion that charlock cannot be cleared out of the land. The aim of the tenants is to produce as much as possible, and to purchase as little as possible. They use no artificial manures, and they find it cheapest and most satisfactory to purchase the best seeds from Messrs. Sutton. To keep the land in the state it now is must require a great amount of labour. Mr. Wright, from the nature of the land, and its difficulties in winter, cannot enter the milk trade. Were it otherwise, he has estimated that, at present prices, the difference between the sale of milk and his present proce- dure, Would enhance his receipts by some £6O to £7O per. annum. On a rough estimate, he calculates that it takes 14 quarts of milk to the pound of butter. Mr. Wright, senior, Was both a good and a bad farmer, the latter simply by reason that he never asked his landlord for any repairs, consequently the buildings and the gates now require a COM- plate overhaul, some of the roofs, in wet weather, bearing a striking likeness to a sieve. The work of renovation is about to be taken in hand. There are strange anomalies in farming, and Greenhill presents one of them. The rent, I believe, is some 30s. per acre, and here an apparent comfort- able living has been made for half a century, and a family brought up in respectability. On the other hand, we have now the spectacle of good land, in favoured localities, and at no more rent, where ends cannot be made to meet. Coald a more convincing proof be given of the truth I stated in an article, and published in the showyard edition of the Agri. cultural Gazette, when the "Royal" was held at Liverpool, that the "farm of the future," the paying ones, would be those devoted to dairying and the production of flesh meats. —R.

WEDDING TRIPS WITRODT THE BRIDE —The Editor of "The Drawer" in Harper's Magazine for July, has the following :—The Drawer, which sits at the receipt of stories, has occasion to muse much upon the fallibility of human testimony. Do the men and women who send in stories which are as old as Solon, and declare that the inci- dents related occurred in their own observation and ex- perience, know that there is another world? Sisters and brothers, why are we made thus? There is a story about a wedding trip that has been knocking about the country for some time. We have tried to keep it out of the drawer, but it is of no use to kick against it any longer. It was first told to the Drawer editor in October, 1883, by a clergyman of strict temperance principles and high character—in fact, a total abstainer—who had it from a friend of his, first hand, who had jest returned from the West. This friend, mind you, saw and beard what he related, and he was a person of undoubted veracity, though perhaps as an abstainer, when travelling, not so total as the clergyman. It was, in brief, to this effect. In the car on a train. from Toledo to Chicago was a man who sat alone, looking absently out of the win- dow, and appearing dejected. During the passage an acci- dent happened to a newsboy, and the generous passengers passed round the hat for him. The solitary man alone of all the earful refused to contribute anything, not even a quarter. Somebody remarked audibly upon his stinginess, when he turned round and said: "Gentlemen, it may ap- pear strange to you that I give nothing; but I haven't a cent of money. The fact is, I was married yesterday, and I am on my wedding trip, and I hadn't money enough to bring my wife along." In December following, the editor of the Drawer was seated with two other gentlemen in a library in New York. One of them said: "I heard a good story the other day from a friend of mine who has just re- turned from Europe. Going down the Danube from Pesth last summer, he noticed on the steamboat a melancholy- looking man, who did not appear to care much for the scenery, but leaned over the guards and vacantly regarded the river. Falling into conversation with him, he facer. tamed that the man was a Prussian. Remarking that the journey did not seem to interest him, the Prussian said: 'No; I'm rather lonesome. The truth is, I'm on my wed- ding tour, and I could not afford to bring my wife.'" The editor of the Drawer said that it was a good story, and that he began to think it was true, as it was confirmed by so many independent witnesses. Thereupon he took from his pocket a letter which he had received that morning from Paris. In it the writer, a gentleman of culture and travel, said that a curious incident happened to him last summer. He and his wife were on a Rhine steamer, when they noticed a melancholy passenger whom all the beauties of the scenery failed to rouse from his dejection. He was an object of in- terest to them all the morning, and at length the wife's sym- pathy was so much excited that she proposed to go and THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT ON speak to the melancholy stranger, and find out the cause of AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION. his sadness. DARK AND LIGHT BRAIIMAS. • The two varieties of Brahma, are thedarks and the lights, the former of which have a dark or black ground colour with a lighter shade of ticking thereon, which gives a some- what grey appearance to them, and the light variety have a white or very pale cream ground work marked here and there with dark stripes, but still the chief colour is the white. Both have very much the same shape, and only differ in point of colour. As a rule, adult cocks weigh about twelve pounds, and hens about two pounds less, whilst it is not difficult to get cockerels at six months up to from seven to nine pounds, and pullets six to eight pounds. At times larger birds have been seen, but these are good weights. Unfortunately, there has been a tendency of late years to a redaction in size, largely due to the seeking after fine pencilling, i.e., marking or lacing on the hens and pul- lets, and in some cases the birds were pounds lighter than the weights we have here stated. Happily there has been a re-action, and size is now made by most judges and breeders a sine qua non. Coming to the actual characteristics of the breed, we find that the bead is very small in proportion to the body, short and fine in its lines, and surmounted by what is known as a peacomb, which may be briefly described as a triple comb, the three small ridges running side by side, with the centre one rather higher than the other two, and not more than half an inch in height. The neck in the cock especially is very full in the hackle, and has a fine arched appearance, so that the head is forward, just in advance of the breast. If the head is thrown back, the bird has an unshapely appearance, and the real outline of the Brahma, so far as the head and neck are concerned, partakes much of that of a spirited horse. The length of neck depends much upon the general contour of the fowl, and if the bird is big all over and full in feather the length of neck does not mat- ter; but a long neck on a small bird gives a modified giraffe look, which is by no means what it ought to be. The back of the Brahma is wide and flat, what there is of it, but from the neck hackle, where the feathers join the shoulders, to the root of the tail, covered there by what is known as the Beadle hackle, the distance ought to be a short one, and have somewhat the appearance of a U, though the upper part of that letter does not adequately reoresent the tree form. It will be see that this shape is different to many varieties of fowls which elope towards the tail, and that then goes off at another angle, like a sickle. Bat the Brahma's does not do so at all, and a sloping back with a whip tail is altogether out of keeping with the contour of the fowl. The tail is different to that of all other fowls of,the Asiatic type, and may be described as a bunch of short feathers with but a slight curve Atha end, and the whole rising straight or almost straight up from the body. The slightest appear- ' anue or tendency to sickle or long sweeping feathers is repressed, and the height should be very nearly that of the head, or as nearly so as is possible. But as the head must:not be thrown back neither must the tail, and the two require to be evenly and properly balanced. The body proper of the fowl is broad and deera with the breast well thrown forward, and the breast-bone set well between the thighs. Shoulders are prominent, and when the bird stands facing you it should have a big massive appearance. The wings are small and well tucked up, for as Brahmas are not flyers, wings are but a small part of their economy. The thighs are covered with soft bluff, and fairly profuse, below which stand out the hocks or the soft feathers which Protrude below the thighs. With these come the leg and foot feathers, which in first class exhibi- tion birds are got as long as possible, in some Cases standing several inches out from the middle toe of the foot. The more foot feather that can be got the better from an exhi- bition point of view; but for ordinary purposes, this is a matter that need not be so much regarded. We are, how- ever, here giving a sketch of the best birds and must state what is required. The legs are yellow in colour, of medium length, and strong in order to support the heavy body. Thus much about the cock. The hen ought to be of the same shape and carriage as the cock, allowing for the natu- ral differences in sex. She should have a rather short neck and short legs, and with this statement we need say no more. In dark Brahmas both sexes have a yellow beak, or yellow with a black stripe, the eye is red, and the comb, face, deaf ears, and witttles are of the same colour, though naturally of a more pronounced hue. In the cock the head may be described as silver White; the hackle white with a heavy stripe of black, and saddle of the same colour. The back and shoulder should be silver white, except between the shoulders, where the black must be laced with white. The upper wing butts are black, the wing bow is white, and the end of every wing weather black. The breast, the under parts, and the thighs should be glossy black, or evenly mottled with white, bat black is preferred, and looks decidedly the better of the two. The tail is pure black, glossed green, and the legs orange. In the hen, the head and hackles are silver white, with a deep stripe black. The tail is black with the top feathers edged gray, and the rest silver gray, dull gray, or steel. The markings or pencillings on each feather is in crescent form, and is black pencilled with gray. The clearer and more even this is the better is it regarded. In the light Brahmas the beak is yellow, with or without a dark stripe; the deaf ears, comb, face, wattles, and eyes red, as in the darks, and shanks of the same colour. In the cock the head is silver white, the hackles, both neck and saddle, white with a black stripe. The tail and coverts are a glossy green black, whilst the body has a peculiarly soft pearly whiteness. The shank feathers are white, but more or less mottled with black. In the hen the head is alto silver white, and the hackles white with a deep black stripe. The tail is black, except the top pair of feathers, which shonld,be edged white, and the body pure pearl white all over. Any yellow tinge in the plumage is regarded as a grave defeat, spoiling, as it does, the appearance of, the fowls.

SEASONABLE HINTS. The earlier chickens will now begin to get into their hobbledehoy-hood, and they need to be well supported with good and nourishing food, as the strain upon the system consequent upon the formation of the adult feathers is very great. To provide for this they must be well fed, and should have some Bone Meal in their soft food every day without fail, and as much liberty as can be given without actually allowing them to dy all over the country-side. It must also be remembered that the day very soon dawns, and that the chicks are out and about by three o'clock in the morning, so that if they have to wait until seven or eight o'Clock before they get anything to eat they will suffer in conse- quence, and it is as well, therefore, to scatter about &little corn, such as dari or buckwheat, the evening before, Care must be taken that too much is not put down, or it will be wasted; but just suffielent to stay their appetites until the proper feeding time, which had better be as early as possible,

div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES. ,

It is interesting to know (says the Atheneum) that the Royal Commission on Accidents in Mines are about to make some experiments on the getting of coal without the use of exploeives. A large -oalowner of the Midland counties has placed his collieries at the disposal of the Commission for the experiments. Under the anapices of the Norwegian Association for the Promotion of Fisheries, says Nature an establishment for the hatchil:g of cod and soles' ova has been prepared near Arendal, in the Christiania Fjord. From the excellent re- sults already obtained, it has been decided to found another hatching station near Christiania.

ETCHING GU GIASS.—A Sydney newspaper Is now illus- trated by typographic etchings done on glass by a process due to Mr. H. a Crocker. The dravring is made by a resist- ing crayon of waxy material, and hydrofluoric acid is used to "bite" the glass on the exposed parts which the crayon does not protect. The glass plates are cemented down on metal blocks for use in the printing machine like the ordi- nary electrotype "block." It a recent meeting of the Philadelphia Academy of Sciences, Mr. Joseph Wilcox described a fish-way designed by Colonel M`Donald, of Virginia, with a view to faaitate the passage of fish up dams. A trough is constructed with covered ways at each side, down which the water Lbws. The partitions are perforated in such a manner that the water spouts from the side passages upward into the central trough, making a current strong enough to propel fishen,. and even properly constructed boats, towards the top of the way. A SINKING Monwram.—An isolated mountain termed Jebel Nalba, about 25,00C1ft. high, situated near Bona in Algeria, is found to be rapidly decreasing in height, and round its base a considerable cavity has formed. The whole mass of the mountain is evidently sinking; and the envi- rons of Bona seem to show that a similar phenomenon has taken place there before. Lake Fezarra, now some thousand acres in extent, did not exist in the time of the Romans, and investigations made in 1870 show that its bed was once the site of a Roman town.—Cassell's Magazine.
• Mr. R. Brough Smyth, of the School of Mines, Sanahurst, colony of Victoria, communicates to the current number of Nature an account of a remarkable fall of atmospheric dust

in that ;3'g-1;W -o;"April -2-47--ii;e-Ksi-w-are-I;rOught down during showers of rain, which were really showers of mud, everything—leaves of trees, roofs of buildings, Sze.—being after the showers more or less covered with red mud. A microscopical examination showed the dust to consist of quartz, oxide of iron, and mica particles. Mr. Smyth be- lieves that the dust came from the north and had travelled far. A FIRELESS LOCOMOTIVE—It Francq, a French en- gineer, has just been awarded a Montvon prize for perfect- ing a fireless locomotive, and applying it to traction on railways and canals. The locomotive in question takes in a sufficient supply of steam from a fixed generator to last a trip of the train or vessel, and thus the necessity of carrying coals and a furnace is obviated. A reservoir containing hot water is charged with steam at the beginning of each trip. A line of tramway between Buell and Marty, another be- tween Lille and Roubaix, and a tow-boat on the Canal de l'Est are now being worked by M. Francq's locomotive.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

LITTERING STRMNBERRIES—by which is understood making provision to protect the fruit from being splashed with dirt in rainy weather; and the better the system of culture the more deeirable is the operation of littering. The finer the fruit the sooner it comes in contact with the soil. Good cultivation demands ample space between the plants to develop; but this increases the area of the soil exposed to the action of the rain, and should urge the grower to litter or mulch, and that speedily. Strawberries once covered with grit seldom free themselves of it entirely. If 1 from the mulching to the time of ripening heavy rain de- scends, the top part of the fruit may get fairly clean, but, the under side, which is usually the worst, remains so.l Where the heedless method of cultivation is practised, if it is worthy to be termed culture, where the plants are al- lowed to spread their runners over the surface so as to thoroughly cover it, mulching is not necessary, neither would the quality of the halt pay for the trouble. The materials in general use for mulching are litter, spent bark and bracken, or the withered fronds of the common fern, collected the previous year and stored in a dry place. Thisl in some districts is plentiful, and grows over sft. high and makes a clean, cheap mulching, except in extra wet seasons, when through absence of fibre it is soon rendered useless by the action ot the feet. Litter such as has been used in stables, with the excrement shaken cut, stands first with growers when they can get it, but it has- one undesirable tendency, that of introducing a quantity of the seeds of weeds into the garden, if it has not undergone a severe fer- mentation. Tan, on the other hand, tends to keep the weeds down, but occasionally particles of the tan may be seen on the fruit after heavy rain. Before the mulching is com- menced we would raise the runners up,. especially those be- longing to the outer rows, to be afterwards placed on the material, and when they have extended themselves suffi- ciently they may be secured to the soil; when they will make plants that will bear a good crop next season. ()motes —This crop promises badly, on account of the dry weather, and we shall have large gaps to fill up if thel maggots will leave us a sufficient number to transplant.' Waterings with weak guano water is the best preventive. Clear water would also do much in that direction, for we do not suffer from the maggot only in dry seasons. Advan- tage should be taken of a moist day to transplant the Onions, also Beet and Scarlet Thinner Beans, which are de- ficient in the roots. Dwarf French Beans are amenable to eimilar treatment. POTATOES.—Our attention has been drawn to a paragraph in "The Garden" of June 14th, which from the context is not a misprint, and the writer appears in earnest when he states that "early potatoes should now be earthed up." There is something wrong somewhere, for on that date we began to unearth ours, and others are doing the same thing in the vicinity of Preston; and we further learn that the Rev. L. C. Wood, of Singleton, commenced to dig the first week in this month. Tag ramie GARLIEN.—ROSES.—If it is obsereed that the leaves of these curl up, it is a sure sign that the rose grub is at work, and if it is not speedily destroyed it will make sad havoc on the leaves and flower buds. There is no better insecticide than the fingers and thumb, between which the leaves should be pressed, and the deadly remains of the grab will be seen to ooze out, so that in a few minutes seve- ral trees may be examined. The green fly on the young growth and flower bads must not be neglected. It is got rid of by using soapy water coloured with tobacco juice. Sweet William sown this time last year is now coming in flower, and some sown a fortnight or three weeks earlier has been in flower that much sooner. For the general sowing this is a good time; but any result that is conducive to a successional crop flowers or vegetables should not be overlooked, and for that reason another small Bowing of Wallflowers should be made at this time, for it occurs with this plant in certain seasons that the first sowing, will make such rapid growth that they will be too forward to with- I stand the wieter's frost, whilst the one made a month later will survive, and should both do so there will in all proba- bility be successional bloom. To provide against these con- tingencies involves no extra quantity of seed; but simply dividing that which would have been sown at once and making two sowings of it. THE WINDOW.—The chief object of the cottagers atten- tion will be those plants which he intends exhibiting, and which we usually see at flower shows. The most popular no doubt is the Fachsia, respecting which we have already informed oer readers that they must not be pinched or stopped after the ninth week previous to the show, as the plants will not have time to make fresh growth to produce flowers to any extent, and all flowers that may appear on previous growths should be pinched off, as they will be use- less in nine weeks after they appear, and they moreover exhaust the plants. A floriferous plant like the Fuchsia, if required at its best on a certe:m date, must not be allowed to flower whilst making its, growth, or the latter will be. come stunted and refuse to make further progress. Where there is space the plants would do well plunged in the ground outside, where they should be attended to daily as to watering, tad manure water every other day.

WOMEM ore VJENNA..—The education of girls in Vienna is somewhat peculiar, and perhaps worthy of note, writes a correspondent from that city. Up to 15 years of age they are kept at their studies. After they leave school they go through a year's, or even two years, teaching in the pantry and in the kitchen, under some member of the family, or even in some cases in another family, under trained cooks. They may never be required to cook a dinner, but they are thus rendered independent of cooks and servants, as they learn how to do everything themselves long before they begin housekeeping on their own account. When married they are most affectionate wives and mothers. An Austrian lady, in fact, is as accomplished and learned as an English governess, as good a housekeeper and cook as a German, as witty in society as a Parisian, as passionate as an Italian, and as handsome as an American—some of the most beauti- ful women in Europe being in Vienna. A meeting of thc Warrington Chamber of Commerce was held on Monday afeernoom in consequence of a requisition signed by a number of members, the object being to anew tain the feeling of the general Chamber on the subject of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill and the attitude that should be assumed by the Chamber with respect to it. The following members were presentl—niessrs. C. Broadbent (in the chair), J. Davies, J. Dunn, W. Pierpoint, T. Jolley, J. Fairclough, A. Mackie, H. Bleckly, Z. Armitage, C. J. Morris, C. Hutch- ings, P. Davies, F. Monks, and W. Carson. The CHAIRMAN said that as the action lately taken by the Council of the Cbamber of Commerce had been subject to comment in the town generally and a subject for platform oratory, be thought that he ought to say something as to what had happened which had not been correctly reported outside. The Council, at their last meeting, had two memo- rials laid before them, one from Liverpool in opposition to the canal and one from Manchester wishing the Chamber to promote the canal. The action that the Council took in reference to thos3 two memorials waseas they knew, a peti- tion to the House of Commons. That petition was, ill the opinion of the Council, a very proper one to send, or they should not have sent it. It was one which in their opinion either Warrington, Liverpool, or Manchester might semd. It was certainly not., as hael been erroneously represented' by some people, hostile in its intention or action to the atip Canal, or to the improvement of the navigation between Warrington and Manshester on the one side or Liverpool on the other. The Council were aware that there had been' very imoertant engineering evidence Oman both for and lagainst the Ship-Canal, and as regarded the effects of ha 'works upon the estuary a the Mersey. It would be a bold' Iran who would attempt to say on which side-such evidence wee most powerful, but it did not seem to them that it was a matter between Liverpool' and Manchester, but the question effett all Lancashire would suffer alike supposing that the works of the Ship Canal injured the estuary on the Mersey , and the port of Liverpool. He wished it to be known that I the feeling of the Council was not hostile to the' canal, but in fevoar of any sciterne wnich would improve the naviga- tion from Liverpool inland and to Manchester. One indica- tion of the absence of any hostility on the part of 1 the Council was the fact that the Mayor, who was present, and wa3 about to take the chair, at a meet- ing in favour of the Ship Canal, supported the resolution that the Council paned: In the excitement of a public meeting the Mayor seemed to have forgotten ex- actly what took place in the Council meeting and 'to have given an incorrect account of what had passed. He (the chairman) was sure that that was entirely unintentional on the part 6t the Mayor, and that he would not wish to, have done so. The idea that any members of the Council wlate were present could or would' have any hostility to-any scheme that was likely to be beneficial to the trade of War- rington was simply ridiccious on aim fame of it! There had been some question whether the Council was a fit and proper body to take the action which them did. but in this case they had taken the course they had done under similar cireurn- stances before, and which he believed was in accordenee with the roles of the Chamber. lie should like to ask Mr. Davies, who was acting as secretary, to read any rules that would give any information am tct how far the Chamber in this respect had acted strictly ineorder. Alderman, DAvIES having remarked that he should be glad to make a statement justifying the course taken by the Council, proceeded to detail the rules of the Chamber, as he thought it was best to have them before such an important meeting as that one. Proceeding, he said that unfortua nately the Council had, in exercising their powers, resolved upon all petitions and memoriale, as representing the Chamber. Mr. Davies then read a coinmunication that had been received from the Secretary of the Liverpool Incor- porated Chamber of Commerce, enclosing the copy of a petition to the House of Commonenurging the rejection of the bill, and asking the Chamber to adopt the petitien. In con- sect...lmmo a meeting of the Council was- called and he d, when Mr. Broadbent produced a letter from Mr. Daniel Adamson asking the Chamber to support the bill. Mr. Davies then read the minutes messed at the meeting, which were published in our last issue, the resolution adopted being to the effect that a petition be forwarded to Mr. McMinnies for presentation to Parliament, praying that the House would not assent to any proposal which might endanger the navigation of the Mersey or reduce the flaw of water which at present gavethe petitioners and the- other traders of War- rington a free navigable channel to the port of Liverpool. He (Mr. Davies) believed that no member of the Chamber had any antagonistic feeling to the promoters of the Ship Canal— (hear, hear)--indeed, they were the rather imbued with the opinion that they were men who frone their own lights were doing their, best to promote the interests of Lan- cashire and the north of England altogether. He could speak with some propriety as to why he did not take*, such a warm interest in the promotion of the canal as he did last year, Mont the faet that there were few who would he more benefited by its entension than he would be. He had nearly a mile of front teethe existing river Mersey, and by the extension of the works—or inten- ded works—that front would become available and ap- proachable to the, new canal. He could not do better than state the reasons why, from a public point of view, he hesi- tated to take the same amount of interest in the zuestion as he did last year, as expressed by him, to one of the pro- moters in a communication in which he said "that as re- garded Warrington the course of the canal was entirely altered from last year, and for no material reason. They were up in arms about two swing bridges, and new they had five within a distance of two miles. That was a serious m itter to.. the canal proper. The main canal was more than half a mile further away, and the proposed local dock would be a sealed book for Warrington, as it would be un- approachable except over the Wilderspoal level crossing— an intolerable nuisance even to a suburban road: On look- ing at the plan he saw that it would be convenient for a railway tip from Preston Brook or London, but as regarded Warrington manufacturers carting to the doe/ they must either go over a dangerous railway level crossing closed to the public hours in the day, or go three miles round by Wash-lane, Stockton Heath, past the- Wilderspool Brewery, and encountering two swing bridges over the canal. In the face of these con- tradictory statements it is impossible to say that any report is " official." THE SUEZ CANAL—Mr. Bertemarr asked in the event of the neutralisation of the Suez Canal if the war vessels of a foreign State with whom this countreemight be engaged in hostilities would have the same rights as English vessels of passing through the canal, and whether the British Govern- ment would neither be able to stop these hostile men of war nor to fortify the canal against possible injury or destruc- tiom—Lord E. Ft said the word neutralisation as applied to the canal was misleading. the proposal being in the nature of an agreement to secure the free passage of all ships under all circumstances. it was contemplated that provision would be made for the immmediate repair of may damage to the canal caused by a war vessel at the cod of the Power to which she belonged. THE NOTE OF C hIeISURE DECLINED. EXTRAORDINARY SCENE. Questions were over pretty early, Mr. GLADSTONE rising at ten minutes prat five to move that the Orders of theTay be postponed till after Mr. Brace's motion. This he did without comment. —Mr. FORSTER immediately followed, and said he was still of opinion that the discussion upon which they were about to enter was most inopportune, and inconvenient. He had, therefore, risen for the purpose of appealing to Mr. Arnold to withdraw his amendment, and to permit the division to be taken on the previous guection. —Mr. Anemia) said he thought it was his duty to persevere with his amendment—Sir W. Lawson rose to support Mr. Forster's appeal, and Mr. LABOZCHERE asked what the Go- vernment were going to do.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Go- vernment had, yielded to the demand of the Leader ,of the Opposition for a day on which to discuss the Vote of Cen- sure with a very deep sense that they were furnishing facili- ties for a proposal most inopportune and most injurious to the public interests, a description of the motion hailed with loud cheers -from the Liberal benches.—At this stage Mr. GOSCREN appeared upon the scene, and gave a new Vern to affairs. Rising hurriedly, the right hon. gentleman declared his opinion that, looking to the. circumstances of the case, the House of Commons would best do its duty if it were to refuse to agree to the postponement of the Orders of the 'day with the specific object of furnishing an opportunity of bringing on the Vote of Censure. The House of Commons ought not to be driven into the division' lobby at an inopportune time to decide upon an in- complete ease. Mr. Goschetee speech made a profound sen- sation. growing as—observing the wideding assent en the Liberal side—he more firmly stated his view. At first when the approving cheers were, only partial, but when tie sat down there was unanimous applause both above and below the gangway on the Liberal side. On the Treasureebench a rapid interchange of views took place between Mr. Glad- stone Sir William Harcourt, and Mr. Childers, who sat on his left hand. They were evidently as much taken aback as the main body of their supporters, and hastily discussed this startling proposal. Sir S. TiORTHCOTE, who plainly shared in the prevailing excitement, said the course of the Opposition was quite clear. They could not consent to the postponement of the question.—Mr. CHILDERS said the Government were bound to provide a day for discussing the Vote of Censure when notice haddeeen given by the Leader of the Opposition; but in the opinion of the Government debate would be most inischievous,—BAßON DE WCRMS said a few words amid cries fore division—Mr. HENEAGE agreed with Mr. Goschen, as did Mr.lezeterowourn, who, amid loud cheers, said the simplest and most straightforward course was to prevent the opening of a debate from which nothing but mischief would come.—Mr. BAIKES asked whether the public out of doors would believe that the couree suggested by Mr. Goochen was not prompted by a Government afraid to face the dis- cussion, a suagestion received with laughter and ironical cheers from the Liberal benc'ces.—Sir W. HARCOURT, amid renewed cheering, retorted that there was no man outside the HORSe Elle,DD one in it except Mr. Raikes who would have made a suggeetion equally dishonourable to Mr. Gosdhen and the Government —He left Mr. Raikes in the sole mon- opoly of the insinuation, an erclusive position from which Mr. Warzrote generously hastened to rescue him by intima- ting that be took the same view. The House was in no humour for further discussion, and at twenty minutes to six the question was put that the Orders of the Day be postponed. There was a half-hearted cry of " Ave " from the Conservative side and a thunderous shout of" No " from the Liberals. Amid a buzz of excited conversation, the House was ,cleared for the division. The speaker naming Lord Richard,Grosvenor and LorcLii en- Sington, the Government whips, to " tell " in favour of the motion, there was much laughter and cheering. Mr. Ges- chen and Mr. lilingworth "told" for the neee. Lesson as the Speaker cried "ayes to the right, noes to the left," the Liberals above and below the gangway rose in a mass, and amid repeated cheering moved out to the left. At the same time Mr. Gladetone rose, and heading the long filecf Minis- ters, moved off to the right to support a motion which the long established-etiquette of Parliament forced upon his acceptance. In a quarter of an hoar members had 'returned, the whips telling for the supporters of the motion coming in first, thus indicating how the day had gone. A minute or two later the tellers 'for .the other side came in, and the paper being handed to Mr. Goschen in token of victory, enthusiastic cheering rrose from the Liberal Eenches repeated again and agaen when ,the figures were announced showing that by 190 to 146 op- portunity for debating the Vote of Censure had been refused to the House of Commons. Sir S. detortbcote claimed the right to make one observation, which expressed his great •surprise that Mr. Gladstone had not in naming a day for the debate stated that it would he injurious to the public interest. Mr. Gladstone, who was received with loved echeers, said it was the duty of the Government to adhere to the rule which had of late been turned to such extraordin- ary use, and give a day for debating ,a Vote of Censure when it was claimed by the Leader of the Opposition. Having taken that decision, they were bound to give it un- grudgingly. But when Mr. Forster and other members had appealed to him that afternoon for his views he was bound Ito state them. THE MUNICIPAL Erezerions Brute—The House then pro- ceeded to the Orders of the Day, the firet. of which was the consideration of the Municipal Elections (Corrupt and Illegal Practices) Bill as amended by the Standing Com- mittee. ,Ultimately, after a formal stage had been taken,the discussion of the amendments which are 0 be proposed was adjourned. In the course of the discussion it was stated by tlae Home -Cecretary that the London Government Bill would be taken on Thursday. Tao Pomcg BILL—Mr. HIBBERT next moved the second reading of the Police Bill, the main object of which he ex- plaiued to be the pensioning of policemen after 25 Years' service, but at the minimum age of 55.---Mr. SCLATEII- BOOTK objected to the propesed interference with the dis- cretion of local authorities, and the burden to be imposed on the rates.---Sir M. Hicks-Beach and Sir M. Lopes else. dwelt on the expenses which the bill would throw on the rates— Sir W. Harcourt denied this, and after some remarks from Sir H. Selwin-Ibbeteon and General Alexander, who sup- ported the bill, it was read a second time. The Intestate Estates Bill was read a second time. THE MEDICAL AOI.-0n Mr. Mundella proposing to go into committee on the Medical Act Amendment Eill; the objection was again raised that members interested in it had not anticipated its comizg on, and a motion to adjourn the debate was made and negatived by 87 to 55. Ultimately, after several divisions, the bill was committed, but no pro- gress was made. After some other orders had been disposed of, the House was counted out at 1-30.

HOUSE OP LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. PROPOSED RRIF,CTION OF THE FRANCHISE BILL —Lord CAIRNS glve notice, on the second reading of the Represen- tation of the People Bill, to move its rejection, on the ground that it was " unaccompanied by provisions for so apportioning the right to return members as to insure a true and fair representation of the people, or by adequate se- curity in the proposals of the Government that the present bill shall not come into operation except as partof an entire scheme." COLLAPSE OF THE VOTE OF CENSICTRE.—The Earl of CAR- Neßvox, after a recital of his view of what had taken place in the House of Commons on Monday night (in the course of which he observed that he did not know whether the vetoing of the debate on Mr. Bruce's motion was en =col-

dent or a manteutrre), asked 'Earl Gran' i'le if he took the same view as Mr. Gladstone of the corm2quences of going forward with a motion censuring thelpslicy of the Govern- ment in Egyr...—Earl GRANVILLE, Warring to Lord Car- narvon's insinuation, read a letter from Mr. Goschen, in which that gentleman asserted in the most unqualified man- ner that 'to one connected directly or indirectly with the Government had the slightest inkling of any idea on his part to oppose the postponement of the orders of the day. Eael 'Granville expressedlis perfect concurrence with what Mr. Gladstone had said of the injurious tendencies of de- bate at the present juncture upon affairs in Egypt.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, whilst admitting the bona fides of Mr. Goschen's letter; pursued, amid unwonted demonstra- tions of indignation on the part of noble lords opposite, the train of scepticism opened by Lord Carnarvon as to the spontaneity of the action taken by the majority of the House of Commons on Monday nitht.—After some words from Lord Kimberley the subject dropped. One or two bills were advanced a stage, and their lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuasnaY.

The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. MiscEmetvEozs.—Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett attempted to count it out. More than sixty members were present 6.nd business proceeded. In reply to Mr. Forster, vho asked whether the ,Government would take steps to prevent cruel injustice in Egypt, especially cruelty in Egyptian prisons by the imprisonment of innocent people, Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government would continue to do what they had been doing, and up to the present they had no reason to be dissatisfied with the results. In reply to further question- ing, the Premier suggested to Mr. Chaplin that he would do well to withhold his judgment till he was in possession of fuller information. Mr. Chaplin gave notice that he would call attention to the cruelties now being practised in Egypt as described in a letter of Mr. Clifford Lloyd._ Questions disposed of, Dr. Cameron rose to call attention to the smallpox epide,nic in London, and moved a resolution declaring that in view of the alarming increase of smallpox in London, the House calls up.n her Majesty's Govern- ment at once to apply to the metropolis those rational prin- ciples of prompt and direct preveative administration, the efficacy of which in circumscribing smallpox epidemics has been demonstrated by the experience of Glasgow and other large towns. Dr. Farquharson seconded .the resolution. "Sir C. Duke, whilst not asserting that the condition of ,dffairs in London was thoroughty•satisfactory, said it was not desirable while the epidemic existed to change the pre- -sent system. It was impossible to deal with the subject in a satisfactory way except in a general scheme for the government of London. Not desiring to meet the proposi- tion by a direct negative he moved the previous question. After some remarks from Mr. Anderson, Mr. Hopwood rose. and had offered a few observations when, at five minutes past seven, the House was counted out. • HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker entered the House soon after twelve. A quorum was constituted at a quarter to one. Throughout the sitting the attendance was 'very smell. NEW PEERS.—Mr. LABOUCHERE, amid laughter and ironical cheering, gave notice on Monday to ask the Pre- mier whether the House and the country might indulge in the hope that he would advise her Majesty to create such a number of peers of approved Liberal and Radical opinions as would redress the balance of parties in the House of Lords. Paola LAW Bat.—Mr. GRAY moved the second reading of the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill, which proposed various reforms in the system of electing poor law guardians in Ireland.—After some conversation, Mr. THEYELYAN, ap- proving the general principle of the Bill, consented to the second reading, leaving disputed points to be settled in com- mittee.—Mr J. Hurriar M'Castais took the opportunity to make his maiden speech in support of the measure, and the Bill was read a second time. COMPENSATION Bri.x.—Colon'el Nowar then moved the second reading of the Compensation for Improvements (Ireland) Bill, to which Mr. WANTON noisily objected on the score that the Bill was not printed.—Colonel NoLetr speaking on this point, Mr. Wanvrmq, after his accustomed manner, said: "Sir. I rise to order."—" I must ask the hon. member," said the &TAXER with unusual severity, "not to rise to order when there is no ,cuestion of order before the House." The Speaker scent on. amid cheers, to add that if Mr. Warton persisted in his habit he would be bound to call the attention of the House to it.—On the motion of Mr. TREVELYANt the debate was adjourned. HIGH Cotrwrs •fiouse took up the High Courts of Justice (Provincial Sittings) Bill, tbe second read lug of which was moved by Mr. WHITLEY. The Bill pro- posed to create a judicial district, comprising the county of Lancashire and part of the county of Chester, with power to extend the system to other communities, such as Bristol. —Mr. MORGAN 'LLO7O moved the rejection of the bill, which was supported by Mr. Arnold, Mr. West, Mr. Tomlin- son, and Sir R. Cross. It was opposed by Mr. Charles Russel, Mr. Gregory, and the Solicitor-General, who dwelt upon the fact that a scheme bad already been framed for giving extended sittings in Lancashire.—After some further conversation the House divided* and the second reading was carried by 8.7 votes against 64, a result hailed with cheers from the Opposition.—The House adjourned at ten minates to six.

- _ The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. Brms CONFLETED.—The Royal assent VMS given by Commission to 39 public and. private Acts, including the . Customs and 'lnland -Revenue, the National Debt (Conver- sion of Stock), Settled ,Land, Greek Marriages, Summary Jurisdiction over Children (Ireland), and the Sea and Coast Fisheries Fund Acts. The Lords Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, Earl S 7 dney, and Lord Monson. MISCELLANEOUS. The principal business before the House of Lordo last evening wao the correction by Earl , GRANVILLE of astatement made the other evening by the Marquis of Salisbury in-support of his contention that the collapse of the vote of censure, in the House of Commons was "arranged" between ,the Government whips and their unofficial supporters.—Lord DEITLAN brought in a Bill to confer the franchise on women, and several measures re- ceived the Royal assent,—The Duke of Argyll having given , notice of an amendment to the Secretary for Scotland Bill, 1 it was agreed on the suggestion of ere Marquis of SALE9NURY to postpone theconsideration of that Bill from Tuesday, on the understanding that the discussion of the Franchise Bill would entend over that day. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes after five o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS..—Tgurameser. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE CONFERENCE, SHIBMIG Rail, &C.—Lord E.. FITZ- MAURICE said in reply to a question that Mr. Clifford Lloyd left Egypt owing to differences of opinion between himself and varions high officials. Her •Mi:escy's Government did not intend to assome the entire internal administration of Egypt, bat they would continue to claim the rieht to advise on all important subjects.—Mr.' GHILDERS said he could not state at what date the plenipotentieries intended to resume the labours of the Conference until further progress had been made with the inquiries which were being made into details of finance.—Answering Sir S.Vorthocte, the Fuming eaid it would hardly be decorous for him to presume that the Conference would leave its work undone. When the financial matter with regard to -Egypt was disposed of, Her Majeetee t Government worth.' deem it their dutv to forward by any means in their power any desire the right hon. gentleman might have for dieouaioing the subject. En .reply to another question, Mr. Gladstone said the seamen .might not outlive the Conference, but his impression was that it wouId.—LordvELDNIOND IirerZILICOCICE told Mr. Storey 'that the Rajah of Tenom had been informed that he would be held responsible for the lives of the crew of the Nisero.— Kr. CHAMBERLAIN wanquestioned by Mr. Stanhope respect- ing the Merchant Shipping Bill, and he announced that he should not be able to proceed further with the measure, feel- ing that it would be dmpossible to and time to get it through the remaining stages. He had yesv reluctantly como to the conclusion that the bill must be withdrawn, and on Monday he ohould move that the order for the second reading bidis- charged. 'Eau CREW OF THE NEER° —Me. ISTOHEI having risen te move the adjournment of the House in order to call atten- tion to the perilose position of the captive crew of the Nisero and the dilatoriness of the Foreign Office in taking effectual steps for their rescue, the &WAX= asked whether he was supported by 'forty members, whereupon a large number of Conservative and Irish members steed up ia their places. The hon. member then proceeded with his motion and made serious charges of negligence against the Foreign ,Office. Lord E. Ft:TIMM:MICE maintained that Her Majesty's Government had not shown any indifference in regard to the subject. The tact was that there had been constant communications going on upon the subect and if there was, at had been as- serted, any strong feeling on the matter in the north of England, it was because of the inaccurate state- ments Mr.Storey had hinteelf published in thatpart of the country. He hoped before long ,to be able to lay fur- ther papers on the table and to be then able to.atzte what the view of her Majesty's Government was after they had received the final answer of the.t of the Netherlands. Mr. GLA,ESTONE said he was confident .that it would be found that the charges of neglect and dilatoriness had ncefounda- tion whatever. Eventually the motion for the adjourn- ment of the House was by leave withdrawn. THE 'LONDON GOVERNMENT RILL —Sir W. HARCOURT, in moving the second reading of the London Government Bill, said he was at a loss to understand whether the Metropolitan Board of Works were opponents to the bill or not. He wished to ask this simple viestion—were these in- dependent vestries to be brought under some common con- trol which gave them uniform action for the benefit of the whole constituency? That was the central point of the bill. He feund that the Corporation of London had made every effort to inducoother corporations to petition against the bill. What was the result? He read in the paper that ,morning that Canterbury had refused lay a large majority to interfere. Manclasster had done the same, and the Corporation of Leafs had petitioned in favour of it.. The vital principle of the bill was that it (or the first time established a necessary community of action between the governing bodies of the metropolis. He hoped the House would affirm the principle a the bill by passing the second reading. (Cheers.)—Mr. RLTCHIE moved the following amendment:—" That while ready to consider the question of a reform in the Government of London this House de- clines to assent to a proposal by which the control over the levying and expenditure of rates would be vested in one central body to the practical extinction of the local self- government of the various cities and boroughs of the me- tropolis." The hon member disputed that there was any popular feeling in favour of the bill, and argued that it would be practidally impossible to proceed with so complex a measure at so late a period a the session. Mr. FIRTH da-

FOREIGN NEWS. EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N.. KHARTOUM AND BERBER.—THE POSITION OF KASSALA. SCAEIM,SATUEDAY.—MASOII Bey, Governor of Massowah, has arrived here. The road between Kassala and Massowah appears to be open, several trains of camels having arrived safely at the latter place. SUAKIM, Suenhay.—The Governor of Takrari telegraphs that a party of pilgrims has arrived there, having left Khartoum on May 23rd, and Berber on June 7th, and re- port that all was well at both places when they left. Government troops were still stationed at both Berber and Khartoum, and food was plentiful. There was also a good supply of water on the road. Another party of pilgrims from Gadara and Kassala, who left the latter place on the 14th inst., report that the country in the neighbourhood of Kassala was quiet. The force of rebels outside Souakiin is increasing. Cern% MONDAY.—The news brought to Suakim yester- day by pilgrims is categorically contradicted to-day by the Sheik Saleb, who is ready to stake his reputation on the correctness of his report as to the fall of Berber.—Sfaralarcl. ASSOUAN, MONDAY.—Major Kitchener arrived here this morning, accompanied by an Arab escort, having completed an extended recnnneisance through the Korosko desert, which occupied 17 days. He travelled almost due east from Korosko, within two days of the Red S.ia, visiting the out- lying Arab posts under the Sheik Jibrac, which he found ' in excellent order, Jibran having more men under arms than he receives pay for. Major Kitchener reports the ceuntry quiet. He denies that the Bishareen Arabs havn thrown in their lot with the Mandi.—Daily News. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESEAY.—NO negotiations whatever pending between the Porte and Lord Dufferin regarding the dispatch of Turkish troops to the Soudan. The Ottoman Government denies having considered the question of send- ing troops to Suakim. No Power has expressed its views upon Aseym Pasha's circular proposing a mixed military occupation of Egypt, and the scheme is regarded as aban- doned. REPORTED MASSACRE IN THE SOUDAN. The Daily News publishes the following telegram, dated Assouan, Wednesdayaia 25 pm: The regiment of Egyptian I cavalry, 500 soldiers, arrived to-day. The English batta- lion is expected the dey after to-morrow. All is quiet. 10-40 p m.—A rumour is circulating that Debbeh has been attacked by 12,000 Arabs, and the town captured by assault. Three thousand of the garrison and inhabitants are said to have been killed. The Mudir of Dongela, with a number of officers, has gone in the direction of Debbah, with what object is not known. FRANCE. THE CHOLERA OUTBREAK. Tamale, SUNDAY—Four deaths from cholera have occurred here since six o'clock yesterday evening. TOULON, Mospear.—From six o'clock yesterday evening to eleven o'clock this morning six deaths occurred here front cholera.-7 Pic —Only one death from cholera was re- ported here sincell o'clock this morning. Paws, MONDRY.—The Government Board of Health met this afternoon. Drs. Proust and Brouardel, who had been sent to Toulon to inquire into the nature of the epidemic, were present, and laid their report before the Board. They had come to the conclusion that the disease which has broken out at Toulon is Asiatic cholera of a mild character —that is to say, it has not spread extensively.—Samlard. VIENNA, MONDAY.—The Austrian and Hungarian Govern- ment have, it is said, issued orders that all arrivals by nee from the French ports in the Mediterranean and from Algiers shall he subjected to observation. Bonen, Sueepay.—The Government has issued an order subjecting travellers arriving overland from France to five days, quarantine. BERIZK, TUESDAY.—Dr. Koch will proceed without delay to Paris, and afterwards to Toulon, to offer his services in determining the character of the epidemic prevalent in the latter oily, and also to prosecute further studies into the nature of the disease and the conditions of its propagation. Moira, TUESDAY.—Twenty-otte days' qaarantine has been imposed here on all arrivals from Toulon or Marseilles. COPENRAGEr, TUESDAY..--AR order has been issued tea , dav that all vessels arriving from French ports ac p to undergo quarantine inspection. Masentatns, TUESDAY MOZNING.—There were three cholera deaths here during the night. The station is filed with refugees. At Toulon there were four deaths. Totta,ou, WEDNESDAY.—Five deaths front cholera have occurred here since ten o'clock last night. MAESEILLES, WEDNESDAY.—TWO deaths from cholera occurred here last night. PANIC AT MARSEILLES. IKAESEILLES,'TRUESDAY.—Since yesterday morning three deaths from Cholera have occurred here. At Tonloraduring the same time, the deaths numbered 23. Four hundred poor workmen sent from Toulon to this city are beitig sect back by the Marseilles authorities. The panic here is un- reasonable. No fewer than 6,000 of the int.abitante have left this place. THE BONAPARTISTS. .Baleta, TRUES/9,1.1,—A Jecomist meeting was held yester- day in the Salle De Rivoli. One speaker delivered a vio- lent address, in which he declared that 'Prince Victor had forfeited his rights for having provoked a division in the Bonapartist party. The meeting adopted as order of the day expressing devotion to Prince Jerome. TRANCE AND CHINA., 'VI)3I;NA, MONDA7.—Accordittg to telegraphic ictelligence received here, the Chinese Goventiment has eoleinnly de- clared to the Diplomatic Corps at Pekin that it is entirely innocent in the matter of the attack on the French at Lang- eon, And is preparing to send ale emphatic protest to the Powers against the insinuation that it has violated the treaty with Trance. The generals and officers who are to blame will be tried by cocrt•martial—Stfendarkt. THREA'PENED OUTBREAK OF WAD. Teem, THEIRSDICZ.—A. Cabinet Council was held here this morning. M: Jules Ferry, the Premier, communicated to his colleagues some despatchce receive-I from China, whichstated that tie Chinese Government did not disavow the actien of the Chinese regular troops at Langcon. The '-Chinese also declined to recognise stipulations agreed upon between Li Hung Chang and M. Fournier providing for the -evacuation of Langson, Chatke,Coa, Pang, ancl,Laokai, be- tween the 6th and teth June. M. Patenotre has received instructions to proceed immediately to Pekin im order to -maintain the rights of France. CLUANCaAI, TRUESDAY.—War is threateninc between China and France, an influential party instigating it. Teo- •teung-t'ang, Peng-ya-lin, and the Marquis Teeng are re- solved to repudiate the Franca-Chinese uegotiatiena. rho French • will probably claim at indemnity, guaranteed by Formosa.—Times. ST. PETER'S ROME.

BoarE, .SUNDAY.—An enormous number of people assem- bled to-dny in St. Peter's, to attend the services in celebra- tion of ft. Peter's Day. Thoulandi of carriages drove to the Cathedral. There was no disturbances of any kind, as apprehended. THE ELECT:ONS IN PORTUGAL. LISEOTP, MONDAX.—The total number of members elected is li3B. The Opposition have only 30 eats, includino 28 Progressists and twa Republicans. Of the six members elected for Lisbon four arc Ministerialists and two Republi- cans. Despatches from •fiLadeira announce that the elections in that island have resulted in the victory of the ,Grovern- merit aver the Republicaats. Riots occurred during the pol- ling, and seven persons were killed. Disturhances.cf an im- portaErt character are reported from ether places.

Ngsr Tote, Sul; Folger, secretary of the Trea- sury, notifiez that he will redeem, prior to maturity, the bonds of the 129th call, not exceeding one million dollars weekly, with interest to data of payment. A boiler explo- sion has eecurred in a finer mill near Byron, Ohio, by which six persons were killed and eleven wounded. Three of the latter.stistained fatal in:aries. Three souricus £5O Bank of England notes have been received by a New York Bank from the Otettown Bank. An indivianal has been arrested at Milwaukee while attempting to negotiate nimilar notes. TRE ANTI-JEWISti RIOTS AT ALGIERS. PARIS, SlONCAN.—lntelligence received here fronrAlgiers states that anti-Jewish disturbances have occurred there. The night before last a sanguinary.coniict took place. Several persons were wounded, and the !Jewish quarter ,ef the town was pillaged. The troops were obliged to interfere. Daring Yesterday all was quiet. Energetic measures have been taken to prevent any fresh disturbances. ALGIERS. Tunsaar.—Fearing a rrenewal of the rioting, the Jews still keep their shops shut. One opened. his chop this morning, bat a mob collected and broke the windows. The Israelite Cons:story has addressed a letter to the Mayor of Algiers formally denying that the dews had, as had been alleged, spoken offensively of the French, and protesting the attachment of the Jewish community to France.

E AGTE RN ROU ELZA. PIIILEPPOPOLIS, WZDNESDAY.—Gravriei Pasha Christovics, the new Governor General of Eastern Roumelii, arrived here to-day, and was receive& at the railway station by a large number of the inhabitants. The city is decorated with flags, and triumphal arches bearing appropriate inscriptions are erected at various points. TERRIBLE COLLIERY DISASTER IN VANCOUVER'S ISLAND.
VICTORIA, VANCOUVER'S ISLAND, TUESDAY.—An ex- plosion occurred yesterday in Wellington Colliery, at Naniamo. Twenty-four persons were killed and many in- jured.
NEW ZEALAND. WELLINGTOS, DIMLY EvEwnect —The New Zealand Parliament has been dissolved, and the new elections bare been fixed to take place on July 22nd.

GENERAL NEWS.

_ Earl Spencer arrived in Lundon on Tuesday from Dublin, and proceeded to Downing-street, where his Excellency had an audience of the Prime Minister. • BLACKPOOL RAILWAY BILL.—The hearing of this bill before the Committee of the House of Lords was concluded en Tuesday, and the preamble declared proved. CRUELTY To A FOWL.—A man named Mills was fined at Maidstone, on Tuesday, for sticking a pin in the comb of a cock to inhprove its appearance when exhibited. ACCIDENT AT THE FORTH BRIDGE WORKS.—On Monday', at the Forth Bridge Works, John Fairless, master of the steamer Dina, of Middlesborough, was killed by the fall of a heavy stone into his cabin. The accident was caused by the breaking of a crane. SUICIDE OF AN bum APPROVER.—Thomas Kennedy, one of the men awaiting trial at Galway for the murder of a bailiff at Ballyforan, and who last week turned approver, committed buicide in his cell by hanging himself with his handkerchief from a hook for impending hammocks. On Wednesday some of Miss dialler's household goods were distrained upon in London on her refusal to pay the Queen's taxes as a protest against her exclusion from re- presentation in Parliament. A meeting of ladies was sub- sequently held in Miss Muller's drawing room, at which a resolution was adopted in approval of the course which had

been pursued. THE ALLEGED POISOIIING Cesx.—At Wallasey, on Wed- nesday, Thomas Edmond Morris, optician, Liverpool, sur- rendered to his bail, on the charge of poisoning his wife, who died about 18 months ago. Tile magistrates were in- formed that the Treasury did not see sufficient grounds for proceeding with the charge against Mr. Morris, wlio was accordingly discharged. MINE INSPECTION—A. representative deputation of miners waited upon the Home Secretary on Wednesday at the House of Commons, to present a memorial praying for an increase in the number of inspectors of coal mines. Sir W. Harcourt expressed himself as being by no means unfavour- able to the views of the deputation, and promised to consult _ _

with Mr. Burt, M.P., on the matter,. . T±AIPERI.NCE DEMONSTELTION.-11 demonstration in con- nection with the jubilee of the British Temperance League took place on Wednesday night in Exeter Hall. Mr. Caine, M.P., presiding. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, in moving the first resolution, expressed his conviction that all work towards making England sober would be useless until, the sale of strong drink was absolutely prohibited throughout the land. DXSTRUCTIVE FtnE.—A five-storey workshop at Stannary, Halifax, was burnt down on Wednesday. One of the walls fell outwards and destroyed eight cottages and their con- tents, the inhabitants escaping fortunately without injury. An adjoining pawnshop and Stannary Congregational Church, which is immediately Opposite, caught fire, but were extinguished. Damage was done to the amount, of

about £7,000. SAD SEQUEL TO A FEAST.—On Saturday night a melan- choly incident happened at a public-house dinner in Old- ham. The hands at Horsedge boltworks were haying a dinner, and it was observed that a youth, 18 years of age, named John Downey, drank freely. He was cautioned about this, but be persisted. At 11 o'clock he was nearly insensible, and was carried home on a man's back. He died

I shortly afterwards. THE BISHOP OF RIPON AT WESTMINSTER ARBEY.—The Bishop Elect of Ripon preached at Westminster Abbey on Sunday evening. Amongst the vast congregation were the Archbishop of Dublin, the Bishops of Manchester and Ohio, Canon Fleming, and Zr Stanhope, MP. It is com- puted that as many people wore turned from the doors as those who obtained admission. The 'Bishop preached what is called a gospel sermon, and said the way to reach , the people's hearts was to know and understated their 'necessities. DEATH OF THE REV. CANON &NCH. •—• The death is announced of the Rev Canon Birch, late the rector of Prest- wich, which took place on Sunday. The deceased gentle- man, who was highly respected throughout the diocese, re- cently resigned the living at Prestwich in consequence of ill-health. He waschaplain in ordinary to the Queen, and •chaplain to the Prince of Wales, to whom he was formerly tater. He was Proctor in Convocation for the Chapter of Ripon, and Residentary Canon df Ripon. He was Bachelor of Divinity of King's College, Cambridge. SALE OF a, NEET 'PRESENTLTION —A sale of landed and other property conaected with the Blenheim estate was held at Oxford, on Saturday, amounting in all to nearly7oo acres, and also the disposal of the advowson and next presen- tation of the rectery of Nokc, in the parish of Islip, near Oxford, by the direction of the Duke of Marlborough. The gross value of the living is under £l2O, the population about 120, and the present age of the incumbent is 41 years. Mr. J. B. Clarke, of woke, became the purchaser,of the advow- son for £4BO. The other property sold realised fairly aver- age prices. FM:WEAL ON -rnit Rtev. i. 7. Bamowne-Banaws.—On Mon- day, in the presence of a large company, the funeral of the Rev. 5. Baldwin-Brown (Congregationalist) took place at Norwood Cemetery. 'Amongst those present were Mr. Sam. Morley, M.P.'; Professor Gerald Baldwin-Brown, of Edin- burgh, son or the deceased; Mrs. J. R. Broke, his daughter; and representatives of numerous denominational institu- tions, including the following :—Lonelon Congregational Un(on, Congregational Union of England and Wales. Church of England (well represented), Surrey Congregational Union, and Colonial Missionary Society. , THE BOOTIE WIFE KIIRDER.—kt the Bootle Police Court, on Monday morning, before Messrs. E.. Neap and J. P. M'Arthur, Peter Cassidy was brought up on remand charged with the wilful murder ,4 his wife. Mr. W. Swift (Eaton and•Ewift) prosecuted on behalf of the Treasury, i and the prisoner was undefended. During the whole of the 1 proceedings Cassidy, who appeared to be very dejected, 1 maintained a moody silence. Mr. Swift haying stated the facts ef thocage, evidence was given by the same witnesses who had attended the Coroner's inquest. The prisoner, on being askedif he had any statement to make, said, " There , is many a' little thing on my behalf that I cannot speak thyself atepresent." ' 'So was then committed to the assizes ! for trial. . ' He was She hest debater-in the Howie, end the staunchest ' champion of the party, and they all 'looked totim in the , future, for they knew he had the cause of the National ' Union at hoart.
