ontion. SlymEas..--11,)out 4CG men engaged ir. the Bradford dye- ing trade struck work on Monday for en advance of 10 per cent, in wages. Some IC,OOO miners strrok wcrk in South Stafferdshire to resist a reduction of wages. The ship- builders of StocktoneonVrees are out on.strike to resist a pro- I posed lOper cent, redaction of wages. The decigion arrived at by the Weavers' Association, on Tcesday evening, was

. carriedinto effect at Burnley on Wednesday, when, except attwo or three mills, where the employers had agreed to pay according to the Mackin:at list. three.fourths of the work. people of this district came out on strike. At a meeting of the Burnley employers, ea Wednesday evening,.a:resolution was agreed to offering to discuss any changes that may he desired, but stating their determination to-rasist the dictation of the Weavers' Association. ffLADIES• IN TIER LONDON UNINEREUPY.—For tlscgrst time in this country a lady has just attained the degree of Master of Arts. The lady in question, Mies Mary Clara Dawea, poised the matriculation 'examination in :7anuely, 1879,1 gaining thelorty-seventh place in the Honours Division. Last year,. et the B.A. examination, having obtained a place in the first division at the pass examination, she gained also honours in Classics, with the first plane inlbeseconti class. At the examination just concluded she isplaced fourth in the list of the Masters of .Arts of the year who have taken the degree in the first 'branch of examination--4hat is, in claesics, with ancient and modern history. The two other branches are mathematics with natural .philosophy, and mental and moral philosophy with political economy. Although the ladies have ,s.s yet only one 'M.A., fifty of there have obtained the degree of Bachelor et Arts, three that of Bachelor of Medicine, and eight the degree of Bachelor of Science. No lady has yet attained to the Doc- torate. The ladies wile have passed the matriculation ex- amination amount already to-several hundreds. THE GOIRENMENT Scisneen AND THE COZWERENCE.— The scheme by which the Government propose to regulate the financial position of Egypt was finally delivered on Saturday to the members of the 'Conference. The Observer has reaeon to believe that the following are the main featcres of the scheme :-1. The interest on the Unified Debt is to be reduced from kl.per cent. to $i per cent. 2. The interest on the Preferonce'Lebt is to be reduced from 5 percent. to 411 per cent. 3. The interest on the Datra Debt is not to be reduced at all, supposing the revelues hypothecated to this I debt suffice to pay the stipulated interest. But in the eon- trary event the Egyptian Exchequer is only to be called upon I to make up the amount less i percent. 4. The Domains ' Loan is to be left untouched, in coseideration of the facts that it was advanced to pay off the Floating Deht under conditions which would never have been granted uslese the security had been regarded as abeolute that Egypt derived great benefit from this loan; and that, therefore, it stands 1 in a completely different category from all the other loans. I 5. The Sinking Funds on both the Preference and the Uni- fied Debts are to be suspended for the present. 6. The in- terest paid by Egypt in respect of the flues Canal shares held by England is to be reduced either by or per cent., as circumstances may render advisable. J. The British Government is either to advance itself, or to guarantee the advance of a sum of £8,060,000 to the Egyptian Govern- ment for the payment of the indemnities and ether expenses. This loan is to take precedence of all existing loans. 8. The tanee levied in Egypt are to be reduced by a sum varying from £3,500,000 to £4,000,693. The business at the meeting on Saturday was but preliminary, and the Conference has not met since. England alone has two representatives at the Conference, Earl Granville and Mr. Childers. ByfAlc CHAMPAGNE.—The champagne districts of the Conti- nent produce some 300,000,000 bottles annually. Only °cos- hed( of this quantity is exported, and yet England and America alone are said to consume more than twice this vast production. From whettce does the balance come? From the apple orchards on both sides the Atlantic! Yes, it is these apple orchards that are responsible for most of the cheaper champagees Now CAMMACE & CO. are offering an AMERICAN CIDER CRAMPAGNE—the PURE JUICE of American apples—which they might easily pass off as a champagne at ten times the price: but they prefer to call a spade a spade! They are confident that everyone who tastes this most delicious and wholesouus beverage, will, like Oliver Twist, ask for glom—Advt.

The statement that the Garmoyle-Porteseue case has been settled out of court is contradicted. The action will, it is believed, come On for trlal in a few days. At the adjourned inquest held on Thursday at Middles- borough on the body of Mary Cooper, eight years old, mur- dered in Albert Park 10 days age, the jury returned a ver- dict of wilful murder against some person unknown. At Windsor Castle on Thursday liar Majesty personally decorated with medals eleven men from various branches of the regular service who had been recommended for distinc- ti4ll by reason of special gallantry in the Soudan cam-

_ paigd. The first annual report of the Inspector-General in Bankruptcy under the new Act was issued as a parliamen- tary paper on Thursday. It states that the total coat of administration is little more than half that of the previous

Act. The announcement is made of the retirement of the Bishop of Salisbury. His lordship has filled several dis- tinguished offices with conspicuous success, but at the age of Übe feels himself unable to keep up with the labours

of his diocese. EDINBERGH THEATRE ROYAL has been burned to the ground. No explanation can be given as to the cause of the outbreak, which was first noticed in the gallery during rehearsal. This was the fourth time the building bad suf-

fered frem fire. A young man named George Soulsby is in custody at Sunderland on a charge of murder. Soulsby went last Fri- day into the house of an old man named Fenwick, and struck him on the head with a hammer as he lay asleep. Fenwick . .

died on Wednesday night. THE CONFERENCE ON EGYPT.—A meeting of the finan- cial assistants of the plenipotentiaries attending the Con- ference on Egyptian finance was held on Tuesday, at the Foreign Office. Mr. Philip Currie, C. 8., and Count d'Aubigny, joint protocolists, attended the meeting of the

experts-. - - The case of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Com- pany v. Overseers of Manchester was concluded on Thurs- day. The Judges held that the Overseers were right in assessing the Company for the relief of the poor in respect of their wires, attachments, and posts. Leave to appeal

was given. FALL OF A SCAFFOLD: Two MEN KILLED.—Whilst the builders were at work in constructing the new Angerrack Viaduct, at Hayle, Cornwall, on the Great Western Rail- way, on Wednesday, a scaffold gave way, and two men were precipitated to the ground, 80ft, below, and instan- taneously killed. NORTH WARWICKSHIRE ELECTION —On Tnesdly, the result was announced to be:—P. A. Muntz (C), 5,282; A. Cameron Corbett (L), 3,538; majority, 1,744. There was no contest at the last general election, but in 1874 the num- bers were :—Newdegate (C), 4,672; Davenport (C), 4,322; __ ,

G. L. Mentz (L), 3.189: Six men employed by the Liverpool Corporation were on Wednesday morning taken to the hospital suffering from the effects of inhaling poisonous gas in a sewer in which they were working. The gas, it is supposed, got Into the sewer from a match factory in the neighbourhood. One of the men lies in a dangerous condition. FATAL TEAP ACCIDENT.—Mr. John Jones, solicitor, and registrar of Swansee County Court, was thrown from a trap at Llandyasil, on Wednesday night, throuah the horse bolt- ing on a steep hill, and was instantly killed. His wife and two children were in the trap with him when the accident occurred. Mrs Jones received serious injuries. At a conference of peers, members of the House of Com- mons, and others, at the offices of the Marriage Law Reform Association on Thursday, it was unanimously resolved that a bill etiould at once be introduced into the House of Lords to legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister. Lord 'Houghton consented to take charge of the meanare. IaLLED EY AN REPRESS TRAIN.—On Thursday morning, at nine o'clock, as Mr, James Burden, wine merchant, Dun- dee, was walking on the Caledonian Railway, near Mont- fieth, on his way to the station, he was overtaken by a fast express, and instantaneously killed. His remains were gathered in a skeet. He was 54 years of age. It was his practice to walk en the rails to the station every morning from his summer residence. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT Bnereso.—On Thursday a des- tructive fire broke out in tbe Harbour Commissioners' sheds. Prince's Dock, Belfast, in which dies to the value of £6,000, the joint property of Sir John Preston and Mr. Ewart, M.P.. was stored. The entire stock and shedding was destroyed. and it was with great difficulty that the fire was prevented from spreading te the shipping and to the adjoining warehottses. The stock was only parti- ally insured.. SCENE tsr COURT By MKS. WELTSDN.—In the Course of the hearingof the action on Thursday for £6',000 damages, brought by Mrs Weldon against a London solicitor named Neale.upor. Mr Justice Smith holding that there was no case against the defendant, Mcs Weldon exclaimed that she could plainly see his Lordship andSaron Huddlestone were ' trying to 'rah her by preventing her from coming into court to have ,f-; sti ce. Upon continuing her observations, the judge directed her to leave the court which she did. AU:OWING RAILWATCOLLISION IN LT7ERPOOL.—About nine o'clock on Thursday morning, a passenger train en- tering Lime-street station, Liverpool, from Edge Hill, col- ' lided with a fish truck and guard's van standing in its way. The van was telescoped and smeshed to pieces, and the truck was damaged. Considerable injury was done to the engine of the passenger train, the occupants of which weremech shaken and knocked about. No serious injury, however, was sustained by any, and all were able to pro- ceed. /Leaman) MURDER 11,1 Gramicaree.en Thursday. Robert Black end John letiferma, labourers, residing in Bernard- street, Bridget Sloan and Alice Goff, residing in Marl- borough-street, are in custody 'in Glasgow for examination as to having caused the death of 'Robert Cummings, a pen- sioner, aged 50 years. The deceased and the four prisoners had been drinking in Black's on Thorsday morning, and it is alleged that in the midst of ,a 'fight which ensued Cum- mings received such injuries that he died shortly after- wards. Erenonen His Wtve ALIVE.-011 Saturday, at the Comity Magistrates' Court, Newcastleeunder-Le me, John Rowley. engineman, Chesterton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly. While tipsy the man actually dug a hole in his gardec, with the avowed design of burying his wife alive. As she did not fall in with vise-arrangement Rowley forced her into the hole, and because she would not lie still and be covered with earth he hit her on the head with a spade. He wee fined 103 and costs. Giteme Mompert.—At Gerrerd's Cross, Essex, on Thera- day, Charlotte Emily Reddington and Jane Morris were charged with the wilful murder of a child named Towns- endereged 1 year and 'O months, and with neglecting to pro- vide for two other children. It-was stated that the children were illegitimate, and that the prisoners received six tihillkgs per week in each case. They were discovered in a shacking state of emaciation Enid dirt, and the post-mortem examination showed that death was caused by starvation. The 'prisoners were 'remanded. COLLAPSE OF L MEITOPOIEMN SCNEME.—There has been a sale of the materials of that which was to hare been the Grand National Opera House, upon the Thames Em- benkment. Eighty thousand pounds had been spent on ifoundations and on around-floor work. Some say the pro- ject was killed 'for want, of funds; others that ' the ecice of Big Ben of Westminster was found to be too sonorous. and that no prima derma could venture to sing so near to the great bell. However, the materials, which with labour had cost £80;000, were sold in 289 lots in two days fee £2,050. NEW RAILWAY STATION AT MANCRESTER.—The 1,11/ew London and North-Western Railway Station in Manchester, which is to be called the Exchange Station, was opened for traffic en Monday.. All the North-Western trains to and from'Liverpool, Chester,'North Wales, and Yorkshire went into and departed from the new platform. The station premises, which are very entensive, are by no means finished, but the traffic is working quite smoothly. The floe new road over the Irwell which has been formed as an approach to the new station, and which debouches opposite the Crom- well fkatute, was also opened. ACCIOENT IN MANCELNrER Two MEN KILLED —A sad accident, resulting in the death of two men, occurred on Thursday afternoon near the Victoria Railway Station, Man- chester. The men were employed, in company with other labourem, in taking down come old buildings on the Long Mitigate side of the river Irk, near the Old Swan Hotel. As three or four of the workmen were engaged in remov- ing the broken bricks and raMbish a portion of the arch sod- denly gave way and fell upon two of them, killing them almost instantly. After the lapse of a few minutes they were extricated from the deS Ks and examined by a medical man, who pronounced life to be extinct. AST AERONAUT hapRISONER FOR FELICRY.—Joseph Sim- mono (49), described in the calendar as a "journalist," but better known as a balloonist, was on Saturday charged be- fore the Common Serjeant with wilful and corrupt perjury before the High Court of Justice. The facts, as stated by the prosecution, were, that in a recant action for damages against the Great Northern Railway with reference to in- juries elleged to have been sueteined in an accident on that line, the prisoner deliberately swore various things which were proved to be absolutely falee. The action resulted in a verdict for a farthing damages, the prisoner to pay all the costs. Evidence as to the affidavits sworn by the prisoner in theameent action in tba High Court and the evidence giveu by the prizoner was then produced. The prisoner was sentenced to two years' bard labour. EVICTION IN Tlfft HIGHLANDS.—A. crowded public meet- ing was held on Monday evening at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-streef, London, under the ausp:ces of the High- land Land Law Reform Association, to consider the threa- tened evictions in the Highlands. Mr. C. Frazer Mackin- tosh, M.P., occupied the chair—Mr. Maefarlane, M.P., moved a resolution declaring the condition of the Highland crofters and cotters, as detailed in the report of the Royal Commission, to be discreditable to a great and wealthy cation, and pledging the meeting to support the efforts of the Highland Land Law Reform Association in their efforts to secure such legislation as will enable the Highland people to live on their native soil under equitable conditions. —The motion, which was seconded by Dr. Clark, and sup- ported by Professor Blackie, was enthusiastically adopted. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

A monthly meeting of this Council was held in the Coun- cil Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Tnere were present-,-The Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Davies and Plckmere, Councillors Ashton, Bolton, Broad- bent, Brown, Burgess, Dakiu, Dixon, Prancomb, Greening, Mackie, Marsh, Monks, Wm. Pietpoint, Sutton, Taylor, Wright, and Tinsley.

THE COUNCIL AND THE LONDON CORPORATION. The MAYOR said he had received a communication from the Lord Mayor of London with regard to the proposed legislation affecting the London Corporation, but before reading it he said he might tell them that the communica- tion was precisely similar to the one read last, when the Council resolved to take no action in the matter. (Hear, hear.) Perhaps they would not care about his troubling them with it now. Dr. Macript : May I ask, Mr. Mayor, whether the Lord Mayor in his anxiety to get our assistance has also remem- bered Warrington in connection with his grand banquet that is to take place next week—(laughter)—whether he has in- vited your worship or whether he has passed us by? The MAYOR: I am afraid I cannot impart any informa- tion on that point. (Laughter.) The subject then dropped for a short time, but later on in the meeting Coanaillor BROADBENT asked if no notice was going to be taken of the Lord Mayor's communication. The MAYOR: Would you like me to read it? Mr. BROADBENT thought it would only be cottleons to the Lord Mayor te inform him that the Council did not feel disposed to take any action in the matter, and he moved to that effect. _
Tite MAYOn seconded this resolution, which was carried.

THE DEATH OF MAJOR CARTWRIGHT. The MAYOR said they were all aware that the flag at the Town Hall was floating half-mast high in consequence of the death of Major Cartwright, who was an ex-mayor and an ex-member of that Council. He (the Mayor) thought it would be very agreeable to the deceased gentleman's family if any of them who thought fit should accompany his remains to the cematery the next day. He was quite sure that'they all very much regretted Major Cartwright's death, particu- larly after the terrible and painful illne.ss under which,, he had been suffering so long; and that their sympathy, if not expressed by resolution, was none the less sincere with Mrs. Cartwright and her family in the loss they had Sus- tained. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BROADBENT thought that under the circumstances a resolution should be adopted with sreference to Major Cart- wright's death, and he thought it would co:ne the best from the Mayor. The MAYOR said he should be very glad indeed to move ," That that Council expressed its deep regret in the first place at the protracted and painful illness under which Major Cartwright had been suffering so long, and also its condolence with Mrs. Cartwright at the loss she has sue- tamed, having regard to the fact that Major Cartwright was once Mayor of Warrington and an active member of that Council, together with the fact that he had filled other public offices of an important character, and rendered the State some service." (Hear, hear.) Alderman %Isms seconded this proposal, which was carried nem. con.

div.head: BAD ROADS.
div.p: BAD ROADS.

Councillor TAYLOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and Mr. Masan seconded. Councillor BROADBENT called the attent;on of the com- mittee to the state of the macadamised roads. These roads, he knew, were in a very bad condition lately owing to the dry weather, but he thought the loose stones ought to be picked off the road. This would not involve very much expense and labour and it would make the road very much safer and batter. It was done in many districts, and he thought it ought to be done in Warrington. Councillor TAYLOR thought it would not be an easy matter to do what Councillor Broadbent suggested. The MAYOR was very glad that Mr. Broadbent had called the attention of the Council to the loose stones on the roads, for anything more uncomfortable and wretched was hardly conceivable than driving over them. New macadamised roads was nothing to what was experienced in going over those loose stones, and he really thought something ought to be done to prevent the nuisance. Councillor Taylor thought it would be a difficult matter to clear the stones away, but he (the Mayor) did net think that would be the case, as anybody could collect them together with a wooden rake. With reference to the street roller, they had a roller—some people used to call it the "demon crusher "—(laughter— that cost about £l5O a few years ago. It was never used, and when he inquired about it some time ago he was told that it was cracked and c mid not be used. He thought it ought Lo be repaired, as it did very good work at one time. and made the roads really pleasant and comfortable to pass over. New they were simply atrocious. The committee's minutes were then confirmed, it being understood that the borough surveyor's attention would be called to the subject under discussion.

div.head: SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: THE SCHOOL OF ART.

The minutes of-t—loa-MO-seu-m and Library Committee were moved by Councillor llnnonss and seconded by Councillor BROADBENT. Dr. MACKIE said there was no committee that he felt more pleasure in attending than the Museum and Library Com- mittee, but circumstances lately had been so that he had been engaged on one committee for the time being of greater consequence to him. Therefore he must apologise for asking a question on a subject he ought to have been familiar with as a member of the committee. Some time ago the question was introduced—he was not sure whether as a suggestion or a proposition—as to whether they, as a Museum Committee could not take some interest in the School of Art. lie forgot how the matter was settled, but it struck him at the present time, from whathe knew of the circumstances connected with it, that probably no better time could be found than the present for at least making some inquiry into the propriety and the practicability of associating the School of Art with the Museum and other institutions. They were all aware that for five and twenty or thirty years the Town Council had been a sort of patron stint to the School of Art. They had done for it what they never did for any other schools in the borough. They had paid in the shape of an allowance something like two-thieds of the rent which the Sc hool of Art would have had to pay. lie had been counting it up—as it was a matter in which he felt no little interest—and he should say that since the School of Art was erected the conditions upon which it was placed by that Council had been equal to at least :cow. And now there was practically no committee in existence, for they had not had an annual meeting for some year or two; they had got a splendid building, and they were, he believed, wishing to re-organise matters, and he thought the Council might do well to consider the question as to whether the School of Art should not be the same as the Baths and Museum, part of their public property. He understood that if a proposal of that kind were carried out it would entgl no extra expense to the borough. As he tad eai I, they had been allowing the School of Art £3O a year, which the premises were worth more than the LIO that was paid, and the arrangements which it was proposed making with teachers in future were such that there would be no claim on the Town‘Council for any payment of salary. All they should have to pay was the doorkeeper's salary. They should probably put some members of the Council upon the committee of management the same as in the case of the Museum, and those gentlemen who had for so many years taken the toil of attending to the School of Art should also be kept on the committee. He had no proposal to make in the matter, but as there were changes quite imminent in connection with the School of Art, and it was very desirable that snob a noble gift as that of Mr. Crosfield should be secured to them in perpetuity—(hear, hear)—and not left to the mere chance of accident—of strange accidents—he thought that if they could, even from that point of view, secure it to the town, they would perpetuate its existence in a more satisfactory manner than they could otherwise do, and they would be gi-ing it all that counten- ance and support which only an incorporated body could give. ' The MAYOR said that the General Purposes Committee took the question into consideration, and decided not to take over the building until it was free of debt; it was not quite clear of debt yet. Councillor MACIHR: It is a mere trifle. The MAYOR said that it was agreed that it was desirable to take over the Institution, and he had no doubt that when the little difficulty to which he had referred was overcome it would be so taken over, and no doubt it would be a very I valuable acquisition to the town.

• ---- . Councillor BROADIBENT said that it was the wish and ex- pectation of many that when the new School of Art was built it would be handed over to the Council, and there was an intention, he thought of that kind among at all events most of the members of the council of the School of Art. Be had certainly all along been very favourable to that course, and he quite expected that when the new building was erected—largely owing to the munificence of Mr. Crostield —that it would eventually result in its being banded over to the municipal body. The matter was more than once brought before the General Purposes Committee, and it was received very coldly by that committee, who feared to take upon themselves, he thought he was expressing fairly the opinion of the committee, the responsibility of the undertaking. and on that account, so to speak, the thing lapsed. The General Purposes Committee showed no anxiety to take the School of Art, and no disposition to grapple with the ques- tion. He feared that it was thought by many that the time for transfer had passed by for the present, but he was entirely of Dr. Mackie's opinion that such an institution would be better in public hands, and certainly Mr. Thompson's desire was that it should be handed over to the munici- pality. Councillor BllnclESs said that he believed that every member of the Corporation would agree as to the desirability of the School of Art being taken over by the Corporation, if it were possible. The real difficulty was a financial one. It was not a large matter, but he thought that it would be sufficiently serious to prevent them from doing it. The Museum Committee was in the position that it could only spend a limited amount of money. Only a one penny rate could he levied for all matters connected with it, and it was quite possible that at that moment or for a year or two, to carry on the School of Art as well as the Museum with a penny rate, but he did not think that it would be likely to be a permanent state of things. Although the present committee—for he thought that he might say that there was a committee in connection with the school—had made certain proposals with regard to their telchers which might make it seem probable that they would not require any money from the Council, except a doorkeeper, he was in- clined to think that if the teachers were in the Council it would soon be found that they would want some different tarrangement. If the Museum Committee could lay another
half-penny rate the whole thing could be done, but he .not think it could be done otherwise.

Councillor MACKIE said that the arrangements wh had hitherto existed, and which existed in all Schools of Ace, he believed, were that the teachers were paid in such away by fees and by share of the Government grant, that they would not come upon the Corporation for assistance. There was every chance, he thought, of their being no pecdniary load upon the Corporation. If instructions were given to the General Purposes or Museum Committee to look into the matter, be had no doubt that they would be able to present a satisfactory report in due time. Councillor BROADBENT : Partly by fixed salaries and partly by fees, I think. The MAYOR then read the minutes in reference to the matter, that were passed when it was last before the Council for discussion, and said that Mr. Owen undertook to furnish the committee with a financial statement as to what would he the probable cost, which he thought had not yet been supplied.

Councillor MACKIE : Any wish from the Council would perhaps expedite the matter. Alderman PICKMEIIE suggested that if the Museum Com- mittee would draw up a report and make some proposal to the General Purposes Committee the question could be thoroughly gone into and come before the Council in a pro- per manner. It having been stated that the six months for which Mr. Owen was requested to furnish a statement had not expired, the matter dropped without further discussion. This was all the business before the Council.

HUYTON. • CONGREGATIONAL CRIIRCH.—The annual collections were made on behalf of the" Liverpool Seamen's Friend Society," and amounted to £lO 12s. The Rev J W Walker, B A (pas- tor), was the preacher. A TROUBLESOME Tnavitume.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Alfred Stott, of Kemble-street, was charged with refusing to deliver up his ticket end assault- ing Ticket-collector Blencow, at Slayton station, on Tues- day night.—He was sentenced to 14 days'lmprisonment. TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATIoN.—The monthly meeting of the Temperance Association wes held in the Huyton Park Schoolroom, en Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. S. Eccles, who gave an address on the Temper- ance Congress recently held in Liverpool. The Rev. J. W. Walker, BA., gave readings; and Mr. J. H. Walker en- livened the proceedings with songs. MIS•ADVENTURE wan Frneenees —As two young men, ironworkers, belonging to Huytons Quarry, named Richard Lyon and John Kilshaw, were amusing themselves with a gun on Friday evening last, the first named was shot in the bead, the weapon having been loaded for the purpoee of kil- ling cats. The injured man was attended by Dr. Packer, who extracted the shot, one having penetrated his eye. Several yet remain in hie neck and face. ROBY Cnnacx.—The annual excursion of the church choir took place on Saturday. It was provided by the kind- ness of Mr A M Smith, of Bolton Hey, who is this year one of the churchwardens. It is a commendable feature of the relations between employer and employed that he gives his employees, to the number of about 400 an annual trip to some holiday resort. This year the place chosen was Chats- worth. The Roby church choir were also invited to join, and an omnibus was provided to take them to the Central station, Liverpool, whence the excursion train started. They were favoured with splendid weather, enabling the party to enjoy the outing which was thoteughly appreciate., CAUTION TO BICYCLISTS.—A.t the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before T Earle, Esq, Williaai Biford, an assis- tant stationer at the Old Swan, was summoned for riding his bicycle without a lighted lamp at Huvton.—The defen- dant: I had a lamp but it was not lighted.—Mr Earle: Why not ?—Defendant: It was not dark.—Mr Earle: What time was it?—? C Edgar: It was half-past nine o'clock on the night of the 21st June.—Superintendent Barker: It was sunset at 20 minutes past eight on that night. —Mr Earle: What is the law, is it "after sunset "?—The Clerk: Yes sir.—The defendant: Well it was not dark.—The Chair- man: You must underetand that in future you must have it lighted after sunset whether it is dark or not. We will let • you off this time.—Defendant: Thank you. CLAIM AGAINST AN IRONWORKS COMPLNY.—At a special sitting of the St. Helens County Court, on Friday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson and a special jury, an action was brought by Mr. John Forster, engineer and boiler-maker, St. Helens, to r, cover from Messrs. Maybury, Marson, and Sharpe, proprietors of the ironworks at Hayton Quarry, the sum of £5O for work done and materials supplied; £42 10s being for repairs, as ordered by one of the defend- awe, on behalf of his firm, to a certain boiler at the works, a further sum of £7 103 being charged for supplying a new top half of front to the same, making two new flues or fire- boxes. and extra work not mentioned in the agreement. On the other hand defendants had a counter claim against the pleintiff for £5O, which, however, had been reduced to £43 3s 93, for damages for breach of contract, elleginginfe- rior workmanship, ending in the collapse of the boiler. Mr. T. Swift. B.L. (instructed by Messrs. JO. and W. Swift), . appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Stewart, 8.L., defended. —Mr. Swift, who proposed to aitswer the counter claim after his client's plaint had been heard, said he should be able to prove that the alleged damage arose from ether - ciuses, the boiler being an old one and defective at the ti'me it was purchased by the defendants; further, thet it was not allowed to be properly tested by the latter after the com- pletion of the repairs, and that the boiler was not properly treated.—After hearing a portion of the evidence the case was adjourned. HUTTON-WITH-ROBY LOCAL BOLIID.—The usual monthly - meeting of the above was held on Tuesday, at the Public Offices, Blacklow Brow. Mr. Cooper was in the chair, and there were also present—Messrs. Burnyeate, Sidderley„ Banner, Parker, and Grimshaw ; Swift (clerk), and Worrell (surveyor).—The minutes of the several committees having been read and passed, the Chairman asked for the medical officer's report, but none had been received.—Mr. Parker wished to know bow often the officer attended the Board meeting.—The answer not being satisfactory he moved, and Mr. Grimshaw seconded, a motion that the clerk write to request the medical officer to attend the monthly meeting of the Board. Carried ' • all voting except Mr. Banner.—A letter was read which had been received from the Local Go- vernment Board, drawing toe attention of the sanitary au- thorities to the "Food and Drugs " Act; and asking what steps were taken in the district for carryinK it out—The Clerk believed the police had had cases under the Act.—Me. Grimshaw proposed, and Mr. Parker seconded, a motion that the clerk write to Mr. Barker, superintendent of police. requesting him to take samples of fool, drink, and drugs from this neighbourhood for public analysis, in accordance with the Act. Carried unanitneuely.—During the discussion the Medical Officer (Dr. Hall) entered and /submitted his report, showing the neighbourhood to be in a healthy state : Four deaths for Huyton ; none for Huyton Quarry or Roby. —A letter was read from Mr. Shipley, of Heywood Bank, Liverpool, the newly•appeinted treasurer to the Board, acknowledging the apuointment. The Clerk also pro- duced the bond of security for £l,OOO signed and completed. —A letter from Mr. S. Worthington, ot the London and North-Western Railway Co., was read in reply to a com- munication from the chairman, stating that the directors had decided to carry out the proposed improvements on the south side of Huyten Station. TEE THREE-CARD.TRICE ON THE RAILWAY.—At the. Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Henry Beetock, a young man, of unsettled residence, was charged with playing the three-card-trick on the London and North-Western Railway on Saturday.—Supt. Barker stated that he had been in com- munication with the rairway authorities, and asked them to conduct the prosecution, but as no one appeared to do so he (Supt. Barker) did not feel inclined to prosecute. He might add that the witnesses were present who gave the prisoner into custody, and he thought the railway company ought to have conducted the prosecution on public grounds.—Mr. Geskell, J.P. : Are you under the impression that there should be a miscarriage of justice because they do not come? —Supt. Barker : The offence really occurs on private pro- perty.—Mr. Gaskell : Have you all the witnesses here ? Supt. Barker: Yes, sir; and if the Bench chooses to go On with the case I can put them in the box.—The Chairman (Mr. Earle): Can we prosecute this man for doing it on pri- vate property P—Mr. Spencely (clerk) : The railway and carriages are a public highway —The Ceairman : Weil then go on with the case.—The evidence was to the effect that Henry Horrocks, John Prescott, and James Prescott, all of Bedford Leigh, left Lime-street Station by the 11-15 train on Saturday night, Shortly after they mitered the carriage in which they rode, the prisoner and another man got in. The prisoner commenced to play the three-card-trick, and Horrocks lost is., but when the latter was successful the p•isoner refused to pay. At Flnyton Station the prisoner and his friend attempted to escape, but the prisoner was cap- tured and he was given into custody.—P.C. Cameron stated money.—Supt. a etly Jackson sisimilar that whhen be searched the prisoner he found in hie posses- sion seven cards, a pedlar's certificate, a counterfeit half- si no v emr eoingeny i lea? et do that o e rthe g counterfeitn,and s 7d. in some passed at Tarbock races.—The prisoner was committed to prison for three months.
On Tuesday, at Somerset Quarter Sessions, Capt. Alison, Deputy Chief-Constable of Lancashire, was elected Chief - Constable of So nersetshire in the room of Mr. Gooid, re- signed.

A town's meeting will be held at Northampton next Wed- nesday to hear Mr Bradlaugh, Si P, and to consider certain resolutions arisino: on the verdict of Mondfy. Mr Brad- laugh at that meeting will submit the question to his coa- -1 stiluents of retaining the seat. MOODY AND ,JA AKEY'S Mrsstorr.—A spacious hall, to the cost of which Mr Samuel Morley contributed £5OO, was opened on Monday by the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion, Bristol, by whom it has been built in commemoration of the visit of Messrs Moody and Sankey and the work which they were the means of accomplishing in Bristol. it sf which nearly £l,OOO, thereby clearing debt, ;as raised at the opening ceremony. Mr ihta of f costthe " Moody took part in the proceerlin;s. A MIDNIGHT FLITTING.—TtIO/1189 Honitram Was sum- moned at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, for re- ying his goods to avoid a distraint of rent.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the complainant, Mr. George Hatctiman,, of Huyton. The defendant had occupied the house, 2, Crook-street, Eccleston, and got in arrears with the rent to an amount between £2 and £3. On the oth June the de- fendant paid the rent for one week and promised a sum to- wards the arrears in the week following. But when the complainant went for the money the defendant had left the house, left no address, and had left the key hanging to a nail in the house. The windows had been plastered over with newspapers in order to prevent discover3i as long as pos- sible...-The Bench made an order for the payment of double • the value of goods removed (4110 s and costs.

THE EXAMINER; SATURDAY, JULY 5, 1884.

THE Lords have at last "screwed their courage to the sticking-place," and deter- mined upon the rejection of the Franchise Bill. A meeting of Conservative Peers was held 9n Tuesday, at the London residence of Lord SALisetritv, at which it was finally re- solved that the desperate deed should be done; and in the evening the matter was !placed beyond doubt by Earl CAIRNS giving notice of motion for Monday next, which is the day fixed by the Government for the second reading of the bill. The motion, i which s curiously involved, means, to put it in plain terms, that the House of Lords is to be asked to reject the Franchise Bill because it is not accompanied by a Redistribution scheme. Any excuse is better than none, and having made up their minds that the bill must go to the wall, it is an easy thing to take up the cry, raised by the Conservatives in the House of Commons. It is nothing, of course, to the purpose that the Government have de- monstrated the impossibility of carrying through a bill combining an Extension of the Franchise and a Redistribution of Seats, or that they are pledged to bring in next session a bill dealing with redistribution. It is sufficient that the Conservative Peers detest what Councillor FRANCOMB characteristically styled "the humbugging Franchise Bill," and, hating it as they do, they probably think they need not trouble themselves to be con- sistent in the reasons they give for strangling it. We may take it for granted that they will succeed in throwing the bill out on the • second reading, for the Tories are all-powerful in the House of Lords; and the question will then arise amongst the Liberals—What is to be done? If the PRIME MINISTER were to follow his impulse, he would imme- diately accept Lord SALISBURY'S challenge and instantly appeal to the country. But this would be playing the game of the Conserva- tives, who are feverishly anxious for a disso- lution, and we do not see that the Liberals are called upon to do that. The present Administration have been appointed to carry out a definite policy and to accomplish cer- tain reforms, and it is their duty to do the best they can to accomplish the tasks they have in hand. Reform Bill or no Reform Bill, it would be a calamity for the country if there were to be a dissolution while the financial and general affairs of Egypt are under consideration, by the European Powers, and on the point of settlement. The Afghan campaign was a strain upon India and upon this country, but it would be a small matter as compared with what would happen if the attempt were made to annex Egypt and re-con- quer the Soudan. Then there is the question of the Franchise Bill itself. Lord SALISBURY might go the length of rejecting it once, and he might turn tail when it was presented to him a second time. He has a good deal of fight in him, but his valour, like that of "Bon ACRES " in "The Rivals," has a way at times of "oozing out as it were at the palms of his hands." Assuming the re- jection of the bill during the present seAsion, the wisest course for the Government to take would be to. call Parliament together again in the autumn, and re-present the measure to

WARRINGTON, thanks mainly to the muni- ficence of Mr. JOHN CROSFIRLD, is in pos- session of a splendid School of Art; but somehow matters- in connection with it are not going on splendidly. The Committee have been engaged with a scheme of re- organisation ; but the new scheme cannot be said to be making a good start, seeing that it has led to the resignation of Mr. ; Tnompsorr, the head-master, who has been the life and soul of the institution for nearly 30 years. It is not for us to say where the fault lies, or that fault is to be found with ' anybody, but it would seem there has been some lack of management on the part of the Managing Committee, or they would , not have placed themselves in such an awk- ward position as to find that when they de- sired to retain the services of Mr THOMPSON they were unable to do SD. There is ton, much friction just at present for the ma- chinery to work well, and it would be no worse, perhaps, if it were completely, overhauled. It is getting well on in a; second year since_ there was an "annual meeting ; " and the Committee are there- , fore practically continuing in office with- ' out the full warrant of the body ori- ginally appointing them. A meeting of subscribers ought to be held at least once a I year, when officers and committee may he appointed, and matters discussed with a ' view to furthering the interests of the institu- tion. In the present case, there is special I need for holding such a meeting, for, apart from the hitch in the arrangement with Mr. THomPsort, the question of the School being taken over by the Corporation has again been under the consideration of the Town Coun- cil. The subject was brought before the members at the monthly meeting on Tues- day, and it seemed to be the general opinion that nothing stood in the way except the small debt in which, the Committee are in- volved. As this was not more, we under- stand, than about two hundred pounds, there should be no difficulty in wiping it off ; and what a feather it would be in the cap of the Committee to be able to say they had handed over to the Corporation, free from debt, a handsome building worth- some thousands of pounds. Care would of course require to be taken by the Town Council that the School of Art should not become a drag on the Library rate. The general rates could not be touched for its support, and as the Library rate cannot exceed one, penny in the pound, it would hardly be fair to reduce it to any considerable extent by subventions from it to the Art School. Government contributes liberally to the support of schools. of this class, and the annual grant, with the fees of pupils, should enable the school to, pay its way. The advantages of Corporate control are that the business would be mere publicly conducted, and there would thus be less liability, to mistake and misapprehension. As an institution, the School would gain in dignity and importance,- and, more than, all, a wider and deeper interest would be taken in it by the mass of the people. It is due to the Committee to say that they are willing to take shelter under the Corporate wing, and subject themselves of course to- Corporate control. The time is opportune, and, all things considered, " twere well it were done quickly,"

WE desire to direct the attention or our readers to a copy, in another column, of cor- respondence which has taken place between the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON and Mr. W. CROSFIELD, the Liberal candidate for War- rington, on the question of Disestablishment and Disendowment. Mr. CARLETON set the ball rolling with an air of innocence whih is refreshingly cool this hot weather He says Mr. CROSFIELD'S views would materially

icaoffnecsttittuheents at the next e attitude of ealargleectonni. umbeffritrpoflytinh; that he and others are ready to vote for the Liberal candidate, if he is of their way of thinking on Church questions. There are Churchmen of this class, but we are much Mistaken if the VICAIK of Holy Trinity is of them. Perhaps he will tell us, as he is about to "express his views," whether he would desert Sir GILBERT GRvENALL and vote for Mr. CROSFIELD if the latter were pledged to sup- pori the present connection between Church and State. If not, we should take it that his "attitude" is indeed "affected." Mr, GROS- FIELD thrust his pen throught the weak place in Mr. CARLETON'3 letter by suggesting-- " kinder sarcastic," as ARTEMUS WAEXP would say—that, as the Vicar asks only about- Disendowment, there is substantial agree- ment between them as to Disestablishment, Conscious of his blunder, Mr. CARLETON., inr his next letter, makes "confusion worse con- founded " by saying he spoke only of Dl5 endowment because, "apart from that," manr Nonconformists have "not a clear conception' of Disestablishment ; that is-to say this clear -- minded ecclesiastic gets into a fog in order to accommodate himself to others wbo are similarly situated. But the fog set-ms to have irritated him, for he proceeds to use bad language, describing something a•" ne- farious," which is, we suppose, the Vicar's substitute for " swearing." However, as to this we must point out that the word against which Mr. CROSFtELD justly. protests has mysteriously disappeared from the copy of the correspondence Mr. CARLETON has supplied to the press. Can it be that,he has,repen" ted him of its use, or has it been struck out as something too shocking oven for the " Printer's devil ?" Mr. CROSFIELD very I properly showed the Vicar the door on ,finding that he indulged in rant and misrepre- sentation. One must draw the line some- where, for "evil communications corrupt good manners."

STREET ACCIDENT AT RONCORN.—About noon on Satur- flay, Lily Hulme, five years, the daughter of Win. Hulme, of Halton-road, was knocked down by a conveyance belong- ing to Mr. Wm Hankinson,and driven by John Aspey. One of the wheels of the cart passed over the child's left shoul- der and the side of its face. Mr. Robert Wright, who was Passing at the time, picked the child up and took it home, where Dr. McDougall attended to its injuries, which were not of a very serious character. ButiNswics WESLEYAN SNNDLY Scuoore—The annual services in aid of this school were held in St. Paul's Wes- leyan Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday last. The pulpit was awarded both morning and evening by the Rev W J Daw- son, of London, and his reputation as an orator drew to- gether a crowded congregation on each occasion. A third service was also held on Monday evening when the sacred edifice was again well filled. The choir, aided by the scholars, rendered hymns specially selected in a most praise- worthy manner. Mr G S flazlebu,st was at the organ. COURAGEOUS BEBAVEOTIR AT RUNCORN.—Late on Friday night, last week, a picnic party alighted from a conveyance at the approach to Runcorn Bridge. The animal became restive, aud overpowering the boy attempted to ruts away, but Samuel Walker, a young man who is employed on the bridge, seized the horse's head, and in spite of its rearing and kicking maintained his hold, ultimately ptcifying the terrified animal. The vehicle narrowly escaped being over- turned, and was brought in contact with the ticket office with considerahle violence. As there wets many people in the street, had the animal not been seized by Walker, serious damage would have been done. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY Ca:unix-rex —The monthly meeting was held on "thursday. Mr Briscoe presided, and there were present Messrs. Lake, Riley, and Jones (libra- rian.) The Librarian's report showed that 576 books had been read or consulted in the reference department and bor- rowed from the lending library ; an increase of three OR the corresponding, month last year, classified as follows: Theology 7. philosophy, political economy, law. dtc., 4, history, travels, and biography 59, science and art 19, poetry and the drama 5, prose fiction 460, miscellaneous 22.—0 n the recommendation of the Book Selectien Committee it was decided to supply the reading room with the following papers :—Daily itieir3, Standard, Liverpool Post, and Liver- pool Courier. On Friday morning, at the Manchester County Police Court, before Sir John Iles Mantell, a boatman, named Richard Draper, of Runcorn, Was brought up on a charge of working a horse whilst in an unfit state on the canal bank at Barton, about five o'clock on Friday inornine.—P.C. Bannister stated that about the time mentioned lie was on duty on the canal bank at Barton, when he saw the prisoner working a horse, which was drawing a large barge with 50 tons of "slack." He had the horse examined by a veterinary surgeon, who stated that the animal was in a very poor and weak condition, and totally unfit to work --Sir John remerkrd that it was a most brutal case of inhumanity to work the animal in such a con- dition, and, as cases of a similar character repeatedly came before him, be had determined to send them to prison with- out the option of a fine. The prisoner would have to go to prison for one month with hard labour. DTSEICNESC LODGERS AT HALE. —At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, &WTI; Thompscen, the wife of a platelayer, was charged with steeling a pair of blan- kets, value 12s, the property of George Fairclough, Mersey View, Hale 'Bank. From the statement of Inspector Wood, it appeared that the prisoner and her husband had been lodging with the prosecutor for about a Week. Between ten and eleven o'clock on Saturday morn- ing the prisoner went into her bedroom and shortly after- wards left the house with a bundle in her possession. Mrs. Fairclough having her suspicions aroused, examined the bedroom and missed two blankets. Information was given to the police and a constable discovered that the prisoner had, in the name of Hughes. pledged the blankets at Mrs. Jameson's for 35.—The prisoner pleaded guilty. She said she was pressed for money at the time, and she took the blankets with the intention of returning them the same evening.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's bard labour. BATHING FATALITY AT WIDNES —gn Thursday about DOOR James Mooney, 12 years of age, son of William Mooney, labourer, 34, Nelson-street, Widnes, was drowned in the Mersey. It appears that Mooney and several school fellows went on Caerdley Marsh to play. Mooney, although warned not to do so by his companions, commenced to bathe in the river, and be had not been in the water long before getting beyond his depth, he sank. One of the boys on the bank ran to obtain aid, and a man he met on the way refused to go to the spot, because he could not swim. After Mooney had sank for the last time, William ,Joseph Murray, a youth, residing at 17. Hutchinson-street, arrived on the scene, and imnpdiately divesting himself of his clothing. he plunged into the water and brought the drowning boy to the bank. There were the faintest indications of life in the unconscious body of Mooney, but before any remedy could be applied, be died. Information was conveyed to Constables Murray and Lamb, who conveyed the body to Ihe house of the deceased's parents. ORANGE BALL AT, WIDNES —On Monday night the first annual ball in connection with the local lodges of Orangemen took place in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes. The object of the gathering was to promote social intercourse between the members of the "Invincible" L.O.L , Ne. 429, and the " Beaconsfield Protestant Boys" No, 23, but the success of the gathering did not reach the anticipations of the promoters, only about a hundred couples being present. The hall had been decorated with flags and bunting, the orange colour, of course, predominating, the long silken banner of the Invincible Lodge depending from the centre of the ceiling. - A string band under the direction of Mr. Hawkins supplied the music, and dancing was spiritedly engaged in until two o'clock on Tuesday morning. Bro. P. Davies officiated as M.C., while the duties of secretary were undertaken by Bro. J. Hurst, the committee superin- tending the arrangements, cansisting of Bros. Davies, Ward, Bingham, Joseph Ford, jaa., A. Burgess, and T. Smith. The decorations were the work of Bros. Ford, Hurst, and Ward. Befreetanents were supplied by Mr. and Mrs. Gerrard, of the Alexandra Hotel, Victoria road. THB CIIBSTER AND CONNAR'S QUAY RAILWAY BILL.— Tait PREAMBLE PROVED. The Chester and Connah's Quay Railway Bill passed the Select Committee of the Lords yesterday week, after Mr. Grierson had been called for the Great Western, and Mr. Peinber, QC, had replied for that company. The committee, without calling on the promoters for a reply, declared the preamble of the bill proved. The committee decided that clause 5 should be so modified as (while ietainine the principles of a low-level bridge, with a headway of 15 feet) to leave all the details of construction to the Board of Trade. The time occupied bY Lord Camperdown's Committee on the bill was only one- third of the time consumed by the enquiry in the Commons. The decision of the committee was communicated in the course of the evening, to the Prime Miaister and Mr. Her- bert Gladstone, be both of whom it was received with the greatest satisfaction. It will be remembered that Mr. Glad- stone was to have given evidence for the promoters before the Commone' Committee, but was prevented by his illness. When the news reached Wrexham in the evening great satisfaction was expressed on all sides, and the rejoicing was general. The church bells rang out merry peals ; blasts loud and long, if somewhat nnamscal, were blown upon locomotive whistles and detonators were exploded on the Wrexham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway by hundred& The hope is now expressed that the work of constructing the bridge and railway will be promptly and energetically pushed on. ' EXCURSION rgoot WIDNES TO CAIVARVON.—FOr a period of about 17 years Messrs. Gossage and ion have annually provided an excursion to some interesting locality for their workpeople, and as the years have rolled on the trip has become more popular. Carnarvon was the place selected by the men for this year's holiday, and en Saturday morning, at half-past six, twelve hundred persons left Widnes in two trains of twenty carriages for the North Wales watering place. The trains streamed through dome of the loveliest scenery in the Principality, and the journey was accom- plished in good time. Each adult workman in addition to receiving two tickets for the excursion, was given Is GI to aid him in enjoying his outing, while the boys received the ticket and a shilling. The chief attraction of Carnarvon is its ancient castle, where at least one Prince of Wales first saw the light, and the trippers by virtue of an arrangement made with teir Llewellyn Turner, the Deputy Constable, Were admitted to explore its emaint sorridors and dark tur- rets at the reduced charge of 21 each. The other pleasures within the retch of the vi,itors were a sail on the blue waters of the straits, a walk through the interesting old town, or a drive through the lanes lined on each side with noble trees whose umbrageous branches meeting in the centre formed a leafy arcade, to some village in the vicinity; but large numbers of excursioniste, disappointed with the place, were returning to the railway station by four o'clock, although the trains did not start on the return journey until 6.30 p.m. The renirn journey was safely accomplished, Wid- nes being reached about eleven o'clock. The excursion was in charge of Inspector Carter, of Widnes, the whole of the arrangements being superintended by Mr. Thorpe and Mr. R. Balmer. Mr. Hartland, the respected manager of the works, who no to the present time has never failed to ac- company the excursion was on the present occasion absent through physical infirmitiee, and regret was universally ex- Pressed at the event.

Sufi-PORTS or LlvEgasoote—We understand that in con- formity with the Customs regulations the following five ports were abolished from Tuesday—namely, Preston, Fleet- wood, Chester, Mcietyn, and Runcorn, and are to be considered henceforth as stib•ports of the port of Liverpool. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR CHESHIRE. The following gentlemen have been nominated by His Grace the Duke of Westminster, Lerd-Lieutenant of Cheshire, for the county magistracy :—Mc Stanton Eddowes, West Kirby; Mr Thompson Mane, Tarporley ; elrJoseph Leigh, Brinning- ton Hall, Stockport; Mr. David Meet ure, Heaton Mersey ; Mr Hallam Ronailey, Stockport; Mr A. Solley, Congletun ; and Mr Anthony Shaw, Congleton. STOCK SALE AT FRODSFIAM —Messrs. John Mainwarinir and Co,, stock salesmen, Warrington, held their usual fort- nightly stock sole at the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodsham, on Tuesday. There was a numerous attendance of buyers from Warriugtorn, Runcorn, Chester, and the district, and the bidding was spirited. The entry included 125 fat sheep and lambs, 12 fat and store beasts, calves., dm. and the prices realized at the previous fortnightly sales were fully maintained. MAIN OF BOWLS AT RUNCOI2IC-01 Thursday a main of bowls, open to all England, was played on the ground of the Runcorn Bowling Club, Bridge Hotel, Ashridge- street. The entries numbered 56. and some very good sport WAS witnessed by the numerous spectators. The first three prizes were divided between Bennion (Pendleton), Johnson (Fidler's Ferry), and Stone (Widnes). This division had to take place in consequence of darkness setting in before the gains was finished. PROPOSED POLITICAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN . The heads of the Liberal peas/ in Runcorn are contempla- ting a monstre demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill, in consequence of • the pending conflict between the Commons and the Lords. No definite proposal has yet been suggested to or decided upen by the Liberal commit- tee but it is highly probable that the demonstration will take the form of a huge parade through the streets of the town to Runcorn Hill, where a meeting should be held and addressed by several prominent politicians. WIDNES COUNCIL O'IF EDUCATION AND FARNWORTH GRAMMAR Scnoor...—The Widnee C iuncil of Education have intimated that they will make the following grants in connection with the free scholarships that have been founded at Varnworth Grammar School :—(1) A sum not exceeding twenty shillings per annum will be paid to the head master of the Grammar School for books and school requisites for each boy living within the township of Widnee and holding a scholarship. (2) On being setiefied that assistance is needed, fifteen shillings per month will be paid to the parents or guardians Of each boy living within the township of Widnes and holding a scholarship to assiet in his main- tenance and clothing. Application for this grant must be made to the honorary secretary of the council by the parents or guardians. The first award will be made A boys success- ful at the examination to be held in September next. The council reserves the right of withdrawing or varying these grants; but no boy having gained them will be deprived of the first during the period of his scholarship, nor of the second unless the council is satiefied that it is no longer needed. RUNCORN CASES AT KNUTSFORD SESSIONS.—At Knutsford Sessions, on Thursday, Nathaniel. Boswell, 60, grinder, and John Lewis, aged 10, stepson, were charged with stealing a purse and the sum of 19a the monies and property of Annie Basnett, at Runcorn, on the 10th May; and they were fur- ther charged with feloniously receiving the same, well knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. E. El. Lloyd prose- cuted; the prisoners were undefended.—Boswell was sen- tenced to six months' hard labour, and Lewis to one month, to be followed by seven years' detention in a reformatory. ---Thomas Threlfall, 16, boatman, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment for stealing 10lbs. of rope, four yards of oilcloth, and one boat-hook, the property of George Clay, at Ruucorn, on the 16th May.-- Henry Watkin, of Halton, on bail. was charged with stealing ard leading away a horse, the property of John Riggs Wooer, coal owner, Ludwig-street, Antield, Liverpool.-Mr Burke Wood prosecuted, and Mr Marshall defended.—The prose- cution alleged that Watkin bought the horse and never in- tended paying for it as was evidenced by the way the animal was taken about the country, and the way the prosecutor was put off from time to time by premises of money. It having come out in evidence that the prosecu- tor accepted an I 0 U from the prisoner the jury considered there was no case for them to try, and acquitted the prisoner.

or temporary.—The Medical Officer reported that in Back Cooper-street he found four of the houses (un- occupied) in a most disgusting state of dilapidation, hardly a pine of glass in the windows, the sills broken off, and the doors damaged, the ashpits full, the Sewage grids blocked, and the whole place filthy in the extreme! In Zion-place he found sewage grids blocked, the closet accommodation unsatisfactory, sii privies for eighteen houses, the houses without proper means of ventilation, there being no win- dows at the back, and the privies within a short distance from the front of the houses.—The Surveyor reported that the complaints of the medical officer with reference to the property in Back Cooper-street could be dealt with under the Nuisance. Remove. Act, that notice should be served upon the owner to repair the dilapidated privies, to put in order the drains and pavement, and either repair the unoc- cupied houses, or cleans) them out and board up the doors and windows to prevent them being mede into receptacles of filth. The houses in Zion-place are built in, or on the mar- gin of an old quarry on so low a level that they are beyond the reach of drainage except by some special arrangement. The presentsystem of drainage is into a ceespool, which to some extent makes itself away into the old quarry, but has to be emptied from time to time; the drains are now choked up; the privy accommodation was augmented some years ago, and was at that time considered sufficient. The venti- lation is difficult, there being no place for back windows, but he thought seine airshafts might be inserted in the roofs; he also reported that the nuisances in the brick-field off Bold-screetsheve been abated. It was resolved that the secretary furnish Mr. Lightburn with copies of the reports of the medical officer and the surveyor on the insanitary condition of the property in Back Cooper-street, and to ask him to state before the tfleeting of the Board on Wednesday next; what is proposed to be done to pnt the property in a proper sanitary condition; and that notice be served on the owner of the property in Zion-place ti cleanse and repair the sewers. A letter was reed from Mr. J. F. Killcross stat- ing that the proposed shed in Heath-road is intended to be a temporary structure, and asking to be informed when he can be allowed to go on with it. Consideration of letter ad- journed. Plans recommended for approval : Kitchen at No. 9, Bold-street, for Mrs. Anderton; six houses in Parker- street for Mr. W. Nixon ; alterations to shop property in Church and King-str-ets for Mr. I. Bowyer.—Mr. Norman moved the confirmation of the minutes, and observed that Mr. Cliffe had been doing his work better since the commit- tee had met.—Mr. seconded the motion, which was carried. The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con- tained a tender from Mr. R. Hampson, to repair the street lamps for a period of three or five years from September let next, at £26 for the first year, and an advance of £1 each succeeding year. Recommendation that Mr. Hampsone tender to repair the lamps for a period of five years be ac- cepted. Resolution appointing a sub-committee, consisting of Messrs. Dobson, Briscoe, Fairhurst, and Norman, to con- ' elder and report upon the Fire Brigade organisetion and charges. Recommendation that the Market Inspector be al- lowed fourteen days' leave of absence.—Mr. P. Kelly the prisoner was fined 10s and costs, 15s. DRUNKENNESS AT WIDNES.— Mr H Gaskell and Mr J. Brock at the Widnes Police Court on Monday inflicted the followingvenalties for drunkenness :—Hugh Kennell; 5s and costs; Peter Gaffiney, 58 and costs, or 7 days; Sarah Riley, Sc and costs; William Mack, 5s and costs; Patrick McGee, 5s and costs; Charles Large, 58 and costs; Thomas Gray- lish, Sc and costs; John Mannion, 5e and costs; Ann Kelly. 53 and costs; Rebecca McDonotagb,ss and costs; Edward Morgan, 58 and Costs; and Henry Munaford, fis and costs; Catherine Carey, who made her 14th appearance, was fined ICH and costs. MEETING OF PRIMITIVE METHODISTS AT OVERTON.— The first annual meeting of Primitive Methodists in the Preston Brook Circuit was held on Wednesday afternoon, at Mersey View pleasure grounds, Overton, and there was a good gathering assembled from all ports of the circuit, and other places. A public tea was provided at four o'clock, and a meeting watafterwarde held, when the Rev. J. Pickwell, superintendent of the circuit presided. Addresses were de- livered by the chairman, Rev. L. Miles, Frodshana, Mr. Jos. Spruce, Preston Brook, Mr. T. Sprucefellow, Runcorn, and Mr. Davies, Manchester. The united choirs rendered effi- cient service in singing a selection of sacred music, accom- panied on the harmonium by Mr. James Hough, of Prod- sham. GOOD TEmPIARISM AT WIDNES.—The weekly meeting of the Widnes Samaritan Lodge was held at 96, Victoria road, on Monday evening, when there was a good atten- dance, and two friends were proposed for membership. During etre eveeing an excellent tea was provided by the sisters, and an entertainment followed. At the weekly meeting of. the Haste to the Rescue Lodge, on Tuesday evening, a Candidate WAS initiated and two propesed for membership. The committee having had charge of Hi, Southport trip, with a few friends, sat down to a supper pro- vided by Mr. R. Petitt, of Waterloo-road. A pleasant even- ing Was afterwards apent. On Wednesday evening the Star of Widnes Lodge held their weekly meeting. Two candi- dates were initiated and four proposed. A musical entetein- ment was gone through. WIDNES C E.T.S.—In connec'ion with this society an opeu-air meeting WAS held on Thursday evening. The mem- bers assembled in the National schools, and having been formed into processional order; proceeded. headed by the society's band, to the vacant spice of land at St. Paul's Church. To a large assemblage of people the Rev. J. Wright Williams and the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson delivered ad- dresses. The vicar announced, amid the cheers of the au- dience, that Mr. T. S. Timinis, chairman of the School Board, had promised to defray the cest of erecting a boun- dary wall round St. Paul's Church, and a Widnes contrac- tor had been engaged to do the work. At the call of the Chairman three cheers were heartily given for Mr Timmis. Subsequently an entertainment was given in the school- room, and at the close several pledges were made. SHOOTING MATCH AT RUNCORN. A shooting match took place at the Runcorn Rifle Range on Saturday between F and G Companies, Earl of Chester's Rifles (2nd C RN.), seven rounds being fire at 200, 500. and 600 yards; Wimbledon targets and scoring, regulation position. Great interest was shown in the match, as there has been several attempt in former years to get up a separ- ate team for each company. This year it has been taken up by the officers of the detachment, who have succeeded in bringing forward the above match, the result being a victory for G Company. After the match both teams sat down to an excellent tea provided by Colour-Sergeant 11. Coward, the remainder of the evening being spent in a social mannet. The following is a list of the competitors and cores:

WARRINGTON BOROUGH. POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—There were no cases down for hearing. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair. Mr. John Fairctough, and Alderman Davies. DRUNYENNESS.—Peter Thompson. for being drunk in Hill. street. on Saturday, was fined 55, including costs; and Emma Howard, for being drunk and disorderly on the same day, was lined 5s and costs, or seven days.—Patrick Hoarty. for being drunk and disorderly in Naylor-street, on the 20th Met, was fined 55 and costs. or seven days; and John Hoarty. his brother, was similarly dealt with for being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street, on the same day.—The follow- ing were also lined for drunkenness. viz.:—Mark McGann, ss, including costs; Williana Caveney, 5s and costs; Thomas Tickle and Emma Lee. 5s and costs each; Jane Lee, Sarah Ann Lee, and John Bail, 5s and costs each; Ann Luffy and Ellen Roberts, ss, including costs. BrONE-THROWISG.—George Tilling, a boy, was fined 2s ed for throwing stones on the 22nd inst. BREACHES OF THE PEACE —Mary Cokeley, Elizabeth Bow- yer. John Hoyles, William Hambiett, Letitia Ellis, and Emily Richardson were all charged with committing breaches of the peace by fighting, and were bound over to be of good be- haviour. MOYnay.—Before Messrs. 11. Reynolds and A. Thomas. FURIOUS DRIVING.—John Carter, a young man, was charged with furiously driving a horse and cart in Greenway.road.— P.O. Kelly said about six o'clock on Thursday ev ning jut he saw the defendant furiously driving a horse and cart up Green- way-road. Two or three People were nearly run over. The horse was not galloping, but the defendant was thrashing it with a whip.—Mr. Kitchen, who appeared for the defendant, said the horse had made a refusal, and the wh;p was a, plied to it as punishment for this behaviour. The animal then started off at a good rate, but the defendant had full control over It. He left the case entirely in their worships' hands.— Mr. Reynolds said they could not look over this case as the lives of several people were endangered —The defendant was fined 10s and costs us 6d. Tat NEW ASYLUM.-At a meeting of county magistrates at the Livetpool Quarter Sessions, yesterday week, mort- gages of the county rates for several sums of money, amounting in the whole to £25,848, were approved for the asylum at Rainhill. RAINEILL ASYLUM—TiIe inmates of this institution were trelted to their annual pie-nic on Tuesday, when nearly 250 of them were conveyed in wagonettes to Knowsley Park. Dancing was sreely indulged in to the strains of the asylum band, and other amusements were afforded.

div.head: ATHLETIC SPORTS.
div.p: ATHLETIC SPORTS.

The annual sports in connection with the Rainhill Ath- letic Club, took place on Saturday afternoon, in brilliant weather, and in the presence of a large number of spectators from Rainhill and the towns and villages adjacent. Prizes to the value of nearly £lOO were competed for, and the arrangements gave perfect satisfaction, everything being conducted as laid down in the programme of events, and due attention being paid to the proper and expeditious post- ing of the winning numbers—a duty which is sometimes a little neglected. A band was in attendance, and on the con- clasion of the sports, the prizes were distributed by the Mayoress of St. Helens, Mrs. Baxter. The following acted as officials in a very competent and courteous manner:— Judges, Rey J Barton and Messrs H W Collins and J Tickle; referee, Mr W Lowe; starter, Mr J Little; clerk of the course. On the conlusion of the sports the prizes were distributed to the successful competitors by Mrs. Baxter, Mayoress of St. Helens, in introducing whom the Rev. Mr. Baxter said that it was necessary to say only a very few words in re- ference to a lady who was so very well known as was Mrs. Baxter—the wife of a gentleman who was known and re- spected by them all—(hear, hear)--and he was glad that she had sanctioned the sports by her presence. He wished that a larger number of the gentry of Rainhill had been present, as he thought it was a duty upon them all to encourage such meetings. Some people shrank hem them because of what was called the " rough element," which was, after all, only human nature with a little superficial difference. Those in a good position had various means of enjoyment, but working people had but few, and a meeting like that was, as it ought to be, one of them. (Applause.) He was entirely antagonistic to skrinking from the " rough element," which he thought was not calculated to do the working classes any good. He did not think any reasonable objection could be raised against the manner in which the sports had been conducted. They had endeavoured to prohibit betting, and the races had been contested in a fair and upright manner. He trusted that another year they might be even more heartily supported than on the present occasion.—A vote of thanks having been heartily recorded to Mrs. Baxter, Mr. Baxter, in replying on her behalf, remarked on the general satisfaction that had been manifested in regard to the pro- ceedings of the day, which were shortly afterwards brought to a conclusion.
