INFECTIOUS DISEASES.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter, in answer to a communica- tion sent by the Board, from the Netherfield-road Hospital, Liverpool, stating that the authorities would be glad to re- ceive any cases of fever, measles, dc., excepting smallpox, which might arise in the Board's district, on certain terms specified in the letter. No resolution was passed thereon. THE NUISANCE QuEsriox.—The Nuisance Inspector re- ported that the nuisances complained of behind Mr. Hewitt's premises and in Barrow's field had been abated; he had nothing further to remark upon.—The Surveyor said that with respect to the general inspection of the township Mr. Dickinson and himself were making progress and were go- ing over ever'.' place in the township, but had nist yet com- pleted the survey. If the Board remembered they under- took that duty, and he might say tat there were two or three places that they could mention just now. There was one matter that they observed that was that pig-keeping was increasing again. They saw oil. Saturday five is: six places where people were beginning toleep pigs and they tried to frighten them a little, but, as he understood it, the only thing was that if they were kept so as to be a nuisance the Board could make them be removed. He did not think that there were above two places that they might say caused any nuisance. A report on the matter would be submltted next month. . _

Puals.—A number of plans were examined, and the Chairman remarked that the Board were constantly in difficulties by reason of people building without duly sub- mitting plans. He thought that proceedings should be taken against same offenders so that it would be understood what is required. ENCROACHMENTS —Some discussion cropped up ,:elative to numerous encroachments by shop-keepers and others in the township, and it was eventually decided to take pro- ceedings against one person whose encroachments most war- ranted that course being taken. The remainder of the business was of a routine chara'Aer.

EARLESTOWN. ENTERTAINMENT.—Mr. John Clarke presided at a meet- ing under the auspices of the Earlestown Gospel Mission, held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance. The string band, conducted by Mr. Tripp, gave a few selections, the choir sang several pieces, and Mr. Cordinglv gave a reading. THE EARLESTOWN WANDERERS' 'FOOTBALL CLIII3.—A general meeting of the members of the Earlestown Wan- derers' Football Club was held at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Earlestown' on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance of members. JarnewLowe was re-elected hono- rary secretary. W. Litnond, assistant•secretary, W. Lord, treasurer, T. Champion, captain,and James Shaw, vice- captain. JUVENILE Goon TEMPLART.—A. meeting in connection with the Earlestown Juvenile Temple of the lcdependent Order of Good Templars was held in the .Good Templars lodgeroom, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday even- ing. There was a vary good attendance, and Brother E Newman superintendent of the Temple, occupied the chair. An excellent programme of songs, readings, recitations, &c, was nicely gone through by members of the Hope of Earles- town (adult) lodge, a very enjoyable evening being spent. WESLEYAN METHODIST TEA MEETING.— A tea meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Society classes was held in the Lecture-hall beneath the chapel, Cross-lane, , Earlestown, on Wednesday evening. About 45 persons sat down to a most enjoyable tea, which was pleasantly waved by Mrs. Stringer, Mrs. Atkinsoy, and Miss Newman. At the subsequent proceedings the Rev. J. M. Fairbourne presided, and interesting addresses were given by Mr. John Roberts, Mr. Clare, Mr. Gosling, Mr. Cordiegly, and others. The , meeting was a good and pleasant one. L OBSTRUCTING THE Roan.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday. Henry Woods was summoned for obstructing , the highway with a horse arid wagonette at Newton on the 17th June.—P.C. Spencer deposed that on the date named, the first day of Newton races, there were 40 or 50 vehicles in Mill-lane' waiting to convey passengers to the race course. The defendant drew out from the rank, and. thereby , blocked the road for some minutes.—lle was fined 2s 6d 3 and costs.—John Platt was summoned for a similar of- fence committed on the same date and was also fined 2s 6d. I and costs.

THEFT OP TIMBER AT SANKEY.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Michael Farrington and John McHugh, young men, were charged with stealing on the 23rd ult, two pieces of timber, value is 3d, from a field at Sankey, the property of Joseph Tyldesley.—Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the defendants, and pleaded not guilty.—The defendants were observed walking away from the direction of the field with two pieces of timber in their possession. The prosecutor charged them with stealing the timber but they denied the allegation.—For the defence it was maintained that the men had found the timber on the side of the Sankey Brook and they picked it up.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs on each defendant. UNLAWFUL GAMES AT EARLESTOWN.—At the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, John Sumner and James Nearey, youths, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss at Earl.istown on the 21st ult.—P C Hunt stated that he saw the defendants in company with other young men on a foot- path near the Haydock railway. He watched them some considerable time and finding that he was unable to get to them with his uniform he took his uniform off and placed it behind a hedge while he walked towards them. The men ran away, however, before he got to them.—The defendants were fined 2s 801 and costs each.--James Donoughoe and George Cosgrove, lads, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss near Sankey-street, on the 21st ult, and were each fined 2s ed and costs. STONE\ THROWING AT WARORAVE. CAUTION TO LADS.—Before R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and J. Pearson, Esqs., at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, George Shaw, a lad, was summoned for throwing stones on the highway at Wargrave, on the 12th ult.—P.C. McMullen stated that he saw the defendant throwing stones in War- grave New-road, on the afternoon of the date named. Several complaints had been made by Canon Whitley about lads throwing stones, several squares of glass having been broken in an unoccupied house. He (P.C. McMullen) had also had complaints from Mr. Tay!ear, of the Vulcan Foundry, and he had cautioned the lads several times besides having asked the schoolmaster to caution the boys, but it took no effect. —The Bench imposed a fine of 2s. 61.

ASHTON GOOD TEMPLARS AT EARLESTOWN.—The mem- bers of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars re- ceived a fraternal visit from Ashton Excelsior Lodge, on Monday evening. The party comprised 18 persons, and a gathering was held in the Good Templars lodgeroom. The chair was occupied by Bro. Crompton, W.C.T., of the Ash- ton Lodge. After a few general remarks on the good feeling engendered by such fraternal visits and the good work done by the Good Templar lodges, he proceeded to call upon his Ashton brethren to give an entertainment. Songs were ren- dered by Bros. Rathbone, Blinston, Vint, J. Taylor (Earl es- town), Wilkinson, and T. Crompton; readings by Bro. Wil- kinson, J. Merrick, C. Merrick ; and a Lancashire reading, entitled e. Putting th' axins in," was given by Bro. Willis, who also gave a short address. At the close of the proceed- ings a deserving vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the Milton friends. THE Ruv. J. M. WALMSLET ON THE WORLD AND WICKED- NESS —Preaching in the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Cross. lane, Earlestown, oa Sunday evening, the Rev. J. M. Wamsley (superintendent of the circuit) drew a prospective view of the nations of the world The nations represented different clans, colours, and forms of government, but the race was one; and the first truth impressed on the mind was the brotherhood of the race. But the outlook was not only vast—it was appalling, and they were brought face to face with the greatest of all moral problems. It made manifeet the appalling degradations and miseries of the nations. go where they would in no land and in no age would they dada people naturally virtuous, upright, and pure! Facts were stubborn things, but the most stubborn of all those stubborn things was the fact that man in every age and in every land had proved himself a fallen being, and living in alienation from God. There was no hope for nations and for men until they were led to see and feel their need of their saviour God. THE CHURCH DISPUTE SUGGESTED IRON CHURCH.— The attendance at the services in St. John's Cnurch on Sun- day were no better than what they have been for some weeks past, and there appears to be but little interest taken in the church or its pastor throughout the parish. During the pre- sent week a suggestion has been made to many parties that a movement should be started for the erection of an iron church to be used for Divine worship by the parishioners who have, in a sense, bean driven away from St. John's Church. The suggestion has been well received, and a cordial support to it was promised, but as yet no definite action has been taken in the matter. The large congrega • tion which formerly gathered at St. John's Church has been gradually dispersing themselves among the other places of worship in the neighbourhood; and the loss of so large a church-going community has been sorely felt by the therough church-people of the district. The proposal to gather them in "one fold " by Means of an iron church, and thus keep them within the pale of the Church of Eng- land is one which meets the approval of many, but there are same dissenting voices to the project. NEWTON RACES; CRUELTY TO HORSES.—At the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Alfred Harris, cabman, Manchester, was charged with torturing a horse at Newton, on the, 17th June.—lnspector Campbell of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, deposed that he saw the defendant furiously driving the horse in a cart containing passengers from the races to Earlestown Station. He was flogging the horse in a violent manner.— Defendant was fined ss. and coste.--Martin Mannin, cab- man, Widnes, was charged with working a horse in an un- fit state on the 18th ult. The defendant was driving two horses in a waggonnette from the Common towards Newton Station. One of the animals was suffering from a wound on the shoulder.—lnspector Campbell spoke to the defen- dant about it, and the defendant said he did not know it was wounded. He was fined 20s, and costs.--Georee Wild, cabman, Manchester, was summoned for a similar offence.— Inspector Campbell stated that in this case the animal was very much exhausted and worn. out, and seemed ready to drop in the road. It was an aged horse, lame on both fore legs, in a very poor condition, and totally unfit for work.— A fine of 103. and costs was imposed --Thomas Varey` cabman, Manchester, was charged with working a horse in an unfit condition on the 18th June. The defendant did not appear.—lnspector Campbell stated that the defendant was driving to Newton Station, the horse being completely ex- hausted. It was staggering about the road like a drunken man through being overloaded and flogged. The animal was in a very poor condition and was totally unfit for work. —The defendant was fined 20s. and costs. CAPTURE OF A GANG OF GAMBLERS —Before R. Hough- ton. T. J. Gillespie, and J. Pearson, Esqs., at the Newton TOWII Hall, on Saturday, the following persons, all young men, were brought up on a charge of gaming with cards at Earlestown, on the 20th June :—George Treyham, John Hodkin, Bernard Hodkin, Thomas Downs, Thos. Cosgrove, William Howard, James Downs, Isaac Haskins, and WM. Foy.—Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the de- fendants, and pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Hunt deposed that a little before nine o'cleck on Friday night, the 20th inst., he was on duty in Sankey-street, Earlestown, when he heard a noise coming from the back of Legh-street. He went in that direction and saw all the defendants along with others on the ground, with an old woman keeping " nix " for them. He watched them for a considerable time, but was not close enough to see what they were playing at. He afterwards rushed across the street, and saw they were playing a game called "banking." Copper and silver money was placed on the cards, and the defendants on seeing him gathered up the cards and money and made off. He, however, succeeded in picking up a penny. There was a crowd of persons round the defendants, and the language the latter came out with was somethingdiegraceful. Many complaints had been made by the neighbours about Regent-street about men gathering in that neighbourhood from all parts of the town and gambling.—ln reply to Mr. Browne, witness added that the men were not playing a game called "25."—For the defence, Mr. Browne maintained that Thomas Downs,Williarn Rowartl, William Foy, and Haskins were not present ; that the others were playing a friendly game called " 25," and that no money passed between the men.—On being recalled, P.C. Hunt stated that the defendants named were present.— Several young men were then called as witnesses, and they stated that Downs, Howard. Foy, and Haskins were at other places at the time mentioned by the officer.—Mr. Houghton, Do you know anything of the character of these 'wit- nesses 7—Superintendent Jackson No, sir, I do not.—Mr. Pearson: There is perjury on one side or the other.—. Superintendent Jackson : Yes, sir, it is evident.—After some minutes'consultation the Bench dismissed the summonses against Howard, James Downs, and Raskin!, and fined the others 2s. 6d. and costs each.

Tax EARLESTOWN Gown. MISSIOX.—SonIe interest was attached to the services in connection with the Earlestown Gospel Mission en Sunday by the visit of Mr. Thomas Ben- son, of Eccles, better known as " Bishop " Benson. Mr. Benson preached in the Co-operative H.lll to large and ap- preciative congregations, and his addresses were listened te with great interest and attention. "Bishop " Benson was accompanied by a Mr. Thomas Davies, and together, in the evening, they inissioned the principal streets of the town. EXTRAORDINARY DISCOVERY AT THE VIADUCT WOE/13. A sans itional rumour to the effect that one of the workmen employed at the Viaduct Wagon Works, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company, at Earles- town, had discovered bank notes to the amount of £5,000 spread rapidly throughout the town on Monday and Tues- day, and created no small amount of excitement. The re- port was at first discredited, but subsequent inquiries have proved that there was some foundation for it, though, un- luckily, Use value of the " find " is not quite as high as it was at first thought. It seems that on Monday when one of the wagon makers was inspecting an old wagon belenging the company, which had been sent for repairs, he noticed what appeared to be a slip of paper doubled up in one corner of the wagon. He picked up the " bundle " and examined it. There were four slips of piper having the appearance of bank cheques; they were drawn up in proper legal phraseology, and "promised to pay on demand" certain sums indicated, and bore all the necessary signa- tures to give them an appearance of being genuine. As the supposed "bank notes" were respectively for £2 500 £1,245, £725, and £525, or a total of £4,995, a report was soon spread over the works that the sums mentioned had been discovered. The 'notes" were subsequently handed over to Mr F Harwood, manager of the works, and they were afterwards placed in the hands of Mr J W Emmett, superintendent. A thorough examination of the slips revealed the fact that instead of being "bank notes" they were" bills of exchange" representing the transfer of money to the amounts stated from one banking house to another. They were American bills of exchangeto"Messrs John Athya and Son, Glasgow"; while across them was printed in faint letters "accepted by Barnett, Hoares, and Company, London," the latter being a well known banking-house. They were all made out for the year 1862. To anyone but the owner the documents are worthless, but such are gener- ally preserved and filed as receipts and documentary evi- dence that the money transactions have taken place. How they got to the place where they were discovered on Mon- day, and how long they had lain there is a mystery, which has not yet been solved.
ANTI-VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS AT NEWTON: CASES DISMISSED. . .

At the Newton Y.;;;FH:ir,;;-Zt—u;:day, before Robert Houghton, Thomas J. Gillespie, and J. Pearson, Esqs., Daniel Garnett, Robert Roberts, George Howgate, and Thos. O'Neil, all of Earlestown, were summoned for neglecting to have their children vaccinated in compliance with the re- quirements of the Vaccination Acts.—On the case of Daniel Garnett being called, Mr Thomas Duxburv, of Blackburn, stepped forward and said: I represent Mr Garnett, your worships.—The Olerk (Mr White) : In what way—are you a solicitor 7—Mr Duxbury: No, sir. I have written in- structions from him to appear on his behalf.—Mr Duxbury handed a note up to the Bench, and the Clerk asked: On his behalf, do you plead guilty or not guilty 7—Mr Dux- bury : Not guilty.—Alfred Cooper, the vaccination officer for the Newton district, was then sworn, whereupon Mr Duxbury said: I believe, yourworships, a previous objection might settle this matter, as I have an objection to take to the summons. Presuming that it is under the 29th section that the summons is issued, it is an excess of the magistrates jurisdiction to order the child to appear, yet the summons does order the child to appear. I must ask ou on that ground to declare the summons bad.—The Clerk: It is simply doubtful whether it is requisite to bring the child.— Mr Duxbury: The section under which the summons is issued does not enable you to do that, but the 31st section enables you to do it —The Clerk: It is simply so much sur- .plus.—Mr Duxbury: I press it to the migistrates and not to the clerk. I have appeared in 'several courts before—Mr Houghton, J.P.: Our clerk rules th it the summons is quite perfect —The Clerk: It is more than perfect. —Alfred Cooper, the vaccination officer, then stated that he asked the defendant why his child was not vaccinated.—The , Clerk: Are you authorised by the Guardians to appear here? —Witness: Yes, sir.—(He thereupon handed a copy of his instructions to the clerk). Continuing, witness said the de- fendant had disregarded a notice served upon him to have I his child vaccinated, and on asking him for an explanation he would not give any.—The Clerk: Have you received any notice that the child has been vaccinated 7—Witness: The child has not been vaccinated.—The Clerk: What you apply for now is an order for vaccination 7—Witness: No, sir; I apply for a penalty.—Mr. Duxbury: That touches my previous objection, your worships. I ought to press that point again before proceeding with the examination or with further remarks. The summons is legally right under section 31st, and enables the Ngistrates to make an order; but section 29 enables the magistrates to deal summarily with the case this morning. I maintain it is illegal and totally irrevalent. I must ask the magistrates to deal with that objection and take the summons under the 31st and not the 29th section. I have a copy of a summons under section 29, which is entirely different to the present one.— Alfred Cooper: Cannot the summons be amended, your worships 7—The Clerk: It does not need alteration. If the child is not produced the defendant is not liable to a penalty for not producing it.—Mr. Duxbury: I maintain that the summons is invalid, and the only alternative Is to declare the summons invalid.—The Clerk: The magistrates have already told you that the objection is overruled.—Mr. Dux- bury: It is evidently a misunderstanding on the part of the) clerk. He asked whether they were to proceed under the 29th section or the 31st section.-The Clerk (to Mr. Cooper): Do you apply for a penalty 7—Mr. Cooper: I apply for a penalty under the 31st section.—Mr. Duxbury : I still press for the magistrates' decision upon that point —The Clerk You must know by this time that when you appear to the summons any trivial informality is done away with.—Mr. Duxbury: I will ask the magistrates to amend the sum- mons and enable the party to have another opportunity of having the child vaccinated, and prevent you giving a penalty this morning.—Mr. Houghton, J.P. : The parents have had an opportunity already if they felt so diposed.— The Clerk : Do you wish to cross-examine the Witness ?- -Mr. Duxbury: Have Ito go under the 29. h or the 31st section 7—The Clerk: The 29th section.—Mr. Duxbtery then handed to witness a notice paper and asked him if he had served it upon the defendant —Witness : Yes.—Mr. Duxbury : Does it contain the proper date 7—Witness : It's there.—Mr. Duxbury: Does it contain the proper date ' I ask 7—Witness : Duxbury : Has it the year on in which you sent it 7—Witness : You can see that.— Mr. Duxbury : Has it the year en 7—Witness: No.—The notice was then handed to the clerk, who asked witness when he served the notice.—Witness replied : Either the Bth or 9th of --Mr. Duxbury: Or some othee date, your worship. It does not show the (lite when it was served nor the vaccination officer's address, which the Act requires it should do —The Clerk : This notice is not a proper notice—Witness: Do you think not P—The Clerk : Ido think not —Mr. Duxbury : I think it prevents the magis- trates inflicting--The Witness : It is a Government copy. The Clerk : But you have not tilled in the date.—Mr. Dux- buty (holding a paper in his hand): Here is a Government copy, and it gives the vaccination iiifficer's address as well. Mr. Houghton, J.P. : There is an evident informality in this summons.—The Clerk: The notice is baBl.—Mr. Houghton. J.P. : We give you the benefit of it.—Mr. Duxbury: May I understand, then that the case is dismissed ?—Mr Hough- ton, J.P.: Daxbury : On that question, then, the whole of the cases are similar, except that a few of them are a little bit worse.--The case of Roliert Roberts was then cal:ed.—Mr. Duxbury: Here; I appear for him.—The Clerk: Are all these notices alike in each case 7—Mr. Cooper: Yee, I you? worabip.-eThe Clerk: All one form?-.-Mr. Cooper: Yes.—Mr. Houghton, J.P.: it is a very great irregularity on your part—The Clerk: How many cases have you sitnilar? —Mr. Cooper: Four cases ;and a number of others have bad notices just the same.—The Clerk: Leaving you to fill in the day, the Month, and the year.—Mr.rooper: So I did, with the exception of the year.—Mr. Pearson, it'.: The year is important as well as tlae month.—The Clerk: You are bound ts give them such a notice that gives definite and positive information of the time and place.—Mr. Daxbury : And the notice must contain the officer's addrese, your wor- ships.—The Clerk : You had better consult with the clerk to the Guardians, and get him to give you a model notice.— Mr. Cooper: Then these cases are adjourned 7— Mr. Dux- bury: Not adjourned, but dismissed.—TheClerk : The Bench have decided to dismiss the cases.

A Sr. HELENS APPEAL CLE.—In the Court of Appeal, London, on Friday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Bowen and Fry, the case was heard of the Mayor of the Borough of St. Helens te the St. Helens Col- lieries Company, Limited. This was the appeal of the de- fendants from the judgment of Justices Div and A. L. Smith on a special case. It appeared that by a local Act, called the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869, the Mayor, ttc., of the borough of St. Helens were constituted the local authority in and for the said town. By section 351 the borough rate should not in the aggregate exceed in any one year the sum of le in the £ on the yearly rateable value of the rateable property without the consent of the ratepayers. On the 27th of November, 1882, the Corporation made and assessed a borough rate on the rateable property in the borough for the year ending the 31st August, 1883, at the rate of is 6d In the pound, no consent of the ratepayers of St. Helens being obtained, nor was any exception made from the rate in respect of coal mines or other property. The defendants are the occupiers of a colliery mine within the borough, and they were assessed to the said rate in re- !meet thereof at the sum of £417 18s, being at the rate of Is 6d in the pound. The defendants paid on account of that rate the sum of £278 12s being Is in the pound on their valuation; and they contended that a special exemption was created in respect of coal mines by the 352nd section of the St. Helens Improvement Act, and that such exemption was still in force, notwithstanding section 227 of the Public Health Act, and that they were not liable to pay any greater rate than Is in the pound. The plaintiffs sued them for the balance, £139 61, and the question for the court was— Had sections 351 and 352 of the St. Helens Improvement Act been repealed by section 227 of the Public Health Act. 1875? The divisional court gave judgment on the special case for the plaintiffs, with costs, subject to an inquiry to be made by one of the masters of the court as to the inci- dence of the rate. Mr. Bighorn, Q C., and Mr. R. S. Wright appeared for the appellants; and Mr. Vesey Fitzgerald for the respondents. The Master of the Rolls in giving judg- ment, said the decision of the Divisional Court most be up- held. The general Act took away the limitation in the local Act, and there was now no limitation whatever of the amount of the borough rate. The appeal would be dismis- sed with costs. Lords Justices Bowen and Fry concurred.

TH.Erf FROM A PAWNBROKER'S SHOP.—Before Messrs. T. Earle and H. Gaskell, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Catherine Hanley, a middle-aged woman was charged with stealing a child's frock, value 31. from the shop of Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, Prescot. On the 20th ult. the priacner visited the shop, and after she had left the frock was missed. She afterwards attempted to pawn the same frock and she was thereupon given into cultody.-51le was committed to prison for a Month POLICE INSPECTION.—On Thursday afternoon the mem- bers of the police for the Premt Division of the county, which comprises the disfetct of Prescot, Wavertree, Wool- ioe) And BratAen,were inspected by Captain Alison, assistant chief Constable, at the police station, Prescot. There were present on parade Superintendent Barker, Inspectors Fowler and Mayho' Sergeants Townend, Hill, Crawford, Edgar, Piotat, and Dingley, and 38 constables. The inspector hav- ing minutely inspected the uniforms and accoutrements ot the men, then entered the station and inspected the books, and appeared pleased with the result of the inspection. SCHOOL TREATS.—On Monday the scholars in connection with the Prescot Wesleyan Sunday School, to the number of about 400, marched in procession, under the charge of Superintendents Atherton and Cartwright, to Knowsley Park. On the way to the park they stopped in front of the house of Mr. Whitfield, one of their teachers, who is sick, ' and sang a couple of hymns. On reaching the park they were provided with tea, and during the afternoon indulged in games, &c.—On the same afternoon the scholars in con- nection with the Catholic Schools in Prescot were also given their annual treat. Eirly in the afternoon they assembled to the number of about 240 in the schoolroom in St. Helens- road, and were there served with tea, itc. Afterwards they formed in procession and marched, under the care of Father Brindle, Mr. J. Sanders, Mr. Haydon, and the teachers, and beaded by Fairclough's brass bind, to Knowsley Park. A very agreeable afternoon was there spent in games and sports of various description. A RUNAWAY FATHER PUNISHED.—Themas Bibby, a labourer, residing at Widnes, was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. T. Earle and'''. Gasket!, with deserting his children whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—The defendant: I am not guilty of running away, as I have never been away from the parish at all.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians stated that in August, 1880, the pri- soner left Widnes, Where he bad been residing for some time, and his four children were taken to the workhouse. They had since remained there until about a fortnight ago, when two of them were sent to Canada, the remaining two having been placed in homes with foster parents. The Guardians were now paying 3s. per week for each child, with an additional allowance for clothing and and the school fees. The relieving officer had made many inquiries about the man but nothing was heard about him until about a week ago. He was instructed to ask the Bench to make an example of the prisoner and inflict the highest penalty. The total cost of the children to the Union had been £lBl.—Mr. John Scannel, relieving officer, then proved the case, and the Bench committed the prisoner to two months' hard labour. PRESCOT HI G HWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at Mr. Cross's °Mee on Tuesday forenoon, when there were present Mr. W. L. Evans (in the chair), Mr. R. Tyrer. Mr. Newton, Mr. Goldaworth (surveyor), and Mr. Cross (clerk.)—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. THE RE-APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.—When the Chair- man had taken his seat, he said as that was the first occasion upon which he had been present since his re-appointment as chairman of the Board, he desired to say he was very much obliged to them for again conferring that honour upon him. ITs should endeavour to do his duty to the satisfaction of all parties.—Mr. Tyrer : There is no doubt of that, Mr. Chairman, if you are spared in good health, as I hope you will be. MONTHLY EXPENDITI7RE.—The Surveyor's statement of expenditure for the four weeks ending June 25th showed amounts as follows for the various townships :—Bold £l3 4s, Knowsley £7 8s 2d, Rainhill £8 17s Bd, Whiston .£9 18s 6d, team labour £79 3s 101, new materials £B5 15s Bd, incidentals £2 3s 9d, total £lB6 118 71d. SUGGESTED ArmessmoNs TO A ScHOOLS SEWER.--The Surveyor read a letter from the Rev. J. Barton, vicar of ,Rainhill, asking the Board to make certain alterations in the sewerage arrangements of the Rainhill National School premises. Mr. Goldsworth submitted a plan which he had drawn up in reference to the proposed alterations, which was considered by the Board, the Surveyor remarking that It was rather a serious matter.—lt was ultimately decided that the drainage alterations should ba allowed, but an applicaatiou by the Rev. J. Barton for permission to enclose a piece of land adjoining the footpath was not granted. This was all the business.

LOCAL BOARD MEETING. The ordinary monthly meeting of this body was held at the offices, Derby-street, Prescot. on Wednesday evening, when there were present Messrs. C. Spencely (in the chair), W. Baealey, H. Fogg, T. P. Hewitt, T. S. Preston, W, -4oldsworth (surveyor), Dickinson (nuisance inspector), and El. Cross (clerk). div.p: LATiNG OF MEMORIAL STONE.

On Monday the memorial stone of the /ion new schools, Prescot, was laid by Mr. Alexander Eccles, at Roby. The ceremony was favoured by beautiful weather, and this, no doubt, conduced to a considerable extent to the great amount of public interest which seemed to be taken in he event as shown by the large attendance of spectators. This new building, it may be explained, has become necessary owing to the increase of scholars in connection with the Free Gospel Mission at Prescot. The want of accommoda- tion in the old schools has long been a pressing want, and recently this provision of more suitable premises bad almost become a matter of abeolute necessity. The new erection, which is situated in Kemble-street, is calculated to meet all requirements for some years to come as far as the scholars are concerned, and will in addition provide suitable accom- modations as a meetiug place. The building will be two etories in height, the upper story consisting of an assembly room meaeuring 74 feet by 38 feet, and the lower will com- prise a school-room 44 feet by 22 feet, and three class- rooms 15 feet square with a lavatory attached. There will also be a caretaker's house containing a kitchen, two bed- rooms. scullery and pantry. Access to the upper story will be obtained by staircases at the front and rear of the build- ing. It is estimated that the erection and completion of the schools will cost something like £1,700, of which about £4OO are already subscribed. The architect is Mr. Twist, Whis- ton, and the builder Mr. Roberts, of St. Helens. Prior to the ceremony of laving the stone the teachers and scholars assembled in front of the building, the neighbourhood of which was also decorated with flags and streamers. Amongst those present were the Revs. J. Johnson (Congregational minister, Preecot), A. B. Walker (Congregational minister, Huyton), Messrs J. Blundell (superintendent of the Sunday school), C. B Johnson, J. T. Drinkwater (Liverpool), E. Beesley, J. Eastham (Liverpool), J. Twist, T. 'deckhouse, Haswell Brown (Sunderland). It. H. Menzies, T. P. Hewitt, D. Prescott, Mrs. Johnson, Mrs. Roberts (St. Helen), Mrs. Blackhouse, Mrs. Drinkwater, Misses Tyrer, Mr. and Mrs. Bromilow (Bolton:, The proceedings were commenced by Mr. Blundell giving out a hymn, after which the Rev. J. Johnson read a portion of scripture, and the Rev. A, B. Walker offered up a prayer. Mr. Blundell then said that the reason of their erecting that building was that the present schools were qeite inadequate to their wants, owing to the increas- ing vitality of the schools. They had about 230 scholars on their books, and they had an average attendance of nearly 200. The inspector stated a short time ago that the old schools were only fit to accommodate 68 scholars, its ceiling being only 10 feet 6 inches in height, so that it was objec- tionable on sanitary grounds. Mr. Blundell then handed to Mr. Eccles a silver trowel and mallet, the former of which was inscribed with the words " Presented to Alexander Eccles, Esq., of Roby, on the occasion of his laying the the memorial stone of Zion §chools, Prescot, June 30th, 1884."—Mr, Eccles, who was greeted with applause, then formally laid the memorial stone, which was also inscribed as follows: "This stone was laid by Alexander Eccles, Req., June 30th. 1884." la the course of an interesting ad- dress, Mr. Eccles referred to the greatly superior education of children in the present day over those of former times owing to the legislation as to education within recent years, and he also pointed out the necessity for Sunday Scheol teachers improving themselves in view of the increased and inereasing knowledge of their pupils. He congratulated the members of that church on the noble efforts they had put forth in connection with the erection of that new building. Mr. Drinkwater also gave an amusing and interesting ad- dress, and concluded by hoping that those present would give liberally towards the collection, and that the new building would be a blessing not only to the present genera- tion but likewise to generations yet unborn. After the cere- mony the scholars and teachers formed into procession, and preceded by the Whiston brass band, marched to Knowsley Park, and were there provided with tea, and took part in garnee until evening

div.head: ASHTON LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: ASHTON LOCAL BOARD.

An ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board offices, Ashton, on Wednesday evening. There were present Messrs Gaskell (in the chair), Lathorn, Simp- kin, Crompton, Lowe, Roberts, Laithwaite, Barton, Goldsworth (surveyor), Will (clerk), and Chambers (inspec- tor.) The MLNCI/ESrEll SNIP Cum.—The Clerk stated that he had received a communication from the committee of the Manchester Ship Canal asking the Board to petition in favour of the bill they are promoting in Parliament. The Board. the Clerk stated, sent a petition along with about 300 other Local Boards to the House of Commons last year, ask- ing them to suspend their standing order in favour of the Ship Canal scheme, and now the committee asked them to petition in favour of the bill itself.—Mr Roberts was of opinion that the Ship Canal would be a great adrantage to the country at large, but thought it would interfere with their local prosperity.—After some hesitation Mr. Simpkin moved, and Mr Crampton seconded that the petition be signed in favour of the Ship Canal. This proposal was carried. _

THE SCARLATINA EPIDEMIC.—At a special meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee the Clerk explained that the meeting was called for the purpose of considering what steps should be taken for preventing the further spread of scarlatina, and the Medical Officer of Health having re- ported that in his opinion the epidemic had somewhat abated, it was resolved—That having in view that the whole of the school examinations would be held during the pre- sent month, and that the schools would be closed immedi- ately they were concluded, the Committee do not think it desirable to recommend the Board to issue a compulsory order to this effect.—Confirmed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Medical Officer re- ported to the Highway and Sanitary Committee that since last meeting 6 deaths from scarlitina had been registered, making a total of 37 since the first outbreak up to date. From the information he possessed the epidemic had abated, especially at Situ's-lane End and Downali Green districts, and it Was also much less prevalent in Park-lane. The disease, however, was present in other parts of the town- ship, two of the six fatal cases above-mentioned having oc- curred at Stabshaw Cross and one at Lily-lane Cottages, and there were one or two cases in the town. With this exception the health of the township was satisfactory: (a) He also reported the necessity of structural alterations at Bridge Buildings in connection with the closets and ashpit, and the improvement of the house drains at the same place; (b) foul state of yard at Park-lane from slaughter house ; (c) obstructed ventilation at Board's cottages in the gas yard; (d) nuisance from accumulation of fouled water in the old gasometer tank at rear of same ; (e) and further, that the Ten Row remained as last reported as regarded de- ficient privy accommodation. With reference to the nuis- ance at Bridge Buildings and Park-lane, the surveyor and medical officer were instructed to communicate with the owners, and notice was also ordered to be served for the abatement of the nuisance at gas works. Instructions were given by the committee for the necessary steps to be taken for the abatement of these nuisances.—Confirmed. ORIPPIN'S WATER RENT.—In the minutes of the Finance Committee it was stated that the collector was directed to see Mr. Ellis in reference to this matter, and to inqtruct him to institute proceedings if the amount is not paid by Wednesday next.—Confirmed. GAS WORKS EXTENSION.—With regard to the proposed extension of the gas works, which is estimated to cost about £7OO, it w‘s stated that Mr. Goldsworth had been instructed by the Gas and Water Committee to prepare a plan of the buildings as suggested and report further OR the subject to the next meeting.—ln answer to Mr. Crompton, the Chair- man said it was expected that by the improvements of the gas works they would be able to make them pay by having an apparatus that would enable them to make a profit on their residual products. He also proposed that they apply to the Local Government Board for power to borrow £l,OOO for the gas works extension. They would most probably not need the whole of this sum, but it was better to hove power to borrow if necessary and thus save further trouble. —Mr. Bumpkin seconded this proposal, which was carried. —This was all the business of public interest.

The important railway appeal of the London and North- Western Railway Company has been respited until the Oc- tober Sessions at Chester. A btronetcv has been conferred upon Mr. B. Samuelson, M.P. for Banbury, in recognition of his services to the cause of education. THE SEVENOAKS ACcmarrr.—The inquest upon the two men recently killed by a collision between goods trains on the South-Eastern line was resumed at Sevenoaks on Wed- nesday, when evidence regarding the working of the sig- nals was taken. Ti)o jury returned a verdict of manslaugh- tea against Charles Cramp, signalman, who was committed for trial.

div.p: ST. HELENS.

. ..... THE ALLEGED CORPORATE DEFALCATIONS. The alleged discovery of serious irregularities and defal- cetions in connection with one of the departments of the Ste Helens Corporation is still causing a coneiderable amount of talk throughout the town. The reticence of the authorities tends to increase the uncertainty which exists in relation to the matter, and though the rumour e and reports which have been circulated are looked upon as being generally accurate no definite statement or reliable information has been given to the public in an authoritative manner. At the monthly meeting of the Town Council. on Wednesday afternoon, when the minutes of the Paving and Sewering Committee id came up for confirmation, Councillor Belsher rose and sa there was a matter about which he wished to ask a question, although he did not think it arose upon the minutes. He, however, thought that was the best time to put the qtleetieu' which was with regard to the scandal going about the town at the present time—about the irregularities which bad occurred. Certain inquiries, he understood, had been made of which the Council, as a Council, knew nothing about- He did not know what had been done, but the public outside knew that something was going on, and his opinion Wee that every member of the Council was entitled to know the nature of the inquiries, the sebject in hand, and everything about them. He did not think that any one or two mem- bers of that Council had any right or any authority to go into so important a matter without instructions from the Council.—The Mayor (interrupting) : Mr. Heleher. you rose for the purpose of asking a question If you will ask one we might answer it.—Councillor Belsher : I want to know the nature of the scandals and irregularities that are talked about so prominently in the town, what steps are being taken with regard to them, s°a " whether you are prepared to submit to us a statement as te their nature and extent, and the steps that are being e e tekaerl in the matter.—The Mayor: All these questions which , be answered I will answer at the end of the regular busioei, of this Council.—After the ordinary business of the Celine' had been disposed of, the Mayor said: That, gentlemen. jet the ordinary business of this monthly Council. I suggest now that we resolve into Committee, and beg to move tbei. we resolve ourselves into a Committee of the whole Ceune,l —Alderman Cook seconded the motion, which was Neee-„; and the Mayor called upon the representatives of the Pre"- * to retire; and the reporters did so.—lt was afterwards re; ported that a lengthy document was read, giving details el a system ef fraud which had been carried ma more or lee; for the past four years, and implicating several locally We t known men The defalcations were stated to amount to elle° £1,500. IVe believe no definite action was decided uPee' the matter at present remaining in abeyance. VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT ST. HELENS. There were also present Lieu'enant-Colee Bothwell, commandihg 2nd L.E.V. ; Major Wilcock, Ct,„.' tam, and Adjutant Coode, Surgeon E. F. Hall; Capts'L Ward, Duffy, Rigq, Campbell, and Craik Lieutenam: Lyon, Pendiebury, Bothwell, Atkinson, and Higgiu• 113 field state was as follows :—Present on parade, 14 officer; 27 sergeants, 30 band and buglers, rank and file 366—t° 437. This is stated to rie mainly owing to the exertions of the new adjutant, CAP% Coode, who has been very popular since his attachment _ the corps a few months since. The inspecting officer, ti his arrival at head-quarters, first inspected four models ° bridges which had been made by members, and awarded title prizes as foltow :—Model of different combinations of tree et bridges, two,-legged, four-legged, and tripod, by Sergeal T. Gilman, No. 2 company; and a series of trestle bridieeTi on one frame, by Corporal J. Bennett. These were adjud.g, to be of equal merit, and the first and second PrLez`i amounting to about £5, were equally divided. A single-17. bridge by Corporal Bennett was awarded third prize; ". combination of stiffened sling and trestle bridges by S''e giant Bradbury, though not receiving a prize, deserves _ word of praise. The field works consisted of four bridge_7; The first, a barrel-pier floating bridge; the second, a stiffewr sling bridge; the third, a single-lock bridge; and the fourth, a suspension bridge. Colonel Edwards made a careful el: aminatioa of these bridges, and afterwards proceed to a field near the Waterworks, where the regime!). was put through a variety of movements. At the close, 07_ inspecting officer said it gave him much pleasure to be ther', that day. It was at first expected that the Inspector-Geller'. of Fortifications, Sir James Clarke, would have been there instead of himself, but as circumstances had prevented it, be hoped Sir James would be able to be with them next year He was very pleased to notice the rapid increase of efficr_ ency as shown in the fact that there were 437 efficients thle year as compared with 127 last year, and that although t,eaed inspection was this year a month earlier. He was also el to see that their musketry practice appeared to be bettef than last year, and he wished to impress upon them tha' perhaps it eras one of the most important of their duties. He hoped that during the present year they would be able to devote more time to it than they had been able hitherto. It most be remembered that an engineer'a dutiee in the field were not confined to making bridges and 000: structing defences, but he was often called upon to ace ti: infantry, and unless he could do so it was quite imnosel,e: he could act fully as an engineering soldier. lee doubt many of them were aware that during ti's Franco-German war engineers were called upon to act 3 infantry, and, with the best effect. He (Colonel Edwardsl. made those remarks to impress upon every man the imporse mace of combining musketry with engineering duty. He we. sorry that be had not time that day to sea the men at wore; in the field, but he must say that the works and the mode': were very satisfactory indeed. He considered the turn-00e very creditable, and their movements fairly well executed, and he should have pleasure in reporting such to head: quarters. The corps shortly afterwards left the field rroa marched through the principal streets of the town. Tee men presented a smart appearance. and commanded the re- spect and esteem of the large numbers of persons who assail. blest to see them. _ THE "MAIDEN CIRCUITS" THAT MAIDENS LONG Wedding-rings. Every affliction has its blessing. The man with a wooden log never knows what it is to have rheumatism in that ankle. LATEST BUT NOT LIKELY TO BE THE LAST DEFINITION. --Marriage is described by a French cynic as a tiresome book with a very fine preface. The difference between love and law is this—in love the attachment precedes the declaration; in law the declaration Precedes the attachment. There are some persons who cannot take a joke; but Fogg i 8 not one of them. A " friend " acquainted with Fogg's frequent changes of abode, asked him which he thought was the cheaper, to move or pay rent. "I can't tell you, my dear boy," replied Fogg; I have always moved." A small Aberdeen child, being asked by her Sunday-school teacher, "What did the Israelites do after they crossed the Red Sea?" answered, "I don't know, ma'am; but perhaps they dried themselves." A. contemporary obtained the following story from a tele- graph operator in a country town—. A member of the Ma- eonic order telegraphed to a companion at a distance, ' Make room for ten Royal Arch Masons—coming to-day.' When the companions arrived, they found a pen had been built for their aceomodation, the telegram at its destination reading, Make room for ten R A M's—coming to-day." "SWEET GIRL GRADUATES."—A high-school girl, just graduated, said in her essay : "Let us avoid the frivolities of life, and pursue the noblest ends only." The next day She was moved to tears in an agonising attempt to decide the proper shade of blue for her complexion. TRY Jr.—When there is not a breath of air stirring, and You are in danger of stifling, attempt to light a cigar out- (4-doors, and you will be surprised at the breeze that will Start up. We have seen a man try this experiment in a dead calm, and by the time he had scratched thirteen matches it was really so windy as to be uncomfortable. Aunt Dinah, to Johnny (who is studying French): "I think you are getting on with your lessons very nicely, Johnny."—Johnny: "Yes, aunt, very nicely. I think, but it iU be a good while before I can speak French like the ,putleman who was with papa this afternoon."—Aunt D.: How is that, Johnny, did he speak French very fluently ? " Johnny: "0, yes, very fluently, aunt, in fact it didn't seem the least bit of trouble to him, alai' when I gave him my bit Of French didn't he laugh! "—Aunt D.: "He must have studied the French for a long time, I think."—Johnny: "0, Yes, he started to learn when he was quite young."—Amst "I should have liked to have seen him very much, what 'was his name, Johnny ? "—Johnny: "Papa didn't tell me his name, but I think he said he had lived at Paris."—Aunt D., "At Paris! then he has had a good opportunity of studying the French."—Johnny. "Studying it? Why, he has been studying it all his life, he is a Frenchman you See! "—Aunt D.: "0 Johnny, you are a bad boy." SETTING HER CAP.—The little brother came quietly into the parlour where Mr. Featherly was making an evening call, and after looking eagerly around remarked to hie sister: "Aunt Jane is mistaken."—" What is it!'" his sister asked Pleasantly, patting the dear little fellow on the head, while Peatherly gazed at the two in wrapt admiration.—" I don't see any cap," he replied, "but Aunt Jane just said that you were in the parlour sating your cap for Mr. Featherly." La Fontaine, the distinguished comedian, found himself One day, at a cafe, in the immediate neighbourhood of two Young fellows who recognised him. One of them apparently affected superior smartness, for he said to his companion, I'll lay you a wager I draw him out." " How?" "You titan see." Hat in hand, he went to the table at which La Fontaine was seated. "I beg your pardon, monsieur—are Yoe not Monsieur La Fontaine ?" " Yes ; what can Ido for Yon ?" "I only want to ask you whether it is you who Wrote La Fontaine's Fables?" "No, monsieur; but lam the same family as the fabulist—and you furnish me a Proof of the fact." "In what way ?" Do you not see that, like the fabulist. I know how to make donkeys talk ?" A WORD OF ADVICIL—Sydney Smith was complaining to his friends one day of a young gentleman who, although ,Manv years his junior, was in the habit of addressing him '53, his Christian name, a privilege which, as Sydney Smith lelharked, he allowed only his most intimate friends. Shortly afterwards the younggentleman in question entered the room, and, familiarly addressing Smith as "Sydney," inquired how he thought of passing the day. "For my part," said the Youth, "the Archbishop of Canterbury (Dr. Howley) has often invited me to pay' him a visit at Addington Park, and I think I shall run down, and return in the cool of the even- "Ah," said Smith, with a smile on his face which his r'ends well understood, "then let me give you a word of advice ! I know something of the archbishop; he is an ex- rllent man, but rather proud. Don't you call him 'William'; „!5 might not like it." A roar of laughter followed this sig- ircaut speech, and, as the discomfited yopth left the room, VrleY Smith turned round and quietly remarked, "I think VS settled the'cool of the evening' at last."

Total RUNCORN V. bUTTO V RECREATION (nT, llEtErrs).—Tais match was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, and after a rather exciting finish was won by the visitors by six runs. Winning the toss the home te int took the wickets, but, with the excep- tion of Brown and Gregory, all were singularly unfortunate in making a stand, and the inuirn,s closed for SO runs. On the visitors resuming the offansive, so well did Wood bowl, that eight wickets were down for 29 runs, of which G Prescott had made 13 by some good play. A change then took place in the game, as Clarke. who woe playing as a substitute for Sutton, made a very lucky 12, being missed badly four times, while Neil who had to make a break in his innings through a nasty knock, played pluckily for seven not out. The visitors then won a good match, as above stived, which, however, should h,ve been avoided had the bowling been better manipulated. Wood's five wickels cost 11 runs only. ... Some fine play WAS witnessed at Kensington Oval on Satur- day, when the Gentlemen of England &Arno wledged them- selves vanquished by the eustraliarns after a hard fight for victory'. She colonists, who had made 150 overnight, com- pleted their second innings fa. 219, leaving the Gentlemen to get 188 to win. Grace and Studd male a capital stand for the first w eket ; but Sp fforth's bowling quickly disposed of tilt. remainder, and the total for the second innings only retched 141.—Sutsex met Notts at Brighton, when some remarkable batting was recorded. Sussex went in a second time against a majority of 330, and put ogether a total of 302, mainly con- tributed by the amateurs Ellis, Newham, and Wyatt. The game closed at six o'clock, Notts winning in an innngs with 28 runs to spare, having run up the enormous total of 458, t) which Shrewsbury contributed 209 and Gunn 122.—The Gentle- men of Hampshire defeated the Philadephians by five wickets at Southampton, short scores being the order of the day.—The annual match between Eton and Winchester was concluded at the latter pare, resulting in a victory for the visitors with five wickets to spare. The second Ladoga of the Winchester team closed for 101, and Eton west in with 132 to get to win, which they quickly ran up, the first wicket falling for 39, the second at 68. and the third at 86.—At Oxton Liverpool had an easy time of it, practically defeati- g the home teem, who had gained 81 runs for the loss of six wickets, when the game was drawn, Liverpool having scored 273.—The Oldham team journeyed to Warrington. and after some good play, the match was drawn, the scores being 199 for the home team and 71 for four wickets for the visitors. On Monday and Tuesday the Philadelphians m:t the geltle- men of Gloucestershire at Cheltenham, at d gained a victory with 188 runs to spare. The scores were Philadelphians first innings 162; second, 207; Gloneestershire first innings, 94; second, 107. Clarke, Newell, wad Ititicutt paved good cricket for the Americans, mud Gilbert, toranston. and W G Grace for the home team.—Oxford met Cambridge at Lords, when the cricket was of an interesting character, althcugh Oxford won somewhat easily at the finish. On Monday, Cambridge, with nine wickrts to fall in their second innings, were still 84 runs behind. On Tuesday a good stand was made end the sco4 for the second innings at the fall of ths fourth wicket was 160. Then followed a breakdown, and the whole side were all out for 177, leaving the dark blues only 80 to get to win. The march ended in a triumph for Oxford by seven wickets. Scores :—Cambridge first inning', 11l ; second, 177 ; Oxford first innings, 29; second, 80 for three wickets. Whleby. for Oxford, took ten wickets for 113 runs, a creditable perfo,mance. The two days' match at Manchester between Lancashire and Cheshire termina.ed on Tuesday in brilliant weather. inn win for Lancashire by nine wickets. On Monday Cheshire made 128 and Lancashire 194 when play ceased, which they ran up to I 297 when the innings was concluded the following day. In their second innings Cheshire made 203, leaving th,ir oppo- nents to get 33 to win, which was easily dotained. Scores : Cheshire first innings. 126; second, 208; Landasidire first in- Rings, 297; second, 41. Mr Lancashire, fir Lancashire. put . up 119 runs in the first innings, and for Cheshire Mr Hollins planed a careful Innings. The Australians concluded a three days' contest with the Players of England at Sheffield on Wednesday. when the latter suffered defeat by six wickets. At the earlier stages of the game the Players appeared to have an ea•y victory in prospect, but on Wednesday lost, or as some say, threw away their chance, the fielding being indifferent, and many catches being missed, which tad a material effect upon the game. Score'; —Players first innings, 230; sesond. 134; Australians first in- nings, 1.89; sesond, 178. A total of 37,281 paid for admission dur ng the ...ourse of the match. On Thursday an Eleven of England opposed the Australians at Huddersfield; the English eleven were at the wickets all day, and scored 320 runs for the lms of only five wickets. Bcotton, who went in first, was not out for 101, and Hirst hit brilliantly. Atteweil scored 84, and Grimshaw also reached double figures. —A good day's cricket was witnessed at the Kennington Oval in the first of two annual Gentlemen and Players' matches. The Players won the toss and ran up 299. Ulyett being in while 213 runs were scor -d, and out of that number made 134 by almost faultless cricket. The Gentlemen had nearly an hour at the wickets, and in that time lost one wicket for 51 runs.— A large concourse of people witnessed the open ng of the match between Bastes and Kent at Brighton. Sussex went in first and made 270, and Neat, in about three-quarters of an hour's batting, made 54 for the loss of one wicket.—The match between the Lansdown Club and the Philadelphians was con- tinued at Bath. At the conclusion of the play the Lansdown score stood at 311 for the first innings and 18 for one wicket for the second, while the Philadelphians had made 319 in their first innings.

The islet of Herm, between Guernsey and Sark, is to be sold by acution. GALLANT CONDFCT OF I CONTICT.—A few days ago 25 convicts were marched to work in a bog some distance from Dartmoor Prison under the charge of a warder. One of the convicts suddenly picked up several stones, one of which struck the warder behind the ear, rendering him insensible. His loaded rifle fell from his hand, and other convicts rushed on him. One however, named Stevens, recently sen- tenced to transportation for life hastened to his relief, seized the rifle and ammunitton, and life, on the assailants, wound- ing several in the legs, afterwards using the butt end of the rifle. Other warders soon arrived, to whom Stevens ex- plained what had occurred. Some of the convicts, who were severely injured, were conveyed to the prison infirmary ; the remainder handcuffed, and escorted to the prison. Stevens was placed in a separate cell, and at the end of last week all the convicts in the prison were paraded,and Stevens was informed that in consequence of his courageous conduct the Home Seeretary had ordered him to be released, and re- warded. Stevens was deeply affected by this announcement. In a few days he will be liberated. THE BRADLAUOII CASE —The Lord Chief Justice, Mr. Justice Grove, Mr. Baron Huddleston, and a special jury reassembled on Monday to further hear the action " Attor- ney-General v. Bradlaugh." The Lord Chief Justice at once commenced his summing up, observing that the two important questions were—Did the defendant take the oath within the meaning of the Act? and, was he capable of taking the oath? There could be no doubt that the defen-, dant did not take the oath according to the usual practice. His lordship quoted a number Of definitions of an oath from dictionaries and legal authorities, and asked the jury whether, in the sense of definitions, Mr. Bradlaugh was a person who could swear. It was noticeable that in his evi- dence before the Com:tint e of the House of Commons, Mr. Bradlaugb declined to reply to the crucial question which would fix 'him to a belief in a Supreme Being. The jury re- tired at 1-50, and returned into court at 5-5 with a verdict against Mr. Bradlaugh on all the questions submitted to them. ‘Their Lordships gave leave to Mr. Bradlaugh to move for arrest of judgment, and the arguments, it is understood, will be taken after the long vacation.

GOEBORNE.

------ AGGE4MATED ASSAULT ON A GIRL. At the Newton Petty sessions on Saturday, John Bate, 14 years of age, was charged with committing an aggravated assault on Ellen Jenkinson, nine years of age. at Golborne on the previous evening—The evidence was to the effect that the prisoner enticed the girl into a closet and then committed the assabilt with which he was charged.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty, but the Bench fined him 20s including costs. AN UNFORTUNATE WEDDING PARTY AT GOLBDRNE.-Tho following is taken from a Manchester contemporary :—A rather unpleasant episode occurred at a wedding celebrated at Golborne, near Newton-le-Willows, on Saturday. The con- tracting parties-a young couple from West Leth-with their two witnesses, arrived at Golborne early, and occupied themselves for a considerable time in leirurely sauntering about the streets. Eventually, after carefully taking a note of several places of worship along the route, the " two couples" entered tha Congregational Chapel, where the Rev. H. Wilson. of Ashton-in-Makerfield, was in waiting ,to conduct the ceremony. As no registrar was present the service could not proceed, and an awkward pause of half an hour ensued. About 10-30 the chapel keeper connected with the Independent Methodist Chapel, situate a little higher up the same stmet, was accosted by a gentleman, who inquired if there was not a wedding to be conducted there that morning. Having received no instructions the mart replied in the negative, out added that a wedding party had been seen to enter the Congregational Chapel some time before. The stranger (who, it turned out, was the new registrar for the district) hastily wrote the names of the in- tended bride and bridegroom, and requested the chapel keeper to proceed to the Congregational Chapel to inqulre if such persons were present, and to inform them that they were at the wrong plane The suspicion being confirmed, the registrar lost no time in approaching the wedding party and conducting them and the minister to the Inde- pendent Methodist Chapel, where the service was duly car- tied out. The incident, which was more appreciated by the onlookers than the parties themselves, arose from the fact that in most districts Congregationalists are known as " In- dependents," though not "Independent Methodists."

ST. HELENS. IMPUDENT THEFT BY A LODGER.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, Samuel Cartlidge, a young man, .was charged with stealing a pair of boots, and a purse con- taining £2 ss, belonging to Joseph Parr,beerseller, Sutton- road, Sutton.—Prosecutor stated that prisoner and another man lodged with him. They both returned from work ab nit twenty minutes past one o'clock on the morning of the 21st Inst., and shortly after being admitted they left the house by the back, the prisoner having put on prosecutor's boots and stolen the purse containing the amount stated. Witness and Police-constable Carter gave chase, and the latter caught prisoner at Burtonwood.—Committed for one month with hard labour. PUBLIC-HOUSE Row AT PEASLEY-CROSS.—At the St'l Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Thomas Pilkington and A. Sinclair, Esqs., Patrick Cox, of Sutton, was sum- moned for assaulting Edward Holland and Mary .Holland on the 21st ult.—Mr. Swift appeared for the complainants and Mr. Thomas defended.—The evidence showed that Mr. And Mrs. Holland live at the Stanley Arms, Peasley-cross- Ilene, and on the date named the defendant and his brother entered the house and went into the " snug." Shortly afterwards a row inside that room took place, and it was found that the defendant and his brother had a man named Hunt down on the ground. Mr. and Mrs. Holland pulled them off, and Mrs. Holland got Hunt outside the back-door and be ran away. The defendant and his brother afterwards assaulted Mr. and Mrs. Holland, both of whom were kicked and struck several times.—For assaulting Edward Holland the defendant was fined 20s and costs, and for the assault on Mrs. Holland he was further fined 10a and costs.—John Cox, brother of the defendant, was then charged with as- saulting Mrs. Holland at the same time, and he was fined 12s 61 and costs. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICENCE : SINGULAR CASE, —A singular cAse affecting the keeping of dogs was he ird at the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday morning before Thomas Pilkington and A. Sinclair, Esqs. Win. Burrows, I of Sutton, was summoned for keepiog a dog without a licence, and the defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Heald, Superviser of Taxes, appeared to prosecute, and stated that on the 14th January last the defendant made a declaration to him that he kept a dog solely for use in tending sheep Or cattle on his farm ; and on that declaration he (Mr. Heald) I granted him an exemption paper, authorising him to keep the dog without a licence, whilst it was SO Ussd. At the foot of that certificate there was a note "that this certificate will become void, and must be exchanged for a licence, when the dog ceases to be used for the purpose stated." On the 25th April an officer of the Inland Revenue department visited the desendant's premises and saw a retriever dog chained up in the yard to a kennel. He asked the defend- I ant if he had a licence for it, and he said he had not, but he had an exemption paper. He admitted that he had not tried the dog with sheep or cattle adding that his previous dog had been lost or it had strayed away.—Daniel Murphy, Inland Revenue officer, then gave evichnce in support of Mr Heald's statement. —The defendant said he had the dog I simply chained up because it was not time for the cattle or sheep to be out in the fields, and he strongly asserted that he kept the dog only for attending to the sheep and cattle. —The Chairman said the Bench believed the defendant had got the dog for the purpose of tending to the ctttle and sheep. They did not think he had any intention of infring- ing the law, and they would therefore dismiss the sum- mons.—Mr. Heald gave notice of appeal against the decision. FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS: THE CORONER ON MEDICAL ATTENDANCE—On Tuesday forenoon Mr. Rrighouse, core- net, held an inquest at the Running Horses Hotel, St. Helens, on the body of John Smith, 60 years of age, 61, Liverpool-road, a labourer. Deceased, who was the worse for drink, went to bed about half-past nine o'clock on the morning of the 24th ult, and remained there until two o'clock. He then got up, and on reaching the second stair from the top, fell headlong to the bottom. Although there were two women downstairs and two men in bed upstairs, Smith received no attention until after four o'clock, when he was carried to bed and a doctor sent for. As the mes- senger had no money wherewith to pay him, the medical gentlemen refused to attend. The relieving officer was sought, and eventually a certificate for the parish doctor was obtained. It was half-past twelve next day before deceased received medical attendance, and he had remained unconscious since the accident. He died on Friday from concussion of the brain.—The Coroner said it did seem re- markable that in this civilised country there should be such cases of seeming neglect to attend an injured person. He could only say that perhaps the doctors kept within their strict legal rights in refusing to attend a lemon who had no money. There were both rich and poor in this country, and he (the coroner) thought there ought to be some asso- ciation or some establishment where persons could at once obtain medical aid whether they were rick or poor. He was not blaming anyone specially irs this • case, but it did seem hard that just because the man had no money there should be a delay in rendering assistance, although life was fast ebbing away. He thought with a • juryman, 'that if the police bad power to call in a doctor it might answer the case.—The jury returned a verdict of " Acciden- tal death," and cordially acquiesced in the remarks of the coroner. THE FAILURE OF A ST. HELENS SOLICITOR.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, before Mr Regis- trar Bellringer, Henry Lindon Riley, a debtor, who practised ass solicitor at St. Helens and Liverpool, came up on his adjourned public examination.—Mr Frodsham, who repre- sented the trustee, stated that as the debtor's books had not been written up nothing had been done since the Case was last before the court.—The -Debtor stated that the delay arose from his being dependent upon a late cashier of his to write up the books. . his cashier had gone into business for himself, and he could only give occasional attention to the writing up of the books.—The Registrar did not think that was a sufficient reason. He would adjourn the examina- tion to the 17th inst., and if the books were not completely written up by that time, and further delay was necessary, he would order the debtor to pay the costs of the adjournment. The Debtor: I hope you won't decide that matter now.— The Registrar: I am deciding it now because you ought to have made up your books before.—The Debtor: You have not endeavoured to ascertain if there is any blame attach- ing to me.—The Registrar: I will not allow you to address me in that manner, Mr Riley.—The Debtor: I have no soli- citor to represent me, so I must protest myself .—The Regis- trar: I make the order, and if there is no progress made at the end of that time you most take the consequences. These adiournments ought not to take place at the expense of the estate if the bankrupt has been in default. You are at pre- sent in default, and you must purge your contempt—The Debtor remarked that as a matter et fact there had been no order made for the books to be written out. —The Registrar said he understoed such an order had been made.—The Official Receiver (Mr Gittins) said as Mr Riley was a solci- tor, and knew very well what was required, he (Mr Gittins) had not thought it necessary to have a formal order put on the file.—The Debtor admitted that at his first examination he undertook to write out his accounts.—The Registrar Have you done that ?—The Debtor: I have done all that was possible in the meantime.—Then they must have been in a shocking etate.—The Debtor again explained that he had been dependent upon an old cashier to make up the books—The Registrar said that the debtor could not excuse himself by relying on someone else. He must do it himself.- The Debtor: I did not know it was an absolute personal ob- ligation, but after that statement I will undertake to attend myself at the trustee's office daily.—The examination was then adjourned to the 17th inst.
ANOTHER STABBING CASE.

A serious case of, the use of the knife was investigated be- fore the hlavor,of Warrington (Alderman Harrison) at the Borough Police Ceurt, on Monday morning,when a young man named John Brady was charged with unlawfully cut- ting and wounding Edward Worsley, another young man, in Battersby-lane, on Sunday morning.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Con- stable) said that complainant was a railway chair-maker, who worked'at the Chandos Foundry and resided at 1, Peer- street, Lythgoe's-lane. The prisoner Brady, lOyears of age, was a tanner and lived at 18, Back Crossley-street. It ap- peared that Edward Worsley, Joseph Worsley, and two other young men had been to Brown's Circus on Saturday evening. They left there at 10 o'clock, and called at the Fox public-house, which they left at 11 o'clock, going thence to a fried deb shop in Fennell-street. They remained there about half an hour, and then proceeded up Brick-street in the direction of Bittersby-lane. At the time Constable Evans was on duty at the end of Lytlagoe's-lane, and at about 12 o'clock be heard shouting and screaming, as though something was amiss in the direction of the railway bridge in Battersby-lane. Evans proceeded there, and on getting near to the bridge be saw the prisoner in company with a young woman. Prisoner said to the constable, "I have been cut; someone has been using a knife." Whilst the prisoner was speaking to the constable several young men were making their way towards them, and Edward Lawless said, "A young man has stabbed a young fellow, and he is with a young woman." Worsley then came up, and said that he had been stabbed by a young fellow who was with a young woman, and that he should know him again. Evans turned back hastily and overtook the prisoner and his young woman, and brought him back to the other parties, who identified him at once as the one who had used a knife. Prisoner was then brought to the police station and charged with unlawfully outting and wound- ing Edward Worsley, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, and his answer was " I have never done it; the knife's not mine." Whilst this was going on a young man named Jesse Smith went to the place where it was said that the scuffle took place, and found the knife pro- duced. The prisoner said that it was not his, and the police were not at present in a position to prove that it was 80. ' He had reason to believe that the witnesses would say that they were proceeding along Battersby-lane when they met Brady with a young woman, and Joseph Worsley looked at the two rather Closely. The prleoner on that struck right I and left at Joseph Worsley, and knocked him against the wall. The two then began to tight, and the complainant went to help his brother, vren he was struck with a knife. Through his bat there was a cut corresponding to a wound on his heal—Evidence was then called in support of this statement, aed Dr. Rithmond, of the Infirmary, stated that the wound was upon the left temple of the prosecutor's head, was about three•quarters of an inch in length, and extended obliquely to the bone.—ln defence prisoner denied having used a knife, and said that the prosecutor and his friends made an attack upon him. He called a girl named Glynn, , his sweetheart, who said that he did not use a knife.—Pri- soner was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions.

COBDEN CLos Dm:mt.—The Cobden Club held their annual dinner at the Ship Hotel, Greenwich, on Saturday, when nearly 200 gentlemen attended. Lord Carlingford, who presided, expressed the opinion that the recent legisla- tion on, cattle disease would exclude disease from this coun- try without disturbing the supply of healthy cattle. He replied to Lord Salisbury's advocacy of "Fair Trade," and urged that the club should continue to edudate in Free Trade principles the classes soon to be enfranchised, espe- cially as a Tory democracy was capable of doing much harm. Referring to foreign affairs, be said a commercial treaty with Mexico will probably be signed within the year, and the Government hope that Spain will consent to more Liberal relations with this country. He thought Mr Cob- den would have approved the efforts of the Government to make Egypt and the Canal a neutral territory under the pro- tection of the Powers.
