SIR GILEEIT GREENALL AND THE SHIP CANAL. Sir,—Tne following sentence appoars in your issue of Saturday last as a portion of the speech of Sir Gilbert at the recent Ship Canal meeting:—" With respect to himself, he might say he had not a particle of hostility to the ship canal. He had done nothing to oppose it, although it was put into his vitals rather unceremoniously. (Laughter.) But he forgave all that." What does the "odd old fellow" mean by this mysterious statement? I had the pleasure of seeing the hon. baronet only a few hours ago, and certainly he did not appear to have had anything so formidable as a ship einal "pot into his vitals." Perhaps it was after all "only pretty Fanny's way" of explaining that as the new canal bill will take a very large portion of "certain pro- Ap-rty," for which of course a good sum of money as com- pensation will have to be paid by the promoters, Sir Gilbert can now see his way to support a proposal which, if success - 4ul. is of momentous importance to Warrington, whereas year ago, when under the former bill a very small portion of his wooerty was scheduled, he refused either to sub- scribe a single penny towards the Guarat.tee Fund, or even to allow his name to appear as a supperter of the scheme. —Yours truly, LYNX.

" HECK LING." Sir,—An old philosopher once said "Ministers are but men, and the best of men are bat men at best." And I agree with him, and why? I have just been reading some correspondence between Mr. William Crosfield and the Rev. Mr. Carleton respqcting Disestablishment. whick has forced me to the above conclusion. I think the Tories, at the next election, may well appoint Mr. Carleton " Heckler-General " of their party. He seems to tke naturally to it, though, sooth to say, he makes a sad mess of it. If I had not seen the rev. gentleman's signature, I should have concluded that some fourth-form boy bad been, in his youthful indiscretion, addressing our future candidate by letter. Of course, one can feel for his anxiety, since it is "within measurable distance "that the State Church will have to go "the way of all nesh." But Mr. Carleton's red-hot haste has brought him trouble, and Mr. a.:rosfield has administered to him such a rep on the knuckles that I think will tend to keep him quiet for some little time; and if not, I can assure him that Mr. Crosfield has "more paint is his brush." I need say no more, for " . . who would rush at a benighted msn, And give him two black eyes fir being blind" Styx, July 7th, 1884. PLUTO. MR. JOSEPH HOWES V. MR. J. H. BOTTONILEY. bir,-1 have pleasure in asking you to publish the ac- companying letter from Mr. Howes. I again repeat the fact that my committee will be most happy to arrange for a public debate between Mr. Howes on the one band and Mr. Bottomlev (or any other better man the Conservatives care to bring forward, on the other hand) upon the question referred to.—Your obedient servant, H. ROBERTS, Liberal Agent. " Dear sir,—l have jest seen Mr. Bottoraley's letter. No one not acquainted with him could conceive it poesible for any man to be so dead to all sense of shame as to write such a letter, having atoll knowledge of the facts which pre- ceded it. .

I have all the correspondence on this Subject in my pos- session, and I shall now publish it, so that the public may see Mr. Bottornley in his true chatacter. The correspon- dence will prove the truth of my assertion, viz., that the delay at Barnard Castle was caused by Mr. Buttomley not consenting to defend Toryism. The challenge to debate the question Is the policy of the Beaconsfield or Gladstone Government most likely to strengthen our position at home or abroad.' I have never heard of until now; and cer- tainly it was not made before I sent you my last letter. Permit me to sly that I at once accept the challenge. There- fore if the Warrington Conservative Association will put Mr. Battonaley forward as their representative to debste this -question arrangements can be made at once. If I can only get the opportunity of comparing. the last Government with the present one, I huve no fear of the result. —Yours. J. HOWES.

SUNDAY CLOSING.

Sir,--I also as a-ra.-eh.se-t;r:anTi-W-itti-arong party politi- cal bias, wish to say a word respecting the important sub- ject of " Sunday closing" A "Social Reformer" threatens that unless the two candidates satisfy him as to the course they are lrk&v to take on this question possibly his vote will be withheld ; or at least given to the one he would term sound. Well, this is likely to be a knotty subj-ct, and it would beia pity for Liberals to oplit upon it. but 1 for one should distinctly refuse to vote for any candidate whose aim is to give Sunday a more lugubrious aspect than it at present wears. We are now spending some three millions of money in educating our youth. Can it be supposed for a moment that the result of this will be a continuance of the drineingetiebits " Social Reformer " has in mind? I' hope not. I should say rather that the public-house will take uo its original postion ; and use, net abase, will make them fit placei for even social reformers to meet in. The fact is the Sunday closing idea sterns to the unco gui,l a kind of whip With which they intend to flog working-men into their churches and chapels. Truer won't succeed in their wishes Having to keep their noses to the grindstone for six days, the people are determined Lo allow no sect or party to rob them of the seventh. If the cry at an election were by any chance to be that of "Sunday closing," I should vote for the men who would vote against it, even though he might be that dear old gentleman from Walton. But there is another way out of the difficulty. I believe in evolution, and thee the Religion of Humanity is gradually taking the ulace of Christianity ; end I suggest to " Social Reformer" that he allow his left-hended scheme for adding to the attendance at churches and chapels to rest in alyiyance, and open out other sources of attraction for the people. The present writer is well aware of the evils that attend drunkenuese. Nay, I may relate an incident that has lust re- cently come under my own notice, its illustrating how unfit some of the publicens era for the positions they hold. Stand- ing at my door the other Sunday evening, a poor man came -up, and asked for some bread. His wants being supplied, he held his hind open, and I saw he was Possessed of two- pence. "See," he seys to me, "1 went into that public- house," peieting to one ht the corner, "and asked for two- pennertii of bread and cheese, and they refused, saying they had no time to bother with me." Now we see this poor fellow c mild have bought ale, but something to set he must beg. A proper vete of things would tumble that: man out of his house. He, like a good many more public ins, evi- dently thinks the public exist for his benefit, and not he foe their convenience. Evolution will alter this, and with the ' view of aiding-it we mast have the Musenre and Library opened on a Sunday, and lame, bright reading-rooms estab- lished in such cenvenient situations that the poor shall not -be able to reeist the st-ring inducement held out by the fasci- nations of a well selected library. We want no more restric- tions on our liberty. We clamor all afferd to keep a half- gallon cask in the cellar, nor can we afford to keep up a system of entertainments ; but we insist upon keeping the right we now have, to meet our friends where we like. when we like, and to drink what we like. If our teetotal friends wish to bring the working-man more under the con- I trol of the police, it is to be hoped a watchful eye will be ' kent on their actions during the delirium of election time. I was very much amused with "Social Reformer'e " re- I ferences to Sir Gilbert, and I am afraid that should these , reformers wait -upon him just now he will promise them I anything. After allowing the Ship Canal to be put into I hie vitals rather unceremoniously," he will most assuredly I consent to the Sunday closing !easiness. One could see I plainly, net reedy from Sir Gilbert's speech at the Ship Canal meeting but from the numerous fresh faces that put in an appeereece on this question, that all the bitter pile "Social Refeemer" could manufacture would be greedily awalkswed by the Tories if only a few votes could be made -eafe. I have no doubt if the Warrington Freethinkers wait -upon them also, they will readily consent to givet Mr. Brad- laugh all the support in their power in return for the Free- thinkers' votes. I am afraid we moderators are going to have orr hands full with these intemperate Sunday cloaers, but they must be pegged back.—Youre ikce June liath, IBS4. CAPTAIN CUrrLE

At the outset of this movement, it was acknowledged'on all Aides that the smployer and his workman were the two oarties most directly to be benefited by the Ship Canal, ahouid it, in its conception and ultimate completion, turn oant to be an engineering triumph It was pointed out through the press and from the platform, tkat, unless some cheaper method could be devised whereby the raw material could be conveyed inland, and the manufactured article again be conveyed to our customers, not only the workmen but the manufacturers would most surely come to grief. Acing upon this information, the work- ing-men did all that lay in their power by en- couraging their representatives in Parliament and in the Town Council and also by meeting in their thousands and applauding the scheme. The brain and lungs were conjested and the vessels of the heart filled with blood, but all the other organs were healthy.—The jury returned a verdict of •• Found drowned." MARRIAGE AT EMMANUEL REFORMED CHURCIL-011 Thursday, the marriage of Mr. vlenry Gandy, Cairo-street, and Miss E. Allen, Bewsey-road, was celebrated in Em- manuel Reformed Church, Bold-street, the officiating minieter beigg the Rev. W. Mules. Both the bride and bridegroom having been teachers in the Sunday school con- nected with the church, the marriage had excited consider- able interest amongst the members of the congregation and their friends, and there was consequently a large gathering in the church. The bridesmaids were Miss Jane Allen and Miss Mary Gandy, the wide being given away by her father Mr. T. Allen, and Mr. John Gandy acting as best man. At the conclusion of the nuptial service, the Rev. W. Mules mentioned that that was, the first marriage celebrated in that new church, and he presented, OR behalf of the wardens and vestry, the bride and bridegroom with a teacher's Bible and a copy of the Prayer Beok. In making the presenta- tion, Mr. Mules added, they were not only following in the wake of a very popular custom, but they were also giving tokens of their esteem and regard. • He exhorted them to make God's Word the basis of their life, for just as there was no foundation for individual peace like the Word of God, so there was no foundation for domestic happiness like the Bible. On leaving the church the newly-united pair were greeted by a plentiful shower of rice from their well wishers. Before and after the service suitable music was rendered on the organ by Mies Brown. .. BANKRUPTCY EXAMINATION. The adjourned eximie nation of John Theophilus T. Taylor, brewers' traveller, of A'triucham, came before the Deputy Registrar, Mr. EL B. White, on Monday afternoon, when the bankrupt was further examined by Mr. Ridgway, the official receiver.—ln answer to questions, he said be was present at the last adjournment of the public examination, when he heard the court make an order that he should file the best statement of his accounts that he could for the last six years. He was on the Wed- nesday previous served with a copy of an order requiring him to file such accounts. He had done so to the best of his ability.—Have you tiled them for the last six years ? To the best of my knowledge.—.re these (statement* pro- duced) what you are refetring to? Far anything I know they are.—Mr. Ridgway, addreseing the Depuiy Registrar, said that what was filed by the bankrupt was simply a state- met or affairs. They were the accounts that were required ti be filed as a matter of course by every bankrupt—The Deputy Registray : There is nothing here showing the accounts for the last six years.—Mr. Ridgway said that they were the only accounts that the bankrupt could be got to produce. As far as he was concerned that was all the evidence that he proposed to take.—Phe Deputy Registrar : ' What application do you make on that 2—Mr. Ridgway : 1 he only course I can apply for is a further adjournment, with leave to apply for the commitment of the bankrupt.— The Deputy Registrar : When will you take the examina- tion P—Me Ridgway: I should think it will be the best way to take it sine die.—Tee examination was then adjourned, it being undeestood that the Official Roc Aver would apply for the committal of the bankrupt for contempt of court. TEMPERANCE MEETING.-00 Wednesday evening an ma air temperance meeting was held en the Fair Ground, Queen-street, Warrington. A wagon was appropriated as a platform, and this was occupied by Councillor. Dixon, who acted as chairman, Mr. Paton, of Glaseow, and Mr. Whit- worth, Liverpool, The Chairman, in a few preliminary re- marks, referred to the social misery caused by indulgence in intoxicating chinks, and as instances alluded to the recent tragedies in Bootle.—Mr. Whitworth, who next briefly ad- dressed the meeting, mentioned his experience of Liver- pool Police Court, where ha had been on the Monday of the previous week and found that with one single exception every case tried there that day was due to drunkenness.— Mr. Paton said he quite sympathised with the chairman as to the social aspect of the drink question. He was con- vinced that unless social and moral reform accompanied and supplemented political reform there would be no proaress. Social and moral reform began and ended in the home life of the people:. Show him a nation in which home life was corrupt; and he would show them a nation which, though politically free, was in a state of slavery and debasement. There was nonatjon politically more freethan our own, but the want of moral reform in the homes of our people was neutralising their political progress. And the political re- form woich did not bring about moral and social reform fell far short of the mark. Both political parties, he said; were alike with regard to the drink traffic, for they both tolerated it for the sake of the revenue it brought. He strongly advised his hearers that when the next election came they should lay aside party feeling and vote for those men who were in favour of repressing the drink traffic. Suocateua DEATIT TO A Ctuirae.—A shocking accident took place at Warrington on Wednesday when a little boy named William Royle, aged six years, was run over on Wilderspool•road. The boy was the son of William Royle, a blacksmith, 4, Taviesryard, Wilderspeol-road, and at about 5-25 on Wednesday evening, he was playing with some other children on the footway of Wilderspool Causeway, with a pet goat, when a carter named Patrick Hussey, em- ployed by John Whitlow, Broomfield Farm, Appleton, came past with a cart laden with potatoes, leading his horse. When passing by where the children were playing the de- ceased by same means or other fell backward in front of the near wheel, which went over his head, killing him in- stantly, his brains being scattered on the road.—an inquest relative to the sad affair was held at the Norton Arms Hotel, i before Mr. Yates, coroner, yesterday, when evidence to the following effect was adduced.—The mother of the deceased ' said that on Wednesday afternoon she left the child in the , care of a relative, as s'oe had to got work. In the evening, ' about 5-30, she received information that her boy was dead. —William Bradbury, a boy, living at Latchford, said that he was in charge of a goat belonging to his master, when the deceased began to tease it. • The goat knocked the de- ceased down and he fell under a passing; cart and was run over. Witness shouted, and the driver, who was leading i his horse, immediately stopped. The accident occurred on i the Wilderspool-road, near the Norton Arms.—Patrick Huseey, the carter, said that on Wednesday afternoon he was going to Bank Quay Station with a load of potatoes. On the Wilderymo!-road he PAW three boys and a goat on ; the parapet. Ile heard someone shouting and found that one of the wheels of the cart had goae over the head of a little boy. he did not see how the accident occurred, and hqd full ennr,l over Ida horse.—The jury returned a ver- dict of " Accidental death," completely exonerating anyone from blame. PRIZE DAY AT HAMILTON HOUSE SCROOL.—Yesterday week the pupils of Hamilton House hchool, Palmyra-square, assembled to receive the prizes awarded to them for 1883. Some of the scholars generally sit at Christmas for the Cambridge Local or the College of Preceptors' examina- tion', and as the results of these are not known for some three months afterwards, and as the preparatien of certifi- cates takes a few weeks longer, the prizes must either wait or the principal trophies must be dispensed with. Of these al ternati ves the Misses Bradbury chose the former. The pupils, who had a day's holiday in honour of the occasion, met in the afternoon and were entertained to tea by the lady principals, after which they adjourned to one of the large school-rooms, where they were soon joined by a few friends, who were present by invitation. The prizes consisted of a number of most beautiful books. The proceedings opened by a miscellaneous entertainment given by Miss S. Hamil- ton Bradbury and the scholars. After this had been very successfully gone through, Mr. Rippon made a few appro- priate remarks, expressing the pleasure he had in being eresent. He spoke very highly of tbe school and ienpressed upon the pupils the necessity of devoting all their energies to their work, pointing out that their present opportunity was not only the very best they would ever have, but that in many cases it would be almost the only opportunity, as after school days the claim upon their time would be so vastly increased. But more than all, he urged them to re- member that to be good was better than to be clever. He then distributed the prizes and certificates as follows :—Eng- list] prizes: 1. W M Smith; 2, BA Bennett; 3,8 A Collin; 4, A Collin; 5, ff Smith. Latin: M Lonsdale. French : W M Smith. Music: 1, W M Smith ; 2, E A Bennett; 3, N Fairclough. Conduct primes: J Eg,linton, S Colin, D imith. H Smith, Elsie Guest, H Kirkconnel, E Bennet, J Moss, C Fletcher, G Roberts. Certificates, College of Pre- ceptors :W M Smith, M Lonsdale. The takers of the cer- tificates of the Cullege of Precentors were Miss Winifred I VI Smith and Miss Mabel Lansdale, each of whom were ex- mined and passed in eght subjects (these being the highest 'amber permitted), viz., divinity, grammar, English history. e•eography, arithmetic, algebra, euclid,and French or Latin When this interesting ceremony was over refreshments were served and the visitors left. The pupils spent the evening inset enjoyably in playing charades and various games.

WOW('tO e 5 war," which always brings incalculable ruin and misery in its train not unfrequently, by what may perhaps be con- sidered as a rude inequitable methed of compensation, brings prosperity to trades and businesses previously stagnant. his proved to be the case with the business in which Major Cartwright was engaged. The Crimean war broke out soon after his partnership with Mr. Deacon had been dissolved, and there being a sudden demand for ale and porter bottles, of which he had a very large quantity on hand, he was enabled to dispose of them at a very handsome profit. After this his business affairs seem to have pros- ev,red. An incident may here be mentioned which honour- ably illustrates bis character. On finding that his business was becoming a remeneretive one he paid off all the debts which bad been contracted in his previous unsuccessful at- tempts, although he was entirely exempt as far as legal liability was concerned. Major Cartwright's public life in Warrington began on his election as a member of the Town Council. lie was also a member of the Board of Guardians, and in 1857-8 filled the office of Mayor in a most satisfactory manner. Later on in life he was appointed a borough magistrate; and for many years was a popular officer of volunteers, but retired some time ago on the brevet-rank of Major. Some years ago he retired from the Town Council, but he retained his seat on the Board of Guardians until the time of hie death. and it was in connection with this latter body that his pub- lic reputation was chiefly won. Ile was most regular in his attendance at the meetings of the Board and the various committees on which he served, and none are likely to lament his 108 S more than the infirm and helpless inmates of the Workhouse. In politics Major Cartwright was a staunch Liberal, and was always ready to help forward the ause of Liberalism and Progress. THE FUNERAL. On Wednesday afternoon the remains of the deceased aentlernan were interred in the Cemetery. Manchester-road. The funeral cortege which consisted of eleven carriages and the hearse, left the residence, Fir Grove, shortly after two o'clock and reached the cemetery at five minutes to three. Amongst these who were conveyed in the carriages were Mr T J Cartwright and Mr W Cartwright (sons of de- ceased). Mr Lowe, Mr A Jack, Mr Ashe ankelon, Che- shire), Mr Astle, the Revs S Wilkinson and J U Richards, Dr Spinks, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Pick- mere, Webster, and Davies; Cauncillors Greening, Brown, Mackie, Dixon, Bolton, W Piettoint, Sutton, Francomb, Taylor, Marsh, Ashton, Caldwell • Messrs T Jolley, S Sut- ton, Hunt (chief constable), Blackhorst, Fairclough, W Curry, T Longdin (borough surveyor), W Robinson, W Owen, E Bolton, W Fairhurst. The private carriaees of Mr McMinnies, MP. and Me Jos Davies were also present. At the cemetery the children from the Union Industrial school were drawn up, under the charge of Mr Mines, on both sides of the path leading to the church. There was also a considerable number of persons who had evidently come together to witness the obsequies of the deceased gentleman.. The funeral service was performed bv the Revds 0 W Quekett and RW P Montgomery. At the con- clusion of the service the hymn "When our heads are bowed with woe " was sung in an afftcting manner by the children of the Industrial School. The funeral arrange- ments were carried oat in a most efficient menner by Mr E Conner, Sankey-street. The coffin which was of polished oak with black panels and brass mountings, was surmounted by a brass plate which bore the simple inscription" Coaches Henry Cartwright, died June 30th, aged 63 years." MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, pn Monday morning, after the hearing of the cases had been partly pro- ceeded with, the Mayor, addressing the clerk to the m.gis- crates, said that he was sure he (the clerk) in common with every one else who vieited that court, would be sorry to hear of the death of Major Cartwright. They had just re- ceived an intimation of the death of that gentleman, and he took that opportunity of expressing his own sincere regret at ths death of 31,jer Cartwright, and particularly for the long and peieful illness he had endured. They all knew that Major Cartwright had been veey attentive to his duties there, and 'he had not the least doubt that he had done the very best he could to discharge the duties efficieatly and impartially. He thought that he should be borne out in that opinion by all the other magis- trates. Sometimes perhaps he might appear to be a little brusque in his manner and sometimes slightly irri- table, but when they considered the suffering that he had for so long a period to endure, that might have had a good deal to do with it He was salistlel that Major Cartwright tried to do the best that he could, and that he acted in every sense of the word as a man should do who wished to die- , charee his duties with integrity and impartialitv. He re- gretted exceedingly the death of Mtjor Cartwright, and he was sure that the sympathies of all of them would go with Mrs. Cartwright and her family in the loss that they had sustained —Mr. Bleckly sold that he would add one word to what the NliVin tied said. A man who had served the town as Major Cartwright had was entitled to be spoken of with respect. They all of them felt sympithy for his family and regret for a man who had to the best of his ability, as they b.lieved, done his duty to the town in which be lived, and who had worked his way in a steady and progressive manner, and although he might have had his troubles and difficulties, they would not detract from the respect that they had for a man who had acted uprightly.--LAlderman Davies said that, speaking for himself, perhaps none of the magistrates had been so near and dear triends as tied he and Major Cartwright. Outside persocel friendship, he might say that Major Cartwright had at all times acted efficiently as a public servant to Warrington, and bad fu'filled the duties that had fallen mem him with every energy. He was sure that tbe feeling of the Bench in this respect was unanimous and that it would be acceptable to the family of Major Cartwright, to hear that they had appreciated bins so much. —Mr. Fairclough seid that he quite agreed with what had been said. His sympathies were with Mrs. Cartwright and her family.—Alderrean Davies and Mr. Bleckly then left the Bench, and the business was proceeded with before the Mayor and Mr. Feirclough. Boy DTLOWN2D ITIII CANAL.—An inquelt was held at the "Saracen's Read," Wilderspool, og yesterday week, before Mr. T. J. Ridgway. on the body of a boy named Frank Briggs. aged four years, who was drowned in the ctnal on the previous day. It appearad from the evidence adduced, that the deceased was playing with a little girl named Annie 'Thompson, at the turn-bridge over the canal at Wilderspool, when he fell into the water. A young woman named Mtrtha Ads Fleming came up at the time, and was made acquainted with the circumstance by deceased's play- mate. Toey then proceeded to a field where some men were engaged mowing, and told them of the occurrence. One of them named George Cox, assisted by the others, got deceased out, but he did not recover from the effects of his immersion.—A verdict of "Accidentally drowned "was returned.

Robert Dale and Co.'s old factory, St. James-street, Latchford : I have inspected these premises, and find that no work of any kind is being carried on there; that the greater portion of the old factory is being taken down, and that no such stock is kept OR the premises as to constitute them warehouses. The present assessment is gross £ll9 10s, rateable £lOl. I am of opinion the additions would increase the value of the house by gross £2O, rateable £l7, which would give a total assessment of gross £139 10s, rateable £llB. Loudon and North-Western Railway Company— Sankey Canal. As I have no plans through which I could work out the area of the canal, I collected all the informa- tion I could from the overseers of the respective townships, and I also obtained measurement of the width. From this I arrived at a total area of 129 acres 1 rood 18 perches, and sent it on to Mr. Edmonds, who writes me to say that after checking the contents from his plans he makes it 107 acres 1 rood 38 perches, a difference of 211 acres. Not having any plan. I cannot be certain of my figures, for where the area in the old rate books exceeded my calculations of the width I adopted the larger figures, though I did not know how they were originally arrived at. lam powerless to disprove Mr. Edmonds's figures, and propose to accept them provided lain assured the area he gives is entirely free from lock-houses, gardens, and pastures, which can be separately rated.—This report was adopted. TRH LATE MAJOR CARTWRIGHT.—The Chairman said that before they concluded the business he should like to al- lude to the death of Major Cartwright. It was a matter which they all felt deeply. At the last meeting of the As- sessment Committee he mentioned to Mr. Cooper that Major Cartwright was looking very ill, and afterwards he could scarcely get him out of his mind; and soon afterwards he beard he was very ill. There had, eta the Chairman of the Rural Sanitary Authority said, been differences of opinion at those meetings and also at the Board of Guar- dians; he for one had never had any unkind feeling towards Major Cartwright alth•ugh there was a little bit of teeling on his part against him (the chairman.) It was not for him to reflect at all upon how those differences arose or who was wrong. All he could say was that he very much re- gretted the death of Major Cartwright, who was a zealous atfender at their meetings, and Re far as be could, worked for the benefit of the town. (Hear, bear.) He begged to propose that they express their condolence with the deceased gentleman's family. Mr. McCoruuodale seconded the resolution, which was carried.

MISSION SERVICES —On Sunday open air missions were held in connection with the Independent Methodist Chapel, Lynam, notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather. Services were also held in the Zion Chapel, ' leery-lane, where refreshments were provided for strangers. In the evening a love feast "was held, which was well mem:ed. Messrs. W. Hudson, J. Evans, of Warrington; J. Webster, of Leigh ; and W. Boote, of Liverpool, took part in the proceedings, Mr. Mayhall acting as leader.

WARRINGTON FIELD CLUB EXCURSION. —On Saturday fternoon the mom bers of this club journeyed to Lymm, where they were met by several members of the Lymm Botanical Society. The party had a pleasant walk along the meadows in the lower portions of the district, a consider- able number ot botanical specimens being collected. After tea the grounds set aside as a botanical garden were inspected and a stroll by the side of the lake brought the afternoon's outing to a close.

A BOY DROWNED AT STOCKTON HE Int.—Yesterday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the London Bridge Inn. Appleton, into the circumstances attending the death of a boy named Samuel Smith, who was dtowned in the canal at Stockton Heath, under the following circum- stances, as given in evidence—Sarah Smith, wife of John Smith, labourer, Strettec, and mother of the deceased; said that her son was 12 years old last December.. On the pre- vious morning she went to work leaving him in bed. She did not know that deceased had any business at Stockton Heath, and she had cautioned him about going there,— John Henry Arnold, a little boy, said that he was playing with the deceased near the canal, and the latter, whilst jumping on some timber, fell into the water.—Another bog named Arthur (Heave, corroborated.—Joseph Hamblett, Appieton, a warehouseman at Stockton Heath, in the employ of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, said that he saw the deceased playing on some timber on the canA side. He afterwards noticed a Mr Worthington and the two boys Arnold and Gleave go- ing on the water side and following them; he heard one say "Smith has jumped into the water." Witness got a boat hook and recovered the body in a few minutes. The de- ceased was quite dead.—Verdict of "Accidentally drowned." div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF
WARRINGTON.

The Editor of The Warrington Examiner.—Sir,—As a portion of a correspondence which has passed between the Rev. Mr. Carleton and myself has been published, I shall feel much obliged if you will be good enough to print the c3mplete series of six lettere—and also note the fact that the word "nefarious," agginst which I protest in mine of June 18, has been suppressed in copy of Mr. Carleton's let- ter of June 17th, which he has supplied to the press.

As the question which be has put to me is one of great Importance, I shall take the earliest opportunity of answer- ing it in such a way that there can be no misunderstanding on the part of the electors as to my views.—l remain, yours truly, W. CILOSFIELD. _ Holy Trinity Vicarage, June 10th, DM.

Dear Sir,—As you have been selected to contest the repre- sentation of Warrington at the next election, your political views, I need not say, have become a matter ot interest to every electer in the borough. You will, therefore, pardon the ! inquiry I am about to make, and which, I think, is rendered necessary by an important omission in the address you de- livered to your friends on the occasion of their selecting von as their candidate. In the address you omitted any refer- ence to ecelesiastical questions, beyond intimating your in- tention to support the claims of Mr. Bradlaugh. It would, therefore, put an eed to all doubt if you wonld kindly sty how you are disposed to view any measure which has for its object the disenlowroent of the Church of England. As a clergyman, claiming to speak on behalf of many of my fel- low Churchmen, I may say that your views on this matter would materially affect the attitude of a large number of your constituents at the next election. Your views, I need ant remind you, are of public importance. I should there- fore esteem it a favour it you could furnish me with the in- formation I desire, and which I might communicate to otners.--I am, sir, yours oleediently, William Croslield, Esq. E. C. E. CAIILETON. 6 Stanley-greet Liverpool, W, June 13th, 1884.

. . My Dear Sir,—l have only just returned from Loudon, and must therefore ask you to excuse delay in replying to yours of the 10th. The address which I delivered on the Slst ult. was necessarily brief, and WAS not intended to deal with the whole range of politics; but I hope to have many other opportunities of stating my views fully to the electors of Warrington, and will certainly not overlook the impor- tant question to which you draw my attention. From the form in which you pat your question (seeming to grant ' ths•establishment) I hope that we may find that there is substantial agreement between us,—l remain, yours truly, W. CROSFIELD. Holy Trinity Vicarage Warrington, June 17kb, 1831.

Dear Sir,—l an mach obliged by yoUr letter of the 13th lost, though I can hardly say it is any answer to my in- quiry. I should not have thought that the question I asked was one which von need have had any hesitation in answer log, or even have needed to defer to sonte public meeting to be held in the fears. Pardon me if I ask whether you would have the earns hesitation in saying whether or no you are.a Member of the Lib.ration Society and a subscriber to its funds? You will excuse me, I hope, it I sav t think you were rather rash in conclading from the form in which I put my question that I was prepared to grant " Diseetab- lishment." I spoke only of " Disendowment," for the simple reason that with many Nonconformists, disestablish- ment simply means disendowment. and nothing else. Apart from that, they have no clear conception of its meaning. Many of them are under the impression (and they are in- debted to the Liberation Society for the error) that the church was established in this country by.some Act or Acts of Parliament. Now, I need hardly tell you that this is not so, otherwise the work of the Liberation Society Would be easy; for it would simply be necessary to quote these par- ticular Acts and propose their repeal. But you know vers, well that this is not what they propose to do; they rather propose to single out the Church of Eng- land from all other religious bodies of the country, and subj.mt it to exceptional legislation, among other matters condscating its endowments, while those of the Noncon- formists are to remain untouched. And this they seek to do in the name of religious equality. I need hardly tell you that anyone who is prepared to countenance a proceeding of this nefarious character will have no support from Church men. The Church was not established in the way the Liberation Society would have men believe—it wea not established in entire 'distinction to other religious bodias. The Christian rulers of ancient times in this land simply gave effect to their religious convictions. They recognised Chrietianity as the religion of the people. Of course the only form in which Christianity was presented to the people at that time was a Church form. It may seem to you a grievance that Congregationalism was not established, but remember Congregationalism did not exist. It was the Church or nothing, and like Christian men they gave their voice for the'Church. Crgregationalism, whichis chiefly the creed of the Liberationists, is a tVng of modern growth, and baying no ancient inheritance of its own, it desires to take somebody else's. There is one word which describes how this proposal is regarded by all honest men, and if I for- bear to utter it, it is not that I hesitate abont calling t hingi by their right names, but that I think good to exer- cise my discretion as to the occasion.---Apologising for troublin, you with this letter, I'remain. yours faithfully, E. C. E. Cantacrota. Wm. Crosfield, Esq. 6 Stanley•street, Liverpool, W., June 18, 1884. My de tr dir,—l hive yours of yesterday continuing the subject of your letter of the 10th, in which you asked my Opinion on the Disendowrnent of the Church of Englabd "claiming to speak on behalf of many fellow • Church- men "with a view to guiding them how to vote. As I de- sire to be judged by what I think, rather than what someone supposes that I mean to say, you will not think it unrea- sonable that I should prefer to express my views on a public occasion rather than in a private correspondence. Your secohd letter shows that with the best intentions there is a liability to misapprehension and therefore to mis- representation. You take upon yourself to say that "knew very well " that the Liberation Society " proposes" to do certain things, which I. though a member of that society, never heard of them proposing; whilst you apply the word "nefarious " to the assumed acts of those with whom I have the honour of being associated. Pardon rll9 if I say that I cannot carry on a discussion which is liable to degenerate into the use of such epithets, and again ask you to suspend your judgment on this subject.—l remain, yours, W. CROSFIRLD. _ _ _

Killarney, Ireland, June 25th, 1884. ack-ow- Dear sir,—Absence from home has prevented me ledging the receipt of your last letter, and also from sayiag that! intend sending the correspondence respecting your views on the disendownment of the Church to the Wan.i ng • ton Guardian, without remark. The following week I hope to express my views thereon in a letter to the editor.—l re- main, yours faithfully, W. Crosfield, Esq. E C. E. CARLETON. Devonshire Club, London, June 27th, 1884. Dear sir,—l have yours written from Killarney informing me of your intention to publish the letters which have passed between us. I cannot, of course, dictate to you the time or the method which von should select for explaining , your Ti3W3 on disendownment to your friends, but as far as they affect me, I must still ask the public to wait till I have expressed my opinions before jumping at anv conclusion with regard to them. I write under the disadvantage of raelifseerntcoe; f rbonmt Ih do en ri r, ea to point, herer,fuotr therefore, hear rvner wnonti nonurl !Int ei into your first communication. If I may ask you to take the trouble to re-read what I said with regard to he improper action a the House of Commons, you will find that I vindi- cated the rights of constituencies to the free admission of those whom thav,have elected by a constitutional vote to represent them, and that I said nothing about anybody's claim to sit in his individual capacity in the people's House of Parliament. Please include this in the series of letters when published.—l remain, your. truly, W, CROSFIELD.
Nev. E. C. H. Carleton.

A dissolu- 4A, DEANE-STREET, LIVERPOOfe Near the Central Station. tion would then be inevitable and we should probably be in the thick of an election' con- test at the beginning of nest year. And what a contest it would be! The issue would not simply be the Reform Bill, but the Re- form Bill and the reform of the House of Lords. The struggle would probably be the most momentous and far-reaching that has been witnessed in the present generation— perhaps since the revolution of 1688. It would be a god-send to the cause of the people, and, taking all things into account, it is the best thing that could happen. No one I who, like the poet, "dips into the future far as human eye can see," can fail to ob- serve that the House of Lords is destined toe, be revolutionised. An hereditary and irre- sponsible body of legislators is an anomaly which is becoming every day more and more glaring_; but Englishmen are slow to move in a matter of this kind, and need the impetus to exertion in providing a remedy which is to be found only in such monstrous obstruction I as would be afforded by a second rejection of the Franchise Bill. Anything short of this would most likely end in a good deal of grumbling, but in very little being actually done in the way of putting the Peers in their places. There is nothing like striking whilst the iron is hot;. but the House of Lords requires to be brought to a white heat in the furnace of public opinion, and then there will be some hope of its being re-fashioned according to the will of the people. It has to be done, and the sooner it is done and the better—to say nothing of the advantage of killing two birds with one stone. Judging from the past career of Lord SALISBURY, there are many who .will be disposed to con- clude that he will yield at the last moment; but he has capitulated so often that he will be driven, on this or some other occasion, to "fight it out," if only to save the remnant of a shattered reputation. There is reason to believe, too, that in this matter he will be • well supported by the Conservative Peers. According tO 'the terms of his motion, the House will affirm its readiness to concur in any well considered and csmplete scheme for the extension of the franchise, and will, found its refusal to accept the present measure upon the absence of provisions securing true and fair representation of the people,' or of adequate security that the bill shall not come into operation except as part of an entire scheme. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ANTIQUARIAN SOCIETY,— On Saturday about 50 members of this society, accompanied by a few ladies, visited Lancaster. The natty arrived shortly before noon, and were met at the station by several members of the local committee, of which Mr. W. 0. Roper was hon. secretary. The party East visited the castle, and, they ascended the Norman keep, or "John 0 Gannt'a chair,'" whence a splendid view of the Lake Mountains was obtained. The ancient parish church of St. Mary's was next visited, end its details described by Mr. Paley, F.E.1.8..1 The pattY lunched at the County Hall, and afterwards took train for Morecambe, driving from thenco.in wagonettee to Heyshatn, where the rector, the Rev. C. T. Royds, showed them over the ancient Norman church at that place, and the various antiquities in the adjoining churchyard. /a visit was also paid to the hill close at hand, in which stand the remains of an ancient oratory, coffins hewn in the solid. rock, etc., and from whence a panoramic view of the mountains of West- morland and Cumberland was .had. The return to Lancas- ter was made all the way by wagonette, and was reached shortly before half-past six. At the Arniaable Library tea, was provided by the President, Mr. W. G. Welch. Several old charters of the town, the municipal regalia, a cosy old armour, and a few Roman antiquities fonnd in tile neigh' bourhood were here displayed. Before leaving the Amicable' a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the local aommittee' for its sacCessful arrangements. LATEST NEWS. There is no foundation whatever for the report which has been current of the Pope's illness. - Intelligence received at Leeds states that Mr. Joshua Hirst, of that town, has been 'murdered near Willow City, Texas. Two railway surfacemen were knocked down and killed by a shunting engine at the general station at Perth, yes- terday. • During a thunderstorm at Northampton the lightning struck several dwelling-houses, demolished the turret of a shoe factory, and injured a girl. On inquiry yesterday morning at the Bishop's Palace, a Chester correspondent was informed that Dr. Jacol4son still lies in the same critical condition, Hannah Taylor, the wife of an agricultural labourer, at Tervin, near Chester, has given birth to three children, two sons and a daughter. All are doing well. A shoal of whales was seen off Stornoway, Orkney, yes- terday, and a large number of boats set out in pursuit. After an exciting chase the whole shoal, numbering forty, was captured. ILLNESS OF Mn. Groensmern.—The Central News learns that Mr. Gladstone is suffering from a slight attack of lum- bago, but expects to be in his place in Parliament if not to- night, certainly on Monday. The Press Association says that there is now no chance of the Fortescue-Garmoyle action being tried until the November sittings. It is regarded as exceedingly impro- bable that the matter will be arranged. A LIVERPOOL MYSTERY.—The mystery surrounding the discovery of a female skeleton in an unoccupied house in Liverpool has been partially cleared up. The remains have been recognised by clothing, as those of a seamstress, who has been missing for twelve months. THE BURNLY STRIKE.—Two settlements on the basis of the Blackburn standard list were made at 13urnley.on Fri- day morning, and there are now about nine firms where the weavers continue to work on those terms. The number of workers now on strike is about 14,000. THE CONFERINCE.—A meeting of the financial experts attaehed to the Conference was held at the Foreign Offices yesterday afternoon at two o'clock. 'There were present M. de Beligniers, Her Von Dehrenthal, Baron Velsira, Sir E. Baring, Blum Pasha, and Tegrane Pasha. Mr. Childers was also present for a portion of the time. MAN KILLED AT CHORLEY. On Friday morning a shocking fatality occurred at the Lancashire and Yorkshire Goods Yard at Chorley. Henry Smith, a labourer, was engaged with others unloading a timber waggon, when a number of three-inch planks fell upon him, and he was I shockingly injured about the head, and his right leg and arm were broken. He died in a few minutes. The second day of the Henley Regatta passed of most suc- cessfully. Reeults t—Thames challenge cup, London first, Twickenham second. Visitors' challenge cup, Christ Church first, Oxford second. Public Schools challenge cup, Derby school first, Hereford Grammar school second, Magdalen College third. Wyford challenge cup, Thames first. Mar- low second, London third. Stewards' challenge cup, Hamp- ton first, Twickenham second. Diamond challenge sculls, Unwin first, Smith second, Farrell third. Ladies challenge plate, Eton first, Radley second. Thames challenge cup, Twickenham first, Thames second. Silver goblet, Twicken- ham first, London second, Hampton third. THE CHOLERA OUTBREAK IN FRANCE. MARSEILLES, FRIDAY—Since last night no deaths from cholera have occurred here, but at Toulon since yesterday there have been twelve. In order to relieve the poverty- stricken portion of the Toul-on population, deprived of their means of living by the panic, lotteries are being pro- jected. ARRIVAL OF ROYAL ENGINEERS AT SOUAKIM. SOUAKIM, FRIDAY, 11 A.M —Admiral Lord John Hay has left here in Her Majesty's despatch vessel, Helicon. Her Majesty's troop and storeship Humber is now leaving, have lag landed the Royal Engineers, who are encamped near the site of the projected deep sea pier. The chartered steamer Loch Ard is discharging the railway plant and material. The construction of the pier will be commenced immediately, being shortly followed by the laying of the railway. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—FRIDAY. The House met at four o'clock. THE FRANCHISE BILL.—Earl LIMERICK gave notice for Monday that he would ask for an undertaking from the Government not to force a general election on the Franchise Bill without first passing the Rulistribution of Seats Bill. Earl CAIRNS presented petitions in favour of extending the franchise to women. D• CEASED WIFE'S SISTER BILL—Lord Houghton in- troduced the Marriage with Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, which was read a first time. BILLS ADVANCED. Indian Marine Bill, Post Office Pro- tection Bill, and other orders of the day were dieposed of and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. THE RUMOURED FALL OF DEBBAH.—Lord FITZMAURICE, replying to Mr. Ashrnead-Bartlett, said the Goverment had received no confirmation of the rumoured capture of Debbah ; and of the mansacre there they had no information to the effect that pilgrims who gave in- formation of the safety of Berber on the 7th of Juno were evoisaaries of the Mandi. THE COURSE OF BUSINESS.—Sir W. HARCOURT intimated that the Prime Minister was slightly indisposed. Ques- tions addressed to him would he answered on Monday. Re- plying to Sir S. Northcote, he said that at the moment he could not give the desired information as regarded the London Government Bill. It was certainly the in- tention of the Government to press the bill with a view to its paesing this session. Mr. TRH. VELYAN said the greater part of next week was to be given to Supply. aud IrishVanday Closing and Purchase of Land Bills, which Were regarded as bills of the first im- portance.—Mr H. FOWLER thought the attempt to pass the London Government Bill would re-sett in wasting the re- maining time of the preseut session.—Mr CHAMI3ERLAIN said that excessive talking and votes of censors had wasted the time of the session. The Government were not to blame; they had done their best to forward public business. —A long discussion ensued, and Mr. RAIKES moved adjourn- ment to debate. For the adjournment, 136; against, 189. Further discussion ensued, after which, on the motion of the LORD MAYOR, the debate was then adjourned.—The sitting was then suspended. The House resumed at P. Mr. BURT called attention to the subject of accidents in mines, and pointed out the large number of accidents that oc- curred in iron, coal, and stone mines every yesr He moved "That considering the great development of the mining industries of Great Britain in recent years, the number and exbent of the mines, their increasing depth and the large number of persons employed therein, the House was a opinion that the time had come when there should be an addition to the staff of inspectors of mines."—Mr. JAMES seconded the motion.—Sir W. IlannotneT admitted the im- portance of the subject, but eaid that the inspection was useless unless the men themselves accepted and enforced the directions of the inspectors, which was not the case. However, he thought a case had been made out for an in- crease of inspectors —Sir H. Vivian, Mr. Harris, Mr. Caine. Mr. Broadhurst, and Sir J. Pease expressed pleasure at the 'Horne Secretary accepting the motion.—After a short dis- cussion Mr. BURT asked leave to withdraw his motion.— The motion was negatived. 'The House was counted, and forty members were not pre- sent. The House adjourned at ten minutes to eleven.

The Barton Rural Sanitary Authority have ordered the school to be closed for a period of five weeks, in consequence of the prevalence of scarlet fever in the dis- trict. 4 VIOLENT CONDUCT: INCORRIGIBLE FEMALES.—Vester- day, at the Wartington Borough Court, before _Captain Reynolds (in the chair) and Mr. John White, two females named Margaret Fleming and Bridget Higgins, well known to the police, made their appearance under the following circumstances. Fleming was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on the previous evening, with assaulting Police-constables Monoghan and Corcoran and two persons who came to their assistance, Higgins being charged with resisting the police whilst they were taking Fleming into custody. Both pi-Loners were charged on summonses with being drunk and disorderly on a prior ;oc- casion, and Higgins was charged with usira, obscene lan- guage.—Mr. Hunt (cleief constable) slid that he dil not know what was to be done with these young women. They gave the magistrates and the police a deal Of Veuble, and, in fact, were incorrigible.—The Chair- man : I understood Higgins was going to leave the town.— Higgins: I have been two months in gaol since then ; policeman should have put me beck and not let me come SO far as Warrington.—Evidence was then given that the prisoners behaved most violently when being taken into custody.—Biggins said that she had not been in the town an hour when she came out of prison before when she was again locked up, and she only came out again on Fri- day.—Higgins was fined 203 or a month for being drunk and disorderly. 40.3 or 14 days for using obscene language, and was committed to prison for a month for assaulting the police. Fleming was fined 203 or 14 days for being drunk and disorderly, and was committed for two months for the assault.
